lessons.title: The Rise of Generative AI
lessons.goal: Explain what ChatGPT is, why it spread so fast, and which shift and ingredients made general-purpose generative AI possible.

cards.title: Decoding the Name ChatGPT
cards.text: In November 2022 OpenAI opened ChatGPT to the public, and the name itself is a compact recipe. 'Chat' is the way you use it: a conversation in plain language. 'Generative' says it creates new, fluent text rather than just labelling what you give it. 'Pretrained' means it absorbed broad knowledge about language and the world from enormous text collections before anyone ever chatted with it. 'Transformer' names the neural network architecture doing the work underneath. Every one of these four words becomes a full topic later in this course.
points: Chat = conversational interface in natural language
Generative = produces new fluent text, not just labels
Pretrained = learned broad linguistic and factual knowledge before deployment
Transformer = the underlying neural network architecture
Public launch by OpenAI: November 2022
cards.example: ChatGPT = Chat + Generative + Pretrained + Transformer
cards.say: The name ChatGPT is a little recipe. Chat is how you talk to it. Generative means it writes new text. Pretrained means it learned from huge amounts of text first. And Transformer is the network architecture underneath.
covers: A1: What the name ChatGPT means

cards.title: Why ChatGPT Took Off
cards.text: ChatGPT reached roughly 100 million users in about two months, faster than any app before it. Why? You needed no technical skill: you simply typed. A free tier removed the price barrier. Within a session it remembered what you said, so it felt coherent, almost like a personality. Its answers were grammatical, stylistically consistent and useful across coding, writing, explaining and translating, and people shared the best ones virally. Timing helped too: after the pandemic everyone was used to digital tools, cloud infrastructure was mature, and APIs, plugins and Copilot quickly pushed it into real products.
points: About 100 million users in roughly two months (fastest-growing app at the time)
Zero expertise needed and a free tier
Session memory created an impression of coherence and personality
Strong across many domains; viral sharing on social media
Good timing: post-pandemic digital habits, mature cloud
APIs, plugins and Copilot integrations multiplied real-world impact
cards.example: Growth benchmark reported in February 2023: 100 million users about two months after launch.
cards.say: ChatGPT hit around one hundred million users in about two months. It was free, needed no skills, remembered the conversation, worked across many topics, and arrived exactly when people and cloud platforms were ready for it.

cards.title: One Model, Many Tasks
cards.text: Classic machine learning built a separate specialist for every job: one network classifies images, another translates, a third transcribes audio, a fourth detects sentiment. Each needs its own data, training run and maintenance. Generative AI turns this around. A single foundation model accepts text, images, audio or code and can write, summarise, translate, generate programs, answer questions, analyse pictures and even drive tools and agents. The guiding slogan changes from 'one task, one model' to 'one model, many tasks', and that change is why building AI products now looks so different.
points: Traditional ML: one specialised model per task
Examples: image to class, text to translation, audio to transcript, text to sentiment
Generative AI: one foundation model serves many tasks
Inputs: text, images, audio, code and more
Outputs: writing, summaries, translations, code, answers, image analysis, tool use
cards.example: Four specialists (image classifier, translator, speech recogniser, sentiment model) are replaced by one foundation model.
cards.say: Before generative AI, every task had its own model: one for images, one for translation, one for speech. Now a single foundation model handles all of these and more. One model, many tasks.
covers: B1: From task-specific models to general-purpose AI

cards.title: Why Now? Four Ingredients
cards.text: Generative AI did not appear by magic; four ingredients matured together. Architecture: the Transformer, whose self-attention trains in parallel extremely well. Data: web-scale text, code, documents and multimodal material. Compute: GPU accelerators wired into large clusters for distributed training. Training: large-scale pretraining, better recipes, and post-training alignment that makes models helpful. Then everything was scaled at once, with bigger models, more data and more compute. The result is a general-purpose model that can understand, generate, reason and use tools across text, images, audio and code.
points: Architecture: Transformer with parallel self-attention
Data: web-scale text, code, documents, multimodal content
Compute: GPU clusters and distributed training
Training: pretraining, improved recipes, post-training alignment
Scaling all of them together yields general-purpose capability
cards.say: Why now? Four things came together: the Transformer architecture, web-scale data, huge GPU clusters, and better training including alignment. Scaling all four at the same time produced general-purpose models.
covers: B1: Why now? Drivers of generative AI

cards.title: The AI Race
cards.text: ChatGPT's success triggered a scramble. Big tech companies and a wave of startups hurried to train their own foundation models and launch competing assistants, until the landscape became a crowded wall of logos. This race is a double-edged sword. Competition drives capabilities forward at remarkable speed and gives users many models to choose from, but it also creates pressure to ship products before they are fully tested or understood. For an AI engineer, it means the model you build on today may be outdated next quarter.
points: Many companies compete to build foundation models and assistants
Competition accelerates release cycles and capability gains
Downside: pressure to release before products are mature
Practical consequence: model choices change quickly
cards.say: After ChatGPT, tech giants and startups rushed to release their own models. The race pushes progress fast, but it also tempts companies to ship before products are truly ready.

cards.title: AI in the Headlines
cards.text: Generative AI now shapes society, not just software. Headlines show the range: tech companies looking at nuclear power to feed AI's energy appetite (Meta, 2025), AI tools misused to spread racist abuse online (2025), a lawsuit linking a companion chatbot to a teenager's suicide (Character.AI, 2024), and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton warning of mass unemployment and inequality (2025). Energy, misuse, user safety and jobs are real engineering concerns. They motivate the legal and ethical topics later in the course and remind us that every design decision has consequences beyond code.
points: Energy: AI demand drives interest in nuclear power (Meta, 2025)
Misuse: generative tools used for abuse and disinformation (2025)
Safety: chatbot harm to vulnerable users (Character.AI lawsuit, 2024)
Jobs: warnings of unemployment and inequality (Hinton, 2025)
Leads to the course's legal and ethical topics
cards.example: Sorting headlines into four risk areas: energy, misuse, safety, jobs.
cards.say: The news shows AI's wider impact: huge energy demand, misuse for abuse, chatbots harming vulnerable users, and warnings about job losses. These risks are part of an AI engineer's responsibility.
covers: A1: Societal impact of AI in the news

lessons.title: Predicting the Next Word
lessons.goal: Understand next-token prediction, how language models assign probabilities to text, how they learn from raw text, and why this simple task leads to powerful behaviour.

cards.title: Guess What Comes Next
cards.text: Every language model, from tiny to gigantic, solves one core puzzle: given the text so far, how likely is each possible continuation? The model reads a sequence and outputs a probability for every entry in its vocabulary, and these probabilities sum to one. Modern models work on tokens, the units they read and write as single elements; a token can be a whole word or a piece of one, often with its leading space attached. The simplest way to choose is greedy: take the highest-probability token, the argmax.
points: Input: the sequence so far; output: a probability for every vocabulary entry
All probabilities add up to 1
A token is a word or word piece, often including the leading space
Greedy choice = argmax, the most likely token
Next-token prediction is the fundamental training task of language models
cards.formula: next token = argmax over x of P(x | x_1, ..., x_t), where x_1..x_t are the tokens so far and x is a candidate next token
cards.example: 'The cat sits on the' -> ' mat' 0.70, ' sofa' 0.15, ' chair' 0.10, ' car' 0.05. Greedy argmax selects ' mat'.
cards.say: A language model looks at the text so far and gives every possible next token a probability. For the cat sits on the, mat gets seventy percent. Picking the most likely one is called greedy selection.
covers: B1: Next-token prediction and autoregressive generation

cards.title: The Autoregressive Loop
cards.text: One prediction gives you one token. To write a whole answer, the model runs a loop: predict a distribution, pick a token, append it to the input, and predict again with the slightly longer sequence. This is autoregressive generation, because each output becomes part of the next input. Instead of always taking the argmax, the system may also sample from the distribution, which adds variety. Remarkably, essays, code and conversations all come from repeating this single simple step thousands of times. Nothing else is generating the text.
points: Predict -> select -> append -> repeat
Each chosen token becomes part of the next input
Selection can be greedy (argmax) or sampled
All complex output emerges from repeating one step
cards.formula: x_{t+1} ~ P(x | x_1, ..., x_t): the next token x_{t+1} is drawn from (or the argmax of) the model's distribution given tokens x_1..x_t
cards.example: 'The cat sits on the' + ' mat' -> new input 'The cat sits on the mat' -> predict the following token, e.g. '.'
cards.say: To write more than one token, the model loops. It predicts, picks a token, adds it to the text, and predicts again. Every long answer you have seen was built this way, one token at a time.
covers: B1: Next-token prediction and autoregressive generation

cards.title: Language Models and the Chain Rule
cards.text: A language model, statistical or neural, assigns a probability to an entire word sequence. That sounds hard, but the chain rule of probability breaks it into simple steps: the probability of a sentence equals the probability of the first word, times the second given the first, times the third given the first two, and so on. So predicting the next word is all you need to score whole sentences. Classic language models were usually built for one task or domain, powering text generation, spelling correction and autocomplete, machine translation and speech recognition.
points: An LM estimates the probability of a whole sequence
The chain rule turns it into a product of next-word probabilities
Classic LMs were typically single-task or single-domain
Uses: text generation, spelling correction, autocomplete, translation, speech recognition
cards.formula: P(w_1, ..., w_n) = product for i = 1..n of P(w_i | w_1, ..., w_{i-1}); n = sequence length, w_i = i-th word
cards.example: P('the cat sat') = P('the') x P('cat' | 'the') x P('sat' | 'the cat')
cards.say: A language model gives a probability to a whole sentence. Thanks to the chain rule, that probability is just the product of next word probabilities, one word after another. Classic models used this for autocomplete, translation and speech recognition.

cards.title: Ice Cream or I Scream?
cards.text: Speech recognition shows a language model working as a judge rather than a writer. The acoustic model hears the sound and proposes several transcriptions that match it equally well. For the audio 'ai skreem', both 'I eat ice cream' and 'I eat I scream' fit perfectly. The language model then scores each candidate as a sentence, and the first is far more plausible, so it wins. Here the LM is not autocompleting anything; it re-ranks hypotheses so the final output makes linguistic sense, resolving homophones through context.
points: The acoustic model proposes several candidate transcriptions
The LM re-ranks them by sentence probability
Homophones are resolved using surrounding context
Role here: plausibility check, not autocomplete
Covered in depth in a separate spoken language processing course
cards.example: Audio /ai skri:m/: 'I eat ice cream' gets a high LM probability and is kept; 'I eat I scream' scores low and is discarded.
cards.say: In speech recognition, ice cream and I scream sound identical. The acoustic model offers both, and the language model picks I eat ice cream because that sentence is far more likely.
covers: A1: LMs in automatic speech recognition

cards.title: Learning Without Labels
cards.text: Where do the correct answers come from when training a language model? From the text itself. Slide a window over any sentence: the words inside are the input, and the very next word is the target. Every document on the web becomes millions of free training examples, with no human annotation required. This is self-supervised learning, and it is why training can scale to gigantic datasets. During training, a model definition plus text data produce learned parameters; during inference, those parameters take a word sequence and predict what follows.
points: Training data is raw text; the next word is the label
No manual annotation, so data can scale enormously
Training: model definition + text -> learned parameters
Inference: word sequence + learned parameters -> predicted next word
cards.example: From 'The cat sat on the mat': input 'The' -> target 'cat'; input 'The cat' -> target 'sat'; input 'The cat sat' -> target 'on', and so on.
cards.say: Language models do not need human labels. The next word in the text is the answer. So any text becomes training data, which is why these models can learn from the whole web.

cards.title: The Bigram Model
cards.text: The simplest learned language model looks back just one word. A bigram model counts how often each word pair appears in the training text, divides by how often the first word appears, and stores the result in a table. Prediction is then a table lookup. Train on 'The cat sat on the mat' and 'the' is followed once by 'cat' and once by 'mat', so each gets 0.5. The catch: n-gram tables grow as the vocabulary size to the power n. With 50,000 words, even a bigram table needs 2.5 billion entries.
points: Bigram: probability of the next word given only the previous word
Step 1: count pairs in text; step 2: predict by lookup
n-gram models are probability tables
Table size grows as V to the power n
V = 50,000 already gives 2.5 billion bigram parameters
cards.formula: P(w_i | w_{i-1}) = count(w_{i-1}, w_i) / count(w_{i-1}); number of bigram parameters = V^2, V = vocabulary size
cards.example: Training text 'The cat sat on the mat': the->cat 0.5, the->mat 0.5, cat->sat 1.0, sat->on 1.0, on->the 1.0. With V = 50,000: 50,000^2 = 2.5 x 10^9 entries.
cards.say: A bigram model just counts word pairs. In the cat sat on the mat, the word the is followed by cat half the time and mat half the time. But with fifty thousand words, the table needs two and a half billion entries.

cards.title: Why Simple Prediction Gets So Powerful
cards.text: Next-token prediction explains how text comes out, not why modern models are so capable. Three ingredients answer the why. Architecture: attention and Transformers let every position draw information from the entire context, unlike a bigram's single-word view. Training and alignment: large-scale pretraining soaks up statistical structure from huge datasets, and post-training shapes the model into helpful behaviour. Inference and context: prompts, supplied context, decoding settings and extra test-time computation decide which learned abilities actually appear. To understand a model's behaviour, look at all three together.
points: Next-token prediction is the mechanism, not the explanation
Architecture: attention combines information across the whole context
Training: pretraining learns structure; post-training shapes behaviour
Inference: prompts, context, decoding and test-time compute elicit abilities
cards.say: Predicting the next token is only the mechanism. The real power comes from three things: the Transformer architecture, massive training plus alignment, and smart use of prompts, context and decoding at inference time.
covers: B1: What turns next-token prediction into powerful behaviour

lessons.title: LLMs & Foundation Models
lessons.goal: Distinguish large language models, foundation models, products like ChatGPT and complete AI systems, and explain how scale produces emergent abilities across modalities.

cards.title: What Makes an LLM Large
cards.text: A large language model is still a language model: its training objective remains predicting the next token in context. What changes is scale, by many orders of magnitude, along three axes. Data grows to web-scale text, code and dialogue. Parameters grow into the billions and are used more efficiently. Compute grows to clusters of GPUs running for weeks. None of this would be practical without the Transformer, which trains in parallel and captures long-range context far better than older designs. The architecture itself is the subject of Chapter 3.
points: LLM = a language model scaled by orders of magnitude
Objective unchanged: next-token prediction
Scale axis 1: data (web text, code, dialogue)
Scale axis 2: parameters, used efficiently
Scale axis 3: compute (GPUs, clusters)
Enabled by the Transformer's parallel training and long-range context
cards.say: A large language model is the same next token predictor, just scaled up enormously in three ways: more data, more parameters, and more compute. The Transformer architecture is what made that scaling practical.
covers: A1: What makes an LLM large

cards.title: Emergent Abilities
cards.text: Here is the surprise: a model trained only to predict the next token ends up doing things nobody explicitly taught it. The same network completes sentences, translates words, solves small logic puzzles, writes working code and chats politely about books. These skills are called emergent abilities, because they appear once models become large enough, as a by-product of the simple prediction objective. To predict text well across the whole internet, the model must implicitly learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and programming conventions. One model, one objective, many tasks.
points: One model and one objective yield many tasks
Abilities appear at scale without task-specific training
Examples: completion, translation, reasoning, code, conversation
Good prediction requires implicitly learning grammar, facts and logic
cards.example: 'The cat sits on the' -> 'mat'; 'What is frog in Spanish?' -> 'rana'; John is taller than Mary, Mary taller than Alex -> Alex is shortest; Python: def square(x): return x * x; 'What's your favorite book?' -> 'I don't read, but many people love The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.'
cards.say: Trained only to predict the next token, large models can still translate frog into Spanish, solve height puzzles, write Python functions and hold a conversation. These are called emergent abilities.
covers: A1: Emergent abilities from next-word prediction

cards.title: Foundation Models
cards.text: What should we call models with such broad abilities? 'Pretrained' only names a training stage, 'self-supervised' only names a learning method, and 'general-purpose' hides that the model is unfinished. In 2021 Bommasani and colleagues proposed 'foundation model': a model trained on broad, large-scale data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks through prompting or fine-tuning. The metaphor fits. A building's foundation is not a house, but everything rests on it: a solid one makes every application reliable, while a flawed one makes them all fail together.
points: Trained on broad, large-scale data (text, images, audio...)
Adapted to downstream tasks via prompting or fine-tuning
Unfinished on its own; needs adaptation
Shared base for countless applications: strong base = reliability, weak base = systemic failure
Rejected names: pretrained, self-supervised, general-purpose model
Term from Bommasani et al., 2021
cards.say: A foundation model is trained on broad data and then adapted to many tasks by prompting or fine-tuning. Like a building's foundation, everything rests on it, so its strengths and its flaws spread to every application.
covers: B1: Foundation models, LLMs and AI systems

cards.title: Model vs LLM vs AI System
cards.text: Three terms are easy to mix up. A foundation model is the general concept: broad pretraining, then adaptation. A large language model is one kind of foundation model, specialised for text: it models and generates sequences of tokens and is trained on huge text corpora, often including code. An AI system is what users actually touch. It wraps one or more models with context (prompts, memory, retrieval), data (internal and external), tools (APIs, code execution), application logic (orchestration, agents) and an interface (chat or API) to solve a real task.
points: Foundation model: broad data, adaptable to many tasks
LLM: the text-and-token specialisation of a foundation model
AI system = model(s) + context + data + tools + logic + UI
Context: prompts, memory, RAG; tools: APIs, code execution
Logic: orchestration and agents; UI: chat or API
cards.formula: AI system = model(s) + context + data + tools + application logic + user interface
cards.say: Think of nested layers. An LLM is a text foundation model. An AI system wraps models with context, data, tools, application logic and an interface, so it can solve a real task for real users.
covers: B1: Foundation models, LLMs and AI systems

cards.title: ChatGPT = Model + Alignment + Interface
cards.text: Is ChatGPT a foundation model? No, it is a product built on top of one. Start with a pretrained foundation model. Align it with instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback so it follows what users actually want instead of merely continuing text. Then add an interface layer: the chat system, memory, safety filters and user experience. Swapping the foundation model underneath upgrades the product, which is exactly what happened over the years, from GPT-3.5 at the November 2022 launch to GPT-4 in March 2023 and GPT-5 in 2025.
points: ChatGPT uses a foundation model but is not one itself
Alignment: instruction tuning + RLHF to follow human intent
Interface: chat, memory, safety filters, UX
The underlying model is upgraded over time
cards.formula: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface
cards.example: ChatGPT (Nov 2022) ran on GPT-3.5; ChatGPT 4 (Mar 2023) on GPT-4; ChatGPT 5 (2025) on GPT-5.
cards.say: ChatGPT is not itself a foundation model. It is a foundation model, aligned with instruction tuning and human feedback, wrapped in a chat interface with memory and safety filters. The model inside has been upgraded several times.
covers: A1: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface

cards.title: Foundation Models Beyond Text
cards.text: The foundation-model recipe works for any data type. Vision models such as CLIP learn from image-text pairs, using objectives like image-text matching, masked patch prediction or diffusion denoising, and can recognise images zero-shot or generate them from text. Audio models such as Whisper learn from raw and transcribed speech and handle recognition, speaker identification and translation. Video models such as Sora learn to predict missing or future frames aligned with captions, enabling captioning and text-to-video. Multimodal models such as Gemini learn joint representations, enabling visual question answering, grounding and multimodal reasoning.
points: Image (CLIP): image-text pairs; zero-shot recognition, text-to-image
Audio (Whisper): speech + transcripts; ASR, speaker ID, translation, audio generation
Video (Sora): video + captions; frame prediction, action recognition, text-to-video
Multimodal (CLIP, Gemini): joint embeddings; VQA, grounding, reasoning, tool use
LLMs are the text-based member of this family
cards.example: Training objectives: contrastive image-text matching (CLIP), sequence-to-sequence transcription (Whisper), future-frame prediction (Sora), joint embeddings across image, text, audio and video (Gemini).
cards.say: Foundation models are not just about text. CLIP learns from images and captions, Whisper from speech, Sora from video, and multimodal models like Gemini combine them all to answer questions about pictures.

lessons.title: What Is AI Engineering?
lessons.goal: Define AI engineering, describe the layered stack of an AI system, map capabilities to applications, and explain what separates a demo from a reliable production system.

cards.title: Defining AI Engineering
cards.text: AI engineering is the discipline of building reliable, useful and maintainable systems around AI models, with foundation models as the core component. Classic machine-learning engineering often trained a fresh model for each task; AI engineering usually starts from an existing pretrained model and builds around it. That model brings general abilities, but it becomes a real application only when combined with data and context, tools such as APIs and code, application logic like orchestration and agents, evaluation of quality and safety, and infrastructure for deployment and scaling. The work runs as a cycle: design, build, evaluate, operate.
points: Goal: reliable, useful, maintainable systems around AI models
Foundation models are the core component, usually not trained from scratch
Add: data and context, tools, application logic, evaluation, infrastructure
Lifecycle: Design -> Build -> Evaluate -> Operate
Contrast: classic ML engineering trains a model per task
cards.say: AI engineering means building reliable, useful and maintainable applications around foundation models. You add data, tools, logic, evaluation and infrastructure, and you keep cycling through design, build, evaluate and operate.

cards.title: The AI Engineering Stack
cards.text: Picture an AI system as a six-layer cake. On top sits the application: the user's task, domain logic, experience and requirements. Below it, orchestration and agents control workflows and tools. Next, context and knowledge supply prompts, retrieved documents and memory. In the middle is the model itself, whether a foundation, language or multimodal model. Under that, model access and adaptation covers APIs, fine-tuning and local models. At the bottom, infrastructure handles inference, deployment, scaling and efficiency. Cutting vertically through every layer: evaluation, safety and monitoring, via testing, red teaming, guardrails and feedback loops.
points: Application/User: task, domain logic, UX, requirements
Orchestration and Agents: workflows, tools, control logic
Context and Knowledge: prompts, RAG, documents, memory
Model: foundation, language and multimodal models
Model Access and Adaptation: APIs, fine-tuning, local models; Infrastructure: inference, deployment, scaling
Cross-cutting: evaluation, safety, monitoring (testing, red teaming, guardrails, feedback)
cards.example: 6 stacked layers plus 1 cross-cutting column for evaluation, safety and monitoring.
cards.say: An AI system is a stack of six layers: application, orchestration, context, model, model access, and infrastructure. Evaluation, safety and monitoring run straight through all of them.

cards.title: What Can You Build?
cards.text: A handful of core capabilities, namely vision, language, audio, code, tool use and reasoning, combine into a surprisingly long list of application domains. Software engineering uses them to generate, debug, test and refactor code. Data analytics queries, analyses, visualises and reports. Research assistants search, summarise, compare and synthesise. Science and engineering discover, model, simulate and optimise. Add content and media, enterprise workflows that extract and automate, agents that plan and execute, education that tutors and gives feedback, and robotics that perceives, plans and acts. Few building blocks, many products.
points: 6 core capabilities: vision, language, audio, code, tool use, reasoning
Software engineering, data and analytics, knowledge and research
Science and engineering, content and media, enterprise workflows
Agents and assistants, education, physical AI and robotics
Combining a few capabilities yields many applications
cards.example: 6 core capabilities -> 9 application domains, e.g. education = explain, tutor, practise, give feedback; robotics = perceive, plan, control, act.
cards.say: Six core capabilities, vision, language, audio, code, tool use and reasoning, combine into nine big application areas, from coding assistants and research tools to education and robotics.
covers: B1: What can you build with AI?

cards.title: Three Application Archetypes
cards.text: Most products follow one of three patterns. A knowledge assistant answers from your own documents: it retrieves relevant passages, writes an answer grounded in them, and cites its sources, for instance listing the termination conditions in a contract. A coding assistant turns a request into working software through a loop of generate, test, inspect and refine, say parsing log files and adding unit tests. An autonomous agent completes multi-step tasks with tools, memory and planning: search train connections, compare them, decide, and add the best one to your itinerary.
points: Knowledge assistant: retrieve -> generate grounded answer -> cite
Coding assistant: generate -> test -> inspect -> refine
Autonomous agent: search -> compare -> decide -> act
Ingredients: documents and retrieval; codebase and execution; APIs, planning, memory and state
cards.example: 'What are the termination conditions in this contract?' (knowledge); 'Implement a function to parse log files and add unit tests' (coding); 'Find a suitable train connection and add the best option to my itinerary' (agent).
cards.say: Three common patterns: a knowledge assistant that retrieves, answers and cites; a coding assistant that writes, tests and refines code; and an agent that searches, compares, decides and acts with tools.
covers: B1: From capabilities to applications: three archetypes

cards.title: Demo vs Production System
cards.text: A demo asks: can the model do this? One impressive answer, found by tweaking prompts and checking by eye, is enough. A production system asks: can the system do this reliably, safely and efficiently, for every user, every day? That demands consistent behaviour across many cases, deliberate prompt and context design, continuous evaluation, grounded and up-to-date information from data, APIs and tools, and graceful handling of failures and uncertainty. It also forces trade-offs: quality alone is no longer the goal, because latency, cost and safety matter just as much.
points: Single impressive answer vs reliable behaviour across many cases
Prompt trial and error vs systematic prompt and context design
Manual inspection vs continuous evaluation
Model memory vs grounded, current data via APIs and tools
Ignoring failures vs handling failures and uncertainty
Quality only vs quality plus latency, cost and safety
cards.example: 7 paired contrasts, e.g. demo = simple text interface, system = data, APIs and tools.
cards.say: A demo only asks whether the model can do something once. A real system must do it reliably, safely and efficiently, with evaluation, grounded data, failure handling, and a balance of quality, speed and cost.
covers: B1: AI demo vs AI system

cards.title: What Can Go Wrong
cards.text: Ask a system: summarise our latest customer contract and tell me whether we can terminate it next month. The request flows through data sources, retrieval, context building, the model, optional tools, and finally the answer, and every stage can break. Documents may be outdated. Retrieval may miss the key clause or return noise. The model may confidently invent a clause that does not exist. Repeated runs may disagree. A tool may be called wrongly. Everything may be slow and costly. Across all stages loom data leaks, prompt injection and the hard problem of automatically verifying correctness.
points: Knowledge: wrong or outdated documents
Context: missed or irrelevant retrieval results
Factuality: plausible but invented content (hallucination)
Reliability: inconsistent answers across runs; Tool use: wrong API calls or actions
Efficiency: latency, compute, cost
Security and evaluation: data exposure, prompt injection, no automatic correctness check
cards.example: Pipeline: Data Sources -> Retrieval -> Context -> Model -> Tools (optional) -> Answer, for the request about terminating a customer contract next month.
cards.say: Every stage of an AI pipeline can fail: outdated documents, missed retrieval, invented facts, inconsistent answers, wrong tool calls, high cost, and security risks like prompt injection. Spotting these is core AI engineering work.
covers: B1: What can go wrong in an AI system

lessons.title: Hands-On: Models on Your Machine
lessons.goal: See generative models in action, run an open-weight LLM locally with Ollama, estimate whether a model fits your hardware, and know the frameworks used to chain models into applications.

cards.title: Code Generation and Vibe Coding
cards.text: Programming is one of the most visible uses of LLMs. They complete and write code, hunt bugs, explain unfamiliar functions, translate legacy programs into modern languages, and act as data-science helpers that write SQL queries and plotting code. In February 2025 Andrej Karpathy gave a name to an extreme version of this: vibe coding. You describe what you want in natural language, accept what the AI produces, and barely read the code yourself. It is fast for prototypes, but it shows exactly why the reliability and evaluation concerns of AI engineering matter.
points: Code completion: writing, debugging, explaining
Code translation: modernising legacy languages
Data-science assistants: SQL queries, visualisations
Vibe coding: building software by natural-language instructions with little code review (Karpathy, Feb 2025)
cards.example: Request: 'Write a function that returns the square of x' -> def square(x): return x * x
cards.say: LLMs write, debug, explain and translate code, and even produce SQL queries. Vibe coding, a term from early 2025, means building software by just describing it to an AI and accepting the result.
covers: A1: Code generation and vibe coding

cards.title: From Prompt to Picture to Video
cards.text: Foundation models also create visual media. In the course demo, the text-to-image model DALL-E 3 received a short prompt asking for a university lecture called AI Engineering with students attending, and produced a matching picture. That image then became the starting point for Sora, a video model, which animated it into a 10-second clip of the teacher explaining the words AI and Engineering. Chaining models like this, text to image to video, is a small taste of building pipelines. Both outputs were clearly labelled as AI-generated, a good transparency habit.
points: Text-to-image: DALL-E 3
Image plus text to video: Sora
A generated image can seed a video
Outputs were labelled as AI-generated
cards.example: Image prompt: 'Create a picture. University. Students. Lecture called AI Engineering is ongoing.' (DALL-E 3) -> image -> 10-second Sora clip of the teacher explaining 'AI' and 'Engineering'.
cards.say: A short prompt to DALL E three produced a picture of an AI Engineering lecture. Sora then turned that picture into a ten second video of the teacher explaining the course name.

cards.title: Open Weights Are Not Open Source
cards.text: Many strong models can be downloaded and run on your own computer because their providers publish the trained parameters, the weights, under a specific license. These are open-weight models. Be careful with terminology: open-weight is not the same as open source. The training code, the training data and the full development process may still be secret, so you can use and often adapt the model without being able to reproduce it. The license also matters, since it defines what you are allowed to do with the weights, for example commercial use.
points: Open-weight = trained parameters published under a license
Not open source: code, data and process may remain closed
You can run and adapt the model, but not necessarily reproduce it
The license defines permitted uses
cards.example: Meta's Llama 3.1 8B is an open-weight model: anyone can download its weights, but its full training data is not published.
cards.say: Open weight models publish their trained parameters under a license, so you can download and run them. But that is not open source, because the training code and data can still be private.
covers: B1: Running an open-weight model locally with Ollama
A1: Running LLMs locally with Ollama

cards.title: Running an LLM with Ollama
cards.text: Ollama makes local models almost trivial. Under the hood it relies on llama.cpp, an open-source library for efficient LLM inference on ordinary computers. Ollama adds model management: it downloads open-weight text models once, stores the parameters locally, and lets you chat through a command line, a graphical app, or a local HTTP server that other programs can call. Typing one command starts an 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model, roughly a 4.9 GB download. It then runs on your own CPU or GPU, provided the model fits into your RAM or VRAM.
points: llama.cpp: open-source local inference library
Ollama: built on llama.cpp, adds downloading and model management
Access via CLI, GUI or local HTTP server
Weights are downloaded once and stored locally
Runs on local CPU/GPU if it fits in RAM/VRAM
cards.example: $ ollama run llama3.1:8b (about 4.9 GB). Prompt: 'Explain next-token prediction in one sentence.' -> 'A language model predicts a probability distribution over the next token given the preceding tokens.'
cards.say: Ollama, built on the llama dot c p p library, downloads open weight models and lets you chat with them from a terminal, an app or a local web server. One command runs an eight billion parameter Llama model.
covers: B1: Running an open-weight model locally with Ollama
A1: Running LLMs locally with Ollama

cards.title: Will It Fit? Precision and Memory
cards.text: Before downloading a model, do a quick calculation: weight memory is roughly the number of parameters times the bits per parameter, divided by eight to get bytes. An 8-billion-parameter model needs about 16 GB at 16-bit precision, 8 GB at 8-bit and only 4 GB at 4-bit quantisation. If weights plus overhead fit in GPU memory, inference runs mostly on the GPU and is fast. If not, parts spill over to system RAM and the CPU, which is usually much slower. Remember the extras too: KV cache, runtime buffers and other overhead.
points: Weight memory = parameters x bits per weight / 8
Halving the bits roughly halves the memory
Fits in VRAM -> fast GPU inference
Exceeds VRAM -> offloading to RAM/CPU, usually slower
Total = weights + KV cache + runtime buffers + overhead
cards.formula: Weight memory in bytes = N x b / 8, where N = number of parameters and b = bits per weight
cards.example: 8e9 x 16 / 8 = 16e9 bytes = about 16 GB; at 8 bit about 8 GB; at 4 bit about 4 GB.
cards.say: To check if a model fits, multiply parameters by bits per weight and divide by eight. An eight billion parameter model needs about sixteen gigabytes at sixteen bit, but only four at four bit.
covers: B1: How large a model can you run? Precision and memory

cards.title: Challenge: Find Your Best Model
cards.text: Now experiment like an engineer. First, check how much VRAM and RAM your machine has. Second, try several models of different sizes and quantisation levels. Third, measure memory use and generation speed in tokens per second. Fourth, give every model the same prompts and compare answer quality. You will quickly discover that the biggest model is rarely the best choice: a slightly smaller or more aggressively quantised model may answer almost as well while running far faster. Choosing a model is always a trade-off between quality, memory and speed.
points: Step 1: check VRAM and RAM
Step 2: try different sizes and quantisations
Step 3: measure VRAM, RAM and tokens per second
Step 4: compare quality on identical prompts
The largest model is not automatically the best for your system
cards.example: Metrics to record per model: VRAM usage, RAM usage, tokens/s, answer quality on the same prompts.
cards.say: Your challenge: check your memory, try models of different sizes and precisions, measure speed in tokens per second, and compare answers. You will find that bigger is not always better.
covers: B1: Challenge: find a model that fits your hardware

cards.title: LangChain and LangFlow
cards.text: Once a model runs, you want to build something with it. LangChain is a Python and JavaScript framework that turns LLM applications into composable building blocks: prompt templates, chains that sequence model calls and logic, agents that decide which tools to use, memory for conversation context, and retrievers with vector stores for retrieval-augmented generation. LangFlow is its visual twin: you drag blocks such as an LLM, a prompt, a tool or an agent onto a canvas and connect them, no coding required. It runs locally or in the browser and can export the equivalent Python code.
points: LangChain: Python/JS framework for LLM applications
Blocks: prompt templates, chains, agents, memory, retrievers and vector stores
Goal: programmable, composable LLM pipelines
LangFlow: drag-and-drop GUI for LangChain workflows
Works with models like GPT-4, Claude or Llama; exports Python code
cards.example: A flow in LangFlow: Prompt block -> LLM block -> Retriever block -> Output, exported as a Python script.
cards.say: LangChain gives you building blocks like prompt templates, chains, agents, memory and retrievers to build LLM apps in code. LangFlow lets you connect the same blocks visually, then export the Python.

lessons.title: Course Map & Research
lessons.goal: Get an overview of the course roadmap, the practical lab, and the institute's research on efficient LLMs.

cards.title: The Course Roadmap
cards.text: This chapter moved from the ChatGPT moment through next-token prediction and foundation models to AI systems and running models yourself. The rest of the course follows three parts. Understand the Models: from text to tokens and back, the foundations of LLMs, training and alignment, then inference, reasoning and evaluation. Build with Models: prompt engineering, agents, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning. Engineer AI Systems: LLM systems engineering. The earlier run used eight chapters, grouping the model internals into one block and adding agents, fine-tuning, legal and ethical aspects, and building applications.
points: Part 1, Understand the Models: tokens, LLM foundations, training and alignment, inference and evaluation
Part 2, Build with Models: prompt engineering, agents, RAG, fine-tuning
Part 3, Engineer AI Systems: LLM systems engineering
Newer run: 10 chapters in 3 parts; earlier run: 8 chapters incl. legal and ethical aspects
Chapter 1 path: generative AI -> next-token prediction -> LLMs and FMs -> AI systems -> hands-on
cards.example: Earlier outline: 1 Introduction, 2 Foundation Models, 3 Prompt Engineering, 4 RAG, 5 Agents, 6 Finetuning, 7 Legal and Ethical Aspects, 8 Building Applications with Foundation Models.
cards.say: The course has three parts. First you understand the models: tokens, Transformers, training and evaluation. Then you build with them using prompts, agents, retrieval and fine-tuning. Finally you engineer complete AI systems.
covers: A1: Course title and Chapter 1 agenda
B1: Course title and Chapter 1 agenda

cards.title: Lecture and Computer Lab
cards.text: The lecture takes place weekly on Mondays and ends with an oral or written exam. To be admitted you must pass the AI Engineering computer lab, and you should know the material of a pattern recognition course. The main textbook is AI Engineering by Chip Huyen. The lab runs as Jupyter notebooks in Python on a Jupyter Hub, with an optional warm-up unit on Python and PyTorch and four units on foundation models, LLM workflows and agents, RAG, and LoRA fine-tuning with quantisation. Each graded unit needs at least 50 percent of the points, with a pre-test and a final submission.
points: Weekly Monday lecture; oral or written exam
Admission: passed computer lab; pattern recognition knowledge expected
Textbook: Chip Huyen, AI Engineering (O'Reilly)
Lab: Jupyter notebooks on a Jupyter Hub; Unit 0 Python/PyTorch is optional
Units: foundation models, LLM workflows and agents, RAG (e.g. with ChromaDB), LoRA and quantisation
At least 50% of points per graded unit; fetch, submit, get feedback, resubmit
cards.example: WS2026/27 lab: Unit 1 foundation models 24.11.26 / 07.12.26 / 21.12.26 (release / pre-test / end); Unit 4 LoRA and quantisation 09.02.27 / 22.02.27 / 08.03.27.
cards.say: To take the exam you need to pass the computer lab. It runs in Jupyter notebooks, covering foundation models, agents, retrieval and fine-tuning, and each graded unit needs at least half of the points.
covers: A1: Lecture information and computer lab (admin)
B1: Lecture information and computer lab (admin)

cards.title: Research: Efficient LLMs
cards.text: The institute behind this course researches how to make large language models cheaper to run and adapt. Topics include quantisation, which stores weights with fewer bits, adapter-based fine-tuning, reasoning, and even optical neuromorphic hardware. A highlight is BOF4, a 4-bit block-wise optimal float format that improves block-wise LLM quantisation, published at ICLR 2026. This connects directly to the memory calculation from the hands-on lesson: better 4-bit formats let bigger models fit into less memory with less quality loss. Master's thesis topics in these areas are available.
points: Focus: efficient inference and fine-tuning
Quantisation, e.g. BOF4 (4-bit Block-Wise Optimal Float), ICLR 2026
Adapter-based methods and reasoning
Optical neuromorphic hardware
Master's thesis topics available
cards.example: An 8B model at 4 bits needs about 4 GB of weight memory; formats like BOF4 aim to keep quality high at that size.
cards.say: The institute researches efficient language models: four bit quantisation formats like BOF4, adapters for fine tuning, reasoning, and optical hardware. If this sparks your interest, thesis topics are available.
covers: B1: LLM research at the IfN (admin)

chapters.title: From Text to Tokens and Back

lessons.title: The Text-to-Text Pipeline
lessons.goal: Trace how a sentence travels through an LLM system, from raw text to token IDs, vectors, scores and back to text, one token at a time.

cards.title: An LLM Never Reads Text
cards.text: When you type a question into a chatbot, the neural network at its core never sees letters at all. It sits in the middle of a pipeline with six stations. Text is cut into tokens, each token becomes an integer ID, every ID is swapped for a vector, the model turns those vectors into a score for every possible next token, one token is chosen, and that choice is converted back into readable text. Feed in 'The capital of France is' and, if everything works, 'Paris' comes out the other end.
points: Text -> tokens -> embeddings -> LLM -> logits -> next token -> text
The network itself only ever handles numbers
Each station changes the form of the data, not its content
Only the middle station (the LLM) has most of the learned weights
The same pipeline runs for every single generated token
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' -> IDs [313, 7, 895, 3666, 25] (illustrative) -> vectors -> scores -> ' Paris'
cards.say: Here is the big picture. A language model never reads letters. Your sentence travels through six stations: it becomes tokens, then numbers, then vectors, then scores, then one chosen token, and finally readable text again.

cards.title: Way In: Tokens and Vectors
cards.text: The first half of the pipeline prepares text for the network. A tokenizer splits the string into pieces from a fixed vocabulary and replaces each piece with its integer ID. Those integers are just catalogue numbers, so a second step, the embedding lookup, uses each ID to fetch a learned vector from a big table. After these two steps the sentence has become a sequence of continuous vectors, one per token, which is exactly the kind of input a neural network can multiply, add and transform.
points: Tokenization: text -> integer token IDs
IDs are indices, not meanings
Embedding lookup: each ID selects one learned vector
Output of the input side: one vector per token
Lessons 2.2 and 2.3 zoom into these two stations
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' becomes 5 token IDs, which become 5 vectors of the same length (the model width).
cards.say: On the way in, two things happen. A tokenizer turns your text into a list of integer IDs, and an embedding table swaps every ID for a learned vector. Now the network has numbers it can actually compute with.

cards.title: Way Out: Scores to a Word
cards.text: The model's forward pass transforms the vectors and, at the last position, produces a list of raw scores called logits, one for every token in the vocabulary. The model does not write a word itself. A separate selection step reads the scores and picks one token ID, for example the highest-scoring one or a random draw weighted by probability. Finally, detokenization looks up what that ID stands for and turns it back into characters. Splitting scoring from choosing is what later lets us tune creativity without retraining.
points: Forward pass: vectors -> one logit per vocabulary token
Logits are scores, not yet a decision
Token selection picks one ID (greedy or sampling)
Detokenization maps the ID back to text
Selection rules are covered in Chapter 5
cards.example: For 'The capital of France is', ' Paris' should receive the top score among all vocabulary entries and be selected.
cards.say: On the way out, the model produces one score for every word piece it knows. A separate selection step picks one of them, and detokenization turns that choice back into readable text.

cards.title: One Token at a Time
cards.text: A single pass through the pipeline yields just one new token. To write a full answer, the system runs in a loop: the freshly chosen token is appended to the input, and the whole sequence goes through the model again to choose the next one. Every prediction is therefore conditioned on everything written so far, including the model's own earlier outputs. This style of generation is called autoregressive. The loop ends when the model emits an end-of-sequence token or a length limit set by the application is reached.
points: One forward pass = one new token
The new token is appended and fed back in
Each step conditions on all previous tokens
Stops at an end-of-sequence token or a configured limit
Lesson 2.4 looks at the loop in detail
cards.formula: p(x_1, ..., x_T) = product over t of p(x_t | x_1, ..., x_{t-1}): the probability of a whole text is the chain of next-token probabilities.
cards.example: 'The' -> 'cat' -> 'sat' -> 'on' -> 'the' -> 'mat' -> end-of-sequence
cards.say: One trip through the pipeline gives just one token. So the system loops: it appends the new token, runs again, and repeats until it produces an end marker or hits a length limit. That is autoregressive generation.

lessons.title: Tokenization
lessons.goal: Explain how and why text is split into subword tokens with (byte-level) BPE, and what token counts mean for cost, context and model design.

cards.title: Why Text Must Become Tokens
cards.text: Neural networks crunch numbers, yet human language is messy: words can be ambiguous like 'bank', forms vary, and the supply of new strings never ends, from fresh names and typos to hashtags, emoji, code and dozens of writing systems. Tokenization brings order. It cuts text into discrete pieces called tokens and gives each piece a fixed integer ID taken from a finite vocabulary. The hard part is designing that vocabulary so it stays small enough to store, yet can still represent text nobody saw while building it.
points: Networks need discrete numeric symbols, not raw strings
Language is ambiguous, variable and open-ended
Tokenization: text -> tokens -> integer IDs
The vocabulary must be finite
A strategy for unseen text is required
cards.example: 'Hello world!' -> [Hello, _world, !] -> [313, 3666, 25] (illustrative IDs; '_' marks a leading space)
cards.say: Computers need numbers, but language is endless and messy. Tokenization chops text into small pieces called tokens and gives each piece a number from a fixed list. The trick is handling words the list has never seen.

cards.title: Characters, Words or Subwords?
cards.text: The vocabulary is the complete list of tokens a model can see. How big should the pieces be? Single characters give a tiny vocabulary that never meets an unknown symbol, but sequences become very long and each piece carries little meaning. Whole words keep sequences short, yet the vocabulary explodes and any unseen word becomes out-of-vocabulary. Subwords sit in between: frequent words stay whole, rare ones are assembled from parts. That balance is why modern LLMs use subword tokenizers, though a clumsy split can blur meaning.
points: Character-level: small vocabulary, very long sequences
Word-level: short sequences, huge vocabulary, OOV failures
Subword-level: the balanced choice of modern LLMs
Smaller vocabulary -> more tokens -> more compute
Frequent tokens get more training updates than rare ones
Bigger vocabulary -> more stored vectors -> bigger model
cards.example: 'Hello' as H,e,l,l,o (character) / Hel,lo (subword) / Hello (word); 'computer' as one token vs. the meaning-blurring split 'compu' + 'ter'.
cards.say: How big should a token be? Letters make sequences painfully long, whole words make the vocabulary huge and fail on new words. Subwords balance the two, which is why today's models use them.
covers: B2: Vocabulary granularity and its impact

cards.title: Byte-Pair Encoding: Learning Merges
cards.text: Byte-Pair Encoding was invented as a lossless compression trick and later repurposed to build subword vocabularies. Training is a simple greedy loop. Begin with every character as its own token. Count how often each pair of neighbouring tokens appears across the corpus, merge the most frequent pair into a brand-new token, and rewrite the corpus with it. Repeat until the vocabulary hits the size you want. Common fragments and whole words emerge automatically. The catch: a character never seen during training has no token at all.
points: Origin: lossless data compression
Start: one token per character
Merge the most frequent adjacent pair, then repeat
Stop at a target vocabulary size
Result: data-driven subword units
Weakness: unseen characters cannot be encoded
cards.formula: repeat: (a, b) = most frequent adjacent pair; replace every 'a b' with new token 'ab'; until |V| = target size (|V| = vocabulary size)
cards.example: Corpus 'low lower' starts as l o w _ l o w e r. The pair (l, o) occurs twice, so it is merged first into 'lo', giving lo w _ lo w e r.
cards.say: Byte pair encoding learns its vocabulary by counting. Start with single characters, find the pair that appears together most often, glue it into a new token, and repeat until the vocabulary is big enough.

cards.title: Byte-Level BPE and UTF-8
cards.text: How do you make sure no input is ever unknown? Run BPE on bytes instead of characters. UTF-8 stores every Unicode character as one to four bytes, and a byte can take only 256 values. So a base vocabulary of exactly 256 byte tokens can already spell out any valid text in any language, emoji included. Merges are then learned on top of the bytes, and the final vocabulary is the 256 bytes plus all merged tokens, each remembering which bytes it stands for. GPT-2 popularised this approach.
points: Works on UTF-8 bytes (values 0-255), not characters
UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes per character
256 base tokens give complete coverage of any text
Final vocabulary = 256 bytes + learned merges
Each merged token stores its byte content for exact decoding
Popularised by GPT-2-style tokenizers
cards.formula: base vocabulary size = 256 (all byte values 0 to 255)
cards.example: 'Hi 🙂' -> bytes [72, 105, 32, 240, 159, 153, 130]: H, i and the space take 1 byte each, the emoji takes 4. In a Wikipedia paragraph about Obama, 'Barack' = 66 97 114 97 99 107, a space = 32 and '.' = 46.
cards.say: To never meet an unknown character, modern tokenizers start from raw bytes. Every character in UTF-8 is one to four bytes, and there are only two hundred fifty six byte values, so everything can be spelled.

cards.title: Real Tokenizers in Action
cards.text: Production tokenizers behave much like the toy version, just with vocabularies learned from enormous corpora. OpenAI's online tokenizer shows that common English words usually become a single token, and the space in front of a word is typically glued onto it. The same sentence keeps six tokens for both GPT-4o and the newer GPT-5.x tokenizer, yet one ID changes: the final full stop. That small difference is a reminder that IDs belong to a specific tokenizer. A handy rule for English: one token is roughly four characters.
points: Common words are often a single token
The leading space is usually part of the word token
~4 English characters per token
100 tokens ≈ 75 words
Different model generations may assign different IDs to the same piece
cards.formula: tokens ≈ characters / 4; words ≈ 0.75 × tokens (English rule of thumb)
cards.example: 'Children go to the kindergarten.' -> 6 tokens. GPT-4o: [15295, 810, 316, 290, 92647, 13]. GPT-5.x and o1/o3: [15295, 810, 316, 290, 92647, 558]. Only the ID of the final '.' differs.
cards.say: Real tokenizers turn most common English words into a single token, usually including the space before them. As a rule of thumb, a token is about four characters, so a hundred tokens are roughly seventy five words.

cards.title: Special Tokens and Chat Templates
cards.text: Not every token stands for text. Vocabularies also reserve control tokens. A beginning-of-sequence token opens the input, an end-of-sequence token tells the model it is done and can stop generation, and a padding token fills up shorter sequences so a batch has equal lengths; padding is masked out of the loss and never predicted by decoder-only models. Chat models add role tokens that wrap the system instructions, the user's message and the assistant's reply into a chat template. The exact spelling differs from one model family to another.
points: <bos>: start of the sequence
<eos>: end of the sequence, can stop generation
<pad>: batch alignment only, masked and never predicted
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|>: role markers in chat templates
Formats are model-specific
cards.example: A chat turn might be stored as <|system|> You are helpful. <|user|> Hi! <|assistant|> Hello! <eos> (schematic; real templates vary by model).
cards.say: Some tokens are not words but signals. Start and end markers frame a sequence, padding fills gaps in a batch, and role tokens tell a chat model which part is the system, the user or the assistant.
covers: A2: Special tokens and chat templates

cards.title: Tokens Cost Context, Compute and Money
cards.text: Token counts quietly drive three practical budgets. First, the context window is measured in tokens, so a text that needs more tokens eats more of it. Second, every token is a position the model must process, so longer sequences mean more inference work and memory, with the exact growth depending on the architecture. Third, commercial APIs from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic bill per input and per output token. Because tokenizers differ, comparing per-token prices alone is misleading; measure the cost on your own representative workload.
points: More tokens fill more of the context window
Token count sets the sequence length to compute on
Longer sequences raise inference work and memory
APIs bill input and output tokens separately
Per-token prices across models are not directly comparable
Benchmark cost on a representative workload
cards.formula: cost = n_input_tokens × price_in + n_output_tokens × price_out (prices usually quoted per 1M tokens)
cards.example: The same text needs 120 tokens with tokenizer A but 165 with tokenizer B, about 37% more. Even at an identical price per million tokens, model B costs more for that text. (Price tables compared: claude.com/pricing and openai.com/api/pricing, October 2025.)
cards.say: Tokens are the currency of language models. They fill the context window, they set how much computation is needed, and they are what you pay for. Since tokenizers differ, always compare costs on your real text.
covers: B2: Why tokenization matters in practice
A2: API pricing and tokenizer differences

cards.title: Tokenizer and Model Are a Pair
cards.text: Because the model only ever sees tokens, 'predict the next word' really means 'predict the next token'. The vocabulary size therefore fixes the width of the output layer: the model emits one score per vocabulary entry, and these scores can be turned into a probability distribution. It also means tokenizer and model are welded together during training. Swap in a different tokenizer and the same text maps to different IDs, so the model's learned knowledge no longer lines up; it must be adapted or retrained. Diagrams later often pretend one word equals one token, purely for readability.
points: Next-word prediction is really next-token prediction
Output (logit) dimension = vocabulary size V
Scores can be converted into probabilities
Tokenizer and model are a coupled system
Changing the tokenizer requires adaptation or retraining
Simplification ahead: one word = one token
cards.formula: z ∈ R^V: one logit per vocabulary entry, V = vocabulary size
cards.example: With a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, every forward pass ends in a vector of about 100,000 scores, one per possible next token.
cards.say: A tokenizer and its model are a matched pair. The model outputs one score for every token in the vocabulary, so swapping the tokenizer scrambles everything it learned and means retraining or adapting the model.
covers: B2: Engineering implications of the tokenizer

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.goal: Understand how token IDs become learned vectors, how their geometry encodes meaning, and how cosine similarity compares them.

cards.title: IDs Are Labels, Not Meanings
cards.text: After tokenization a sentence is just a row of integers, and those integers are arbitrary. In 'The bank raised interest rates today', 'bank' happens to be 2317 and 'raised' 751, but that tells us nothing. ID 2317 is no closer in meaning to 2318 than to 57. If a network computed directly on these numbers, it would chase patterns that do not exist. The fix is an embedding: a lookup that swaps each ID for a learned continuous vector, placing tokens in a space where geometry can reflect meaning.
points: Token IDs are arbitrary indices
Numeric closeness of IDs means nothing
Each ID selects a learned vector instead
Vectors live in a continuous semantic space
Tokens are dictionary entries; embeddings express their meaning as geometry
cards.example: 'The bank raised interest rates today' -> [104, 2317, 751, 908, 432, 57] (illustrative). 2317 = 'bank', 751 = 'raised'; 2317 is not more similar to 2318 than to 57.
cards.say: Token IDs are just catalogue numbers. Two neighbouring IDs are not similar words. So instead of computing on the IDs themselves, we swap every ID for a learned vector, where distances can actually carry meaning.
covers: B2: Why token IDs are not enough
A3: Why token IDs need embeddings

cards.title: The Embedding Matrix
cards.text: All token vectors live in one table, the embedding matrix E. It has one row per vocabulary entry, so V rows, and d_model columns. Embedding a token is literally copying the row whose index is its ID. Two numbers therefore shape the table: V sets how many vectors exist and also the size of the output vocabulary, while d_model sets how wide every vector is, and it is the same width the hidden representations keep through all Transformer layers. Wider means more capacity, but also more parameters and compute.
points: E has shape V × d_model, one row per token
Lookup at position t: copy row x_t
Vocabularies are often 100k+ tokens
d_model reaches roughly 10-16k in large models
d_model is also the hidden width of Transformer layers
Embedding parameters = V · d_model
cards.formula: E ∈ R^(V × d_model); e_t = E[x_t], where x_t is the token ID at position t and e_t its vector; number of embedding parameters = V · d_model
cards.example: V = 100,000 and d_model = 4,096 give 100,000 × 4,096 = 409,600,000, roughly 410 million parameters in the embedding table alone (illustrative). Each of the six tokens of 'The bank raised interest rates today' gets its own row.
cards.say: Every token's vector is stored as one row of a big table called the embedding matrix. Looking up a token just copies its row. With a hundred thousand tokens and four thousand dimensions, that table alone holds about four hundred million numbers.
covers: B2: Embedding matrix, lookup and parameter count

cards.title: One-Hot Vectors vs. Embeddings
cards.text: Why not just use one-hot vectors? A one-hot vector is as long as the vocabulary and contains a single 1 at the token's position. It works, but badly: it is enormous and almost all zeros, every pair of one-hot vectors is orthogonal so no similarity can show up, and whatever the model learns about one token cannot transfer to another. An embedding layer fixes all three. Mathematically it is a linear projection: multiplying the one-hot vector by E picks out one row, compressing V dimensions into d_model learnable, shared ones.
points: One-hot: vocabulary-length vector with a single 1
Wasteful: huge and almost entirely zeros
All one-hot vectors are orthogonal: no relations
No generalization: each token learned from scratch
Embedding = linear projection of the one-hot vector
Compresses V dimensions down to d_model
cards.formula: e_t = E^T · x_t, where x_t is the one-hot vector of the token; the product simply selects row x_t of E
cards.example: Toy vocabulary of 6: [The, bank, raised, interest, rates, today]. 'bank' = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]; multiplying by E returns exactly the second row of E.
cards.say: A one hot vector is a giant list of zeros with a single one. It treats every word as equally unrelated. Multiplying it by the embedding matrix just picks one row, giving a compact vector that can be learned.
covers: A3: One-hot vectors and embeddings as projection

cards.title: Meaning Emerges as Geometry
cards.text: Nobody writes the embedding values by hand. E is a trainable parameter: its rows start random and are nudged by gradient updates together with every other weight in the LLM, driven by the training objective. Meaning ends up stored not in single numbers but in distances and directions. Tokens that appear in similar contexts drift toward similar positions, and regularities such as gender, tense or grammar can show up as roughly parallel offset directions, so simple vector arithmetic sometimes lands near the expected word.
points: E is trained jointly with all other parameters
Rows start random, updated by backpropagation
Meaning lives in distances and directions
Similar contexts -> similar vectors
Gender (king-queen, man-woman), tense (walk-walked), syntax (is-was, do-did) as directions
Relations can appear as linear offsets
cards.formula: king - man + woman ≈ queen (an analogy expressed as vector arithmetic)
cards.example: In a made-up 2D picture, the arrow from 'man' to 'woman' is parallel to the arrow from 'king' to 'queen'; both encode the same gender shift.
cards.say: The embedding table starts as random noise and is shaped by training. Words used in similar ways end up close together, and relationships like male to female or present to past can appear as consistent directions.

cards.title: Length Says Frequency, Direction Says Meaning
cards.text: Trained embedding spaces hide a surprising pattern. How often a word appears in the training data correlates with the length, or norm, of its vector. Very frequent words such as 'the', 'and' or 'of' receive many gradient updates, end up with larger norms, and point in similar directions, forming a dense cluster around the centroid of all embeddings, not around the origin. That cluster reflects generic usage rather than meaning. Rare words like 'neutrino' get smaller norms but distinctive directions out on the sparse periphery.
points: Word frequency correlates with vector norm
Frequent words: larger norms, more gradient updates
They cluster densely near the centroid (not the origin)
That cluster reflects generic usage, not meaning
Rare words: smaller norms, distinctive directions at the periphery
Rule of thumb: length ≈ frequency, direction ≈ meaning
cards.formula: ||e|| = sqrt(sum over k of e_k^2): the L2 norm (length) of embedding vector e
cards.example: Frequent: 'the', 'and', 'of' -> long, similar arrows near the centroid. Rare: 'cryptocurrency', 'neutrino' -> shorter arrows pointing in their own directions.
cards.say: Here is a neat pattern. Common words like the and of get long vectors that all point roughly the same way. Rare words get shorter but more distinctive directions. Length tracks frequency, direction tracks meaning.
covers: A3: Vector norm vs. direction (frequency effects)

cards.title: Cosine Similarity
cards.text: If direction carries meaning and length is mostly noise, compare vectors by their angle. Cosine similarity divides the dot product of two vectors by the product of their lengths, so scaling a vector changes nothing. The result lies between -1 and +1: +1 means the same direction, 0 means orthogonal and unrelated, -1 means opposite. Cosine distance is one minus the similarity. A helpful picture: normalise every embedding to length one, and all tokens become points on a high-dimensional sphere where the angle is the semantic distance.
points: Measures the angle between two vectors
Ignores vector length
+1 same direction, 0 unrelated, -1 opposite
Cosine distance = 1 - cosine similarity
Normalised embeddings are points on a hypersphere
cards.formula: cos_sim(e_i, e_j) = (e_i · e_j) / (||e_i|| · ||e_j||), with e_i, e_j vectors of length d_model; d_cos = 1 - cos_sim
cards.example: bank-loan 0.82 (strongly related), bank-interest 0.76 (related), bank-river 0.48 (moderate, the other meaning of bank), bank-banana 0.05 (unrelated); good-bad -0.62, increase-decrease -0.45, up-down -0.71, love-hate -0.58 (opposites). Synonyms like car-automobile approach +1.
cards.say: To compare two word vectors, we look at the angle between them, not their length. Pointing the same way gives one, unrelated gives zero, opposite gives minus one. Bank and loan score high, bank and banana almost zero.

cards.title: Word2Vec: Learning from Neighbours
cards.text: Long before LLMs, Word2Vec showed that useful embeddings can be learned from context alone. Its skip-gram variant is a shallow network: the one-hot vector of a centre word goes in, a hidden layer projects it to a small vector, and a softmax output predicts which words appear in a window around it. Training raises the probability of the real neighbours. Because words with similar neighbours must make similar predictions, their hidden vectors become similar, and those hidden weights are the embeddings. You can explore such spaces at projector.tensorflow.org.
points: Skip-gram: predict context words from a centre word
Shallow net: one-hot input -> hidden layer -> softmax
Training data: (centre, context) pairs inside a window
Maximise the probability of true context words
Hidden-layer weights become the word embeddings
cards.formula: maximise the sum of log p(context word | centre word), with p computed by a softmax over the vocabulary
cards.example: In 'The bank raised interest rates today' with centre word 'interest', the training pairs are (interest -> bank), (interest -> raised), (interest -> rates), (interest -> today).
cards.say: Word2Vec learns word vectors with a simple game: given a word, guess its neighbours. Words that share neighbours are forced toward similar vectors, and those learned weights become the embeddings.

cards.title: One Vector per Token, Whatever the Context
cards.text: There is one big limitation. The embedding lookup ignores neighbouring words entirely: the same ID always fetches the same row. So 'bank' gets an identical starting vector in 'The bank raised interest rates' and in 'They sat on the river bank', even though the meanings differ. Its static vector is a blend of all its uses, which is why bank-river scores a moderate 0.48. Separating finance from riverside meaning requires looking at the whole sentence, and that is exactly what attention in the following Transformer layers does.
points: Lookup is independent of surrounding tokens
Same token ID -> same initial embedding
Ambiguous words get one blended vector
Contextual meaning emerges in later layers
Motivates attention and the Transformer (Chapter 3)
cards.example: Matrix rows such as ID 0 -> [0.12, -0.08, ..., 0.44], ID 1 -> [-0.31, 0.17, ..., -0.06], ID 2317 -> [-0.09, 0.52, ...] with d_model e.g. 4096. Both 'bank' sentences fetch row 2317 unchanged.
cards.say: An embedding lookup is blind to context. The word bank gets the very same vector whether we talk about money or a river. Telling those meanings apart is the job of attention, which comes next.

lessons.title: From Logits Back to Text
lessons.goal: Follow how the model's scores become probabilities, a chosen token and finally text, how the generation loop runs inside a context window, and how the same pipeline is trained.

cards.title: Logits: A Score for Every Token
cards.text: Once the input vectors have flowed through the LLM, the last position produces logits: one raw, unnormalised score for every entry in the vocabulary. With a 100,000-token vocabulary that is a vector of 100,000 numbers. Higher means the model finds that token more plausible as the continuation, but the values are not probabilities yet and can be negative or larger than one. A decoding strategy then reads these scores and commits to one token ID. Crucially, a causal LLM makes exactly one such next-token decision per forward pass.
points: Logits = raw, unnormalised scores
One logit per vocabulary entry
Higher score = more plausible next token
A decoding strategy (Chapter 5) picks the token
One forward pass = one next-token decision
cards.formula: z = (z_0, ..., z_(V-1)) ∈ R^V, one score per vocabulary token, V = vocabulary size
cards.example: After 'The capital of France is': ' Paris' (ID 12345) logit 8.4, ' Lyon' (6592) 3.1, ' France' (156) 2.7, ' London' (398) 1.9 (illustrative).
cards.say: At the end of each pass the model produces a raw score, called a logit, for every token it knows. For the capital of France prompt, Paris gets by far the highest score, but nothing is chosen yet.

cards.title: Softmax: Scores to Probabilities
cards.text: To compare logits as chances, they are passed through softmax. Each score is exponentiated, which makes every value positive and stretches the gaps, and then divided by the sum of all exponentials, so the results lie between zero and one and add up to exactly one. The model's output is thus a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary. Softmax keeps the ranking of the logits, so the top score stays the top probability, but a gap of a few points in logits becomes a huge gap in probability.
points: Exponentiate, then normalise by the sum
Outputs are in (0, 1) and sum to 1
Gives a probability distribution over the vocabulary
Preserves the order of the logits
Small logit gaps become large probability gaps
Basis for greedy decoding, sampling and temperature
cards.formula: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum over j of exp(z_j), where z_i is the logit of token i and p_i its probability
cards.example: If only the four candidates above existed: exp(8.4) ≈ 4447, exp(3.1) ≈ 22.2, exp(2.7) ≈ 14.9, exp(1.9) ≈ 6.7; sum ≈ 4491. So P(' Paris') ≈ 0.990, P(' Lyon') ≈ 0.005, P(' France') ≈ 0.003, P(' London') ≈ 0.0015.
cards.say: Softmax turns raw scores into probabilities. It exponentiates every score and divides by the total, so everything is positive and adds up to one. A lead of five points makes Paris about ninety nine percent likely.

cards.title: The Generation Loop and When It Stops
cards.text: Generating an answer is a loop of four moves: process the current sequence, select the next token, append it, repeat. Each new prediction is conditioned on every token so far, including the ones the model just produced. Starting from 'The capital of France is', the loop adds ' Paris', then '.', then the end-of-sequence token. That last token is one way to stop. The application can also cap the number of generated tokens, or watch for other criteria such as a user-defined stop sequence. A high logit alone never stops generation.
points: Loop: process -> select -> append -> repeat
Each step adds exactly one token
Each step conditions on all previous tokens
Stop on <eos>
Stop at a configured generation limit
Stop on other criteria, e.g. stop sequences
cards.formula: x_(t+1) = select(LLM(x_1, ..., x_t)): the next token is chosen from the model's scores for the sequence so far
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' -> ' Paris' -> '.' -> <eos> (stop). A second illustration: 'The' -> 'cat' -> 'sat' -> 'on' -> 'the' -> 'mat'.
cards.say: Generation is a loop: run the model, pick a token, append it, and run again. It ends when the model emits an end of sequence token, when a length limit is reached, or when some other stop rule fires.

cards.title: The Context Window
cards.text: The current context is the prompt plus everything generated so far, so it grows by one token every step. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process at once; it acts like short-term memory, and each prediction only sees what is inside it. The length is fixed by the model design, and both prompt and output share it, so a longer prompt leaves less room to answer. At the limit, the application must stop, drop old tokens, summarise them or move knowledge into retrieval. Larger windows cost latency, memory and money.
points: Current context = prompt tokens + generated tokens
Window = max tokens processed in one step
Acts as the model's short-term memory
Fixed by the architecture; prompt and output share it
At the limit: stop, drop, summarise or retrieve (RAG)
Bigger windows -> more latency, memory and cost
cards.formula: n_prompt + n_generated <= L, where L is the context window length in tokens
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' = 5 tokens; after one step plus ' Paris' = 6 tokens (illustrative). Window sizes grew fast: GPT-1 512, GPT-2 1,024, GPT-3 2,048, GPT-4 32,768 tokens.
