cards.say: The context window is the model's short term memory, measured in tokens. Your prompt and the answer share it. GPT one could hold five hundred twelve tokens, GPT four up to about thirty two thousand.
covers: B2: Growing context and the context window

cards.title: Walkthrough: A 5-Token Window
cards.text: Let's run the whole pipeline by hand with a tiny context window of just five tokens. The prompt '<bos> The' is tokenized and placed in the window. The LLM predicts an ID, the detokenizer reveals its word, and the ID is pushed into the window for the next round. After four steps the window is full, so the oldest token, <bos>, slides out to make room. On the sixth step the model predicts the end-of-sequence ID and generation stops, leaving a complete little sentence.
points: Tokenizer -> IDs in the window -> LLM -> predicted ID -> detokenizer
Every predicted ID is pushed into the window
Window length 5 in this example
When full, the oldest token is dropped
Generation ends when <eos> (ID 513) is predicted
cards.example: IDs: The=464, cat=58624, sat=963, on=162, the=27, mat=7598, <eos>=513. Step 1: [<bos>, 464] -> 58624 'cat'. Steps 2-4: -> 963 'sat', 162 'on', 27 'the'. Step 5: window full, <bos> removed -> 7598 'mat'. Step 6: [58624, 963, 162, 27, 7598] -> 513 <eos>. Output: 'The cat sat on the mat'.
cards.say: Let's step through it with a window of only five tokens. Each predicted word is pushed in. When the window is full, the oldest token drops out. When the model predicts the end token, we stop with: the cat sat on the mat.

cards.title: Detokenization: IDs Back to Text
cards.text: The final station converts generated IDs back into readable text, and it must use exactly the same tokenizer configuration as encoding. For a byte-level tokenizer, each ID maps to its stored byte sequence; the bytes are concatenated and decoded as UTF-8, which correctly reassembles multi-byte characters such as emoji split across tokens. Because token boundaries are not word boundaries, you cannot just join token strings with spaces; leading spaces live inside the tokens. Merges are deterministic, so the round trip is lossless. Special tokens like <eos> end generation rather than appearing as text.
points: Inverse of tokenization: IDs -> tokens -> text
Same tokenizer configuration for encoding and decoding
Byte-level: IDs -> bytes -> concatenate -> UTF-8 decode
Token boundaries ≠ word boundaries; no naive space-joining
Deterministic merges make it lossless
<eos> ends generation instead of producing text
cards.formula: decode(encode(text)) = text (lossless round trip)
cards.example: [313, 3666, 25] -> [Hello, _world, !] -> 'Hello world!'. Generated IDs [12345, 13] -> ' Paris.'; then <eos> ends generation.
cards.say: Detokenization runs the tokenizer backwards. Each ID turns back into its bytes, the bytes are joined and decoded into characters. Spaces already live inside the tokens, so you never just glue tokens together with spaces.

cards.title: The Same Pipeline Learns
cards.text: Training reuses the exact same pipeline, just with the answer known in advance. Take 'The cat sat on the mat': the input is the sentence and the target is the same sentence shifted one token to the left, so every position must predict its successor. In the forward pass the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary at each position. Cross-entropy compares it with a one-hot vector marking the correct next token, which boils down to minus the log probability of that token. Backpropagation then adjusts the weights so the right token becomes more likely.
points: Target = input shifted by one position
Forward pass: distribution over the vocabulary at every position
Cross-entropy loss vs. a one-hot target
Backpropagation computes gradients and updates weights
Every position gives a training signal at once
cards.formula: Loss = - sum over t of log p(x_(t+1) | x_1, ..., x_t); with a one-hot target, each term is minus the log probability of the correct token
cards.example: Input: 'The cat sat on the' -> Target: 'cat sat on the mat'. If p('cat' | 'The') = 0.5, that position's loss is -ln 0.5 ≈ 0.69; raising it to 0.9 lowers the loss to about 0.11.
cards.say: Training uses the same pipeline. The target is just the input shifted by one word. The model's probabilities are compared with the correct next token using cross entropy, and backpropagation nudges the weights to do better next time.

lessons.title: Sequence Models: RNN & Seq2Seq
lessons.goal: Understand how recurrent networks turn a token sequence into context-aware hidden states, how an encoder-decoder maps one sequence to another, and why a single fixed context vector becomes a bottleneck.

cards.title: Same Word, Different Meaning
cards.text: An embedding table hands every token the same starting vector no matter where it appears. So 'bank' after a talk about interest rates and 'bank' after a walk by the river begin as identical points in space. That is a fine starting point, but real understanding needs contextual representations: vectors that shift depending on the neighbouring tokens because they absorb information from other positions. The big question for this whole chapter is therefore simple to state: how can a network move information between token positions so each vector learns what its context is?
points: Embedding lookup is context-independent: same ID, same vector
The initial embedding is only a learned token-level starting point
Contextual representations change with surrounding tokens
They are built by pulling in information from other positions
cards.example: 'After discussing interest rates, they went to the bank.' vs 'After walking along the river, they reached the bank.' - both 'bank' tokens start with the same embedding, but should end up meaning money vs riverside.
cards.say: An embedding gives the word bank the same vector whether we talk about money or a river. To really understand text, each word's vector must change with its context. The rest of this chapter is about how networks pass information between positions.
covers: B2: From static embeddings to contextual representations

cards.title: Two Ways to Move Information
cards.text: To build context, two jobs must be solved: propagation (getting information from earlier positions to later ones) and selection (finding which pieces matter). Recurrent neural networks, the classic sequence models, solve propagation by reading tokens strictly in order and updating a hidden state after every token. That hidden state acts like a running memory of everything seen so far. Attention, which comes later, instead opens weighted direct connections to any position. In both cases the architecture only fixes which information paths exist; training decides how much flows along each.
points: Propagation: earlier positions must reach later ones
Selection: the model must pick relevant information
RNNs read tokens in order and update a hidden state each step
The hidden state is the network's memory of the past
Attention: selective access through weighted connections
Architecture defines paths; training learns the parameters
cards.say: There are two classic ways to share information between words. A recurrent network passes a memory vector along the chain, one token at a time. Attention instead builds weighted shortcuts directly to any position. Training decides how information flows.

cards.title: Inside an RNN Step
cards.text: Take 'I love machine learning', four tokens processed at steps t = 1 to 4. At each step the token ID x_t selects one row of the embedding matrix, giving the vector e_t. The hidden layer then mixes two ingredients: the new embedding, through input-to-hidden weights, and the previous hidden state, through recurrent hidden-to-hidden weights. A bias is added and a nonlinearity such as tanh squashes the result into the new hidden state h_t. The very first state h_0 is all zeros. LSTMs replace this simple update with a gated, more elaborate one.
points: Pipeline per step: token ID -> embedding -> hidden -> linear -> softmax -> argmax
Embedding lookup: e_t = E[x_t], E has V rows of size d_e
W_he (H x d_e) maps the input, W_hh (H x H) carries the past
h_0 is a zero vector; H is the hidden size
LSTMs use a gated version of this update
cards.formula: e_t = E[x_t];  h_t = f(W_he e_t + W_hh h_(t-1) + b_h). x_t = token ID at step t, E = embedding matrix (V x d_e), W_he = input-to-hidden weights, W_hh = recurrent weights, b_h = bias, f = nonlinearity such as tanh, h_t = hidden state of size H.
cards.example: 'I love machine learning' -> 4 tokens -> 4 time steps; h_1 summarizes 'I', h_4 summarizes the whole sentence.
cards.say: At each step the RNN looks up the current word's embedding, mixes it with the previous hidden state using two weight matrices, adds a bias and applies a nonlinearity. The result is the new memory, passed on to the next word.
covers: A3: RNN forward pass: input and embedding layer

cards.title: From Hidden State to a Word
cards.text: A hidden state is not yet a prediction. A linear output layer projects h_t into a logit vector z_t holding one raw score for every vocabulary entry. Softmax then exponentiates each score and divides by the total, turning the logits into probabilities between 0 and 1 that add up to exactly one. The simplest choice of next token is argmax: take the most probable entry, which is called greedy search. Smarter selection rules based on sampling exist and are explained in the decoding lesson.
points: Output layer: W_0 is V x H, bias b_0 has V entries
Logits z_t: one unnormalized score per vocabulary token
Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution
Argmax picks the most likely token (greedy search)
Sampling-based alternatives come later
cards.formula: z_t = W_0 h_t + b_0;  p(y_t = i) = exp(z_t,i) / sum over j of exp(z_t,j);  y_t = argmax_i p(y_t = i). V = vocabulary size, H = hidden size.
cards.say: To turn memory into a word, a linear layer produces one score per vocabulary token. Softmax converts those scores into probabilities that add up to one, and the simplest strategy just picks the highest one. That is called greedy search.
covers: A3: Output projection, softmax and argmax

cards.title: Encoder Meets Decoder
cards.text: Translation, summarization, captioning and dialogue all turn one sequence into another, often of a different length. One RNN struggles to understand and generate at once, so seq2seq splits the work. An encoder RNN reads the whole input; its final hidden state becomes a fixed-size context vector, and its per-step outputs are thrown away. A decoder RNN starts from that vector as its initial state and generates tokens one by one, beginning with <bos> and feeding its own previous predictions back in. Both networks are trained jointly to maximise the probability of the correct output.
points: Tasks: translation, summarization, image captioning, dialogue
Encoder compresses the input into one context vector c
c = final encoder state = initial decoder state s_0
Decoder input: <bos> plus previously predicted tokens
Encoder and decoder are trained jointly; lengths may differ
Distant information must hop through every intermediate state
cards.formula: c = h_n (final encoder state) = s_0;  p(y_1..y_m | x_1..x_n) = product over t of p(y_t | y_<t, c). x = input tokens (n), y = output tokens (m).
cards.say: Sequence to sequence models use two recurrent networks. The encoder reads the input and squeezes it into one context vector. The decoder starts from that vector and writes the output word by word, feeding each prediction back in.

cards.title: Translating Step by Step
cards.text: Unroll the networks in time. The encoder reads 'I', 'love', 'machine', 'learning' and hands its last state to the decoder. The decoder receives <bos> and outputs 'Jag'; that word becomes its next input and produces 'älskar'; then 'maskininlärning' follows, and finally <eos> stops generation. Four English tokens became three Swedish ones, because 'machine learning' is a single compound word in Swedish. This shows nicely that encoder and decoder lengths are independent. For simplicity the time counter is restarted when the decoder begins.
points: Encoder unrolled over 4 input tokens
Decoder begins with <bos>
Each output is fed back as the next input
Generation ends when <eos> is produced
4 input tokens -> 3 output tokens plus <eos>
cards.example: 'I love machine learning' -> <bos> -> 'Jag' -> 'älskar' -> 'maskininlärning' -> <eos>.
cards.say: Here the encoder reads I love machine learning. The decoder starts with a begin token and writes Jag, then älskar, then maskininlärning, and finally an end token. Four English words became three Swedish ones.

cards.title: The Bottleneck Problem
cards.text: Basic seq2seq forces the entire source sentence through one fixed-size vector, and the decoder has no way to peek at individual encoder states. For short sentences this works surprisingly well. For long or complicated inputs, however, crucial details get crushed or forgotten, and translation or summary quality drops. A fixed-size container simply cannot scale with variable-length input. The cure, proposed by Bahdanau and colleagues, is attention: let the decoder look back at all encoder hidden states and assemble a new, tailored context vector at every decoding step.
points: Whole input squeezed into one context vector
Decoder cannot access individual encoder states
Fine for short sentences, lossy for long ones
Fixed size vs. variable-length input
Fix: attention builds a new context vector per step
cards.say: The weakness of basic seq2seq is that the whole sentence must fit into one fixed vector. Long sentences lose details. Attention fixes this by letting the decoder look back at every encoder state whenever it needs to.
covers: A3: Information bottleneck and motivation for attention

lessons.title: Attention in Seq2Seq
lessons.goal: Learn how attention scores, softmax weights and a per-step context vector let an RNN decoder look back at every source word, and why this beat the fixed-context seq2seq model.

cards.title: Scoring Every Source Word
cards.text: Back to 'I love machine learning', now with attention. Before the decoder writes its first word, the encoder has already produced four hidden states h_1 to h_4, one per source token, and the decoder state starts as s_0 = h_4 = c. For every encoder position the model computes a score: how well does the current decoder state match this source state, i.e. how relevant is that word right now? Luong attention simply takes a dot product. Bahdanau attention learns an additive score with a tiny feed-forward network. Either way, one number per source word comes out.
points: Encoder states h_1..h_4 exist before decoding (h_0 = 0)
Initial decoder state s_0 = h_4 = c
Score a_t,i rates the match of s_(t-1) with h_i
Luong: dot-product score
Bahdanau: learned additive score
Answers: how much should step t attend to position i?
cards.formula: a_t,i = score(s_(t-1), h_i). Luong dot product: score(s, h) = s . h. Bahdanau additive: score(s, h) = v^T tanh(W_s s + W_h h). s = decoder state, h_i = encoder state at position i, v, W_s, W_h = learned parameters.
cards.example: Step t = 1: decoder input <bos>, four scores a_1,1 .. a_1,4, one for each of 'I', 'love', 'machine', 'learning'.
cards.say: With attention, the decoder first compares its current state with every encoder state. Each comparison gives a relevance score. Luong attention uses a plain dot product, while Bahdanau attention learns a small scoring network.
covers: A4: Attention scores, distribution and context vector

cards.title: Weights and the Context Vector
cards.text: Raw scores can be any size, so softmax converts them into an attention distribution: positive weights that sum to one. The context vector for this step is then the weighted sum of all encoder states, a summary of the source tuned to what the decoder needs at this exact moment. At the very first step the slides show a uniform 0.25 for each of the four words; that picture is only illustrative, since real weights already depend on the states. The key change from plain seq2seq: a brand new context vector is computed at every decoding step.
points: Softmax over scores gives weights alpha_t,i
Weights are positive and sum to 1
Context c_t = weighted sum of encoder states
Uniform 0.25 weights at t = 1 are illustrative only
A fresh context vector at every step
cards.formula: alpha_t,i = exp(a_t,i) / sum over j of exp(a_t,j);  c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i h_i. alpha = attention weights, c_t = context vector at step t.
cards.example: t = 1 with 4 encoder states: alpha_1,i is about 0.25 each, so c_1 = 0.25 (h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + h_4) in the illustrative uniform case.
cards.say: Softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to one. The context vector is the weighted average of the encoder states, so every decoding step gets its own custom summary of the source sentence.
covers: B2: Attention distribution and context vector
A4: Attention scores, distribution and context vector

cards.title: Updating the Decoder
cards.text: Now the decoder computes its new state from three ingredients: the embedding of the token it produced last, its own previous state, and the fresh context vector. Bahdanau and colleagues used gated recurrent units, GRUs, for this update. The new state then goes through an output layer to get logits over the target vocabulary, softmax turns them into probabilities, and a selection rule such as argmax picks the word. In the example, step one starts from <bos>, uses context c_1, produces state s_1 and outputs 'Jag'.
points: New state uses previous token embedding, s_(t-1) and c_t
Bahdanau et al. used GRU cells
Output layer -> softmax -> argmax gives the token
The chosen token is fed back as the next input
First output in the example: 'Jag'
cards.formula: s_t = f_dec(e_(t-1), s_(t-1), c_t);  p(y_t | y_<t, x) = softmax(W_o s_t + b_o);  y_t = argmax p. f_dec = recurrent cell such as a GRU, e_(t-1) = embedding of previous output.
cards.example: t = 1: input <bos> + context c_1 -> state s_1 -> output 'Jag'.
cards.say: The decoder now updates its memory using the last word it wrote, its previous state and the new context vector. In the original work this was a GRU cell. Then an output layer and softmax choose the next word, here Jag.
covers: B2: Decoder update and output with attention
A4: Decoder update and step-by-step translation

cards.title: Watching Attention Move
cards.text: The whole cycle of scores, weights, context and state update repeats at every step, so attention can wander across the source. When writing the second word, the weight on 'love' clearly dominates and the decoder emits 'älskar'. At the next step attention shifts onto 'machine' and 'learning', which together become the single Swedish compound 'maskininlärning'. Finally <eos> ends the output. Each target word thus draws on exactly the source words it corresponds to. The weights drawn in the figures are illustrative, but the mechanism is the real one.
points: Scores, weights and context recomputed every step
t = 2: focus on 'love' -> 'älskar'
t = 3: focus on 'machine' + 'learning' -> 'maskininlärning'
Last step emits <eos>
Figure weights are illustrative
cards.formula: For each step t: a_t,i = score(s_(t-1), h_i); alpha_t = softmax(a_t); c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i h_i; s_t = f_dec(e_(t-1), s_(t-1), c_t).
cards.example: <bos> -> 'Jag' -> 'älskar' -> 'maskininlärning' -> <eos>. At t = 2 the weight alpha_2,2 on 'love' is by far the largest.
cards.say: Watch the attention move. For the second word the decoder focuses on love and writes älskar. Then it looks at machine and learning and writes maskininlärning. Finally it produces the end token.
covers: A4: Decoder update and step-by-step translation

cards.title: Reading an Attention Map
cards.text: Collect all weights into a grid and you get an attention map: one row per generated target word, one column per source word, brighter cells for stronger attention. Because the decoder reads a different sequence than its own, this is cross-attention. In translation maps the bright cells often run along a diagonal, since words tend to align in order. Where the two languages order words differently, the bright path bends, showing that attention learned the reordering. Nobody labelled these alignments; they emerge from the input and the trained parameters.
points: Rows = target tokens, columns = source tokens
Cell brightness = attention weight
Often near-diagonal alignment
Bends capture word reordering (non-monotonic alignment)
Patterns are computed dynamically, not hand-coded
cards.formula: A[t, i] = alpha_t,i (row t = output position, column i = input position).
cards.example: Figure 3(a) of Bahdanau et al. 2014: an English-French attention map with a mostly diagonal bright path that bends where word order differs.
cards.say: An attention map shows all weights as a heat grid. Target words are rows, source words are columns. In translation the bright cells often follow a diagonal, and they bend wherever the languages put words in a different order.

cards.title: What Attention Bought Us
cards.text: Attention delivered large accuracy gains in neural machine translation. It removes the bottleneck, because every output step builds its own content-dependent summary instead of relying on one memory vector, a bit like a human translator re-reading the relevant part of the sentence. It creates short, direct paths between distant positions, which also shortens gradient paths and eases vanishing gradients. And its weights act as a soft alignment learned without any alignment labels. Two caveats: attention maps help inspection but are not full explanations, and at this stage encoder and decoder are still recurrent.
points: Large accuracy gains over fixed-context seq2seq
Dynamic per-step context removes the bottleneck
Direct paths shorten information and gradient routes
Soft alignment learned without supervision
Maps aid inspection but do not fully explain predictions
Encoder and decoder are still RNNs
cards.say: Attention made translation much better. It removes the bottleneck, gives gradients short direct paths, and its weights reveal learned word alignments. But the encoder and decoder were still recurrent, which the Transformer will change next.
covers: A4: Advantages of the attention mechanism
B2: What attention adds to RNN seq2seq

lessons.title: Self-Attention: Queries, Keys, Values
lessons.goal: Understand how the Transformer replaces recurrence with self-attention, how queries, keys and values are projected and combined by scaled dot-product attention, and why several heads run in parallel.

cards.title: Attention Is All You Need
cards.text: In 2017 a NeurIPS paper by Vaswani and colleagues asked a bold question: what if we drop recurrence entirely and keep only attention? The resulting Transformer was built for machine translation with two stacks of N layers. The encoder reads the input with bidirectional self-attention; the decoder writes the output with causal self-attention that cannot see future tokens, and cross-attention lets decoder queries read the encoder outputs. With no recurrent chain, all known positions are processed in parallel, so training scales on modern hardware. Generation, however, still happens one token at a time.
points: NeurIPS 2017; about 200,000 citations by Sep 2025 and about 300,000 by Nov 2026
Ranked 7th most cited paper of the 21st century by Nature
Encoder: bidirectional self-attention; decoder: causal self-attention
Cross-attention links decoder queries to encoder outputs
Parallel over known positions; generation stays sequential
Basis of BERT, GPT and other foundation models
cards.example: Layer ingredients: positional encoding added to embeddings, (masked) multi-head attention, feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalization; already familiar parts are token IDs, shifted-right outputs, embeddings, final linear layer, softmax and greedy selection.
cards.say: In twenty seventeen, the paper Attention Is All You Need removed recurrence completely. The Transformer uses only attention, so all positions can be processed in parallel during training. It became the foundation of BERT, GPT and nearly every modern language model.
covers: A4: Attention Is All You Need and the Transformer overview
B3: Attention Is All You Need and the original encoder-decoder Transformer

cards.title: From Cross- to Self-Attention
cards.text: In the RNN translator, attention let the decoder read from a different sequence, the encoder's states; that is cross-attention. Self-attention turns the same trick inward: every position in a sequence gathers information from the other positions of that very sequence. It works in three moves: decide how relevant each other position is, convert relevance into weights, and aggregate the information. Because no hidden state is handed along a chain, all positions can be updated at the same time, and the result is a context-dependent vector for every token.
points: Recurrence: information flows through successive states
Attention: weighted direct access, computed for the current position
Cross-attention reads another sequence; self-attention reads its own
Three steps: relevance, weights, aggregation
No recurrent chain, so positions update in parallel
cards.formula: updated_i = sum over j of w_ij * info_j. w_ij = relevance weight of position j for position i.
cards.example: 'After walking along the river, they reached the bank.' - the updated vector for 'bank' draws heavily on 'river', pointing to a riverbank (illustrative weights).
cards.say: Cross-attention looks into another sequence. Self-attention looks inside the same sentence. Every word decides which other words matter, weights them, and mixes in their information. In the river example, bank borrows meaning from river.

cards.title: Query, Key, Value
cards.text: Attention becomes clearer if we split it into three roles. Think of a library. Your search request, say 'books about quantum computing', is the query. Each book's index card with keywords like 'physics', 'quantum', 'algorithms' is a key. The book's actual contents are the value. You compare the query with every key, normalize the matches with softmax, and read a weighted blend of the values. Bahdanau attention already fits this pattern: the decoder state supplies the query, encoder states supply keys and values. When queries come from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder, we call it cross-attention.
points: Query: what am I looking for?
Key: what can I be matched on?
Value: what information do I hand over?
Dot-product scores, softmax, weighted sum of values
Output = context vector passed onward
Decoder queries on encoder keys/values = cross-attention
cards.formula: q_t = s_(t-1) W_Q;  k_i = h_i W_K;  v_i = h_i W_V;  e_t,i = q_t . k_i;  alpha_t,i = softmax_i(e_t,i);  c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i v_i.
cards.example: Library: query 'Find books related to quantum computing'; keys = index-card keywords 'physics', 'quantum', 'algorithms', 'computing'; values = the books themselves.
cards.say: Think of a library. Your search request is the query, each index card is a key, and the book content is the value. Compare the query with all keys, turn the matches into weights, and read a weighted mix of the values.
covers: A4: Query, key, value: generalizing attention
B3: Queries, keys, values and their learned projections

cards.title: Learned Q, K, V Projections
cards.text: Where do queries, keys and values come from in self-attention? Each token's input vector x_i (embedding plus position, or the previous layer's output) is multiplied by three separate learned matrices. W_Q and W_K map into a shared comparison space, while W_V maps into a space tuned for carrying information. The matrices are shared by all positions inside one layer but differ between layers. Queries and keys must have the same size d_k so their dot product exists; values may use a different size d_v. In the original Transformer, d_model = 512 and d_k = d_v = 64 per head.
points: Three separate linear projections per layer
Shared across positions, different in every layer
W_Q, W_K: comparison space; W_V: information space
d_q = d_k required for the dot product; d_v may differ
Original model: d_model = 512, d_k = d_v = 64
Architecture fixes the shapes; training learns the values
cards.formula: q_i = x_i W_Q, k_i = x_i W_K, v_i = x_i W_V. x_i = row vector of size d_model; W_Q, W_K have shape d_model x d_k; W_V has shape d_model x d_v.
cards.example: Query of 'bank' vs keys of After, walking, river, reached, bank -> weights .08, .07, .65, .08, .12; the largest, .65, lands on 'river'.
cards.say: Each token vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to get its query, key and value. Queries and keys must have the same length so they can be compared. In the original model, the model width is five hundred twelve and each head uses sixty four.
covers: B3: Queries, keys, values and their learned projections
A4: Query, key, value: generalizing attention

cards.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
cards.text: Self-attention for one token runs in three steps. Match: dot the token's query with the key of every position it may see, then divide by the square root of d_k. Normalize: softmax turns these scores into non-negative weights summing to one. Aggregate: add up the value vectors using those weights, giving a new context-aware vector z_i. The division is what makes it 'scaled': dot products grow with dimension, and without scaling the softmax would become extremely peaked, nearly one-hot. Layers after the first simply use the previous layer's output in place of the embeddings.
points: Match: q_i . k_j / sqrt(d_k)
Normalize: softmax over accessible positions A(i)
Aggregate: weighted sum of value vectors
Scaling prevents overly sharp softmax
A(i) can later be restricted by masks
Later layers take the previous layer's output as input
cards.formula: s_ij = q_i . k_j / sqrt(d_k);  a_ij = exp(s_ij) / sum over m in A(i) of exp(s_im);  z_i = sum over j in A(i) of a_ij v_j. d_k = key/query dimension, A(i) = positions token i may attend to.
cards.example: With d_k = 64 the raw dot products are divided by sqrt(64) = 8 before the softmax.
cards.say: Scaled dot product attention has three steps. Compare the query with every key and divide by the square root of the key size. Turn the scores into weights with softmax. Then mix the value vectors with those weights.
covers: B3: Scaled dot-product attention and the attention matrix

cards.title: The Attention Matrix
cards.text: Doing this one token at a time would waste hardware. Instead, stack all n token vectors into a matrix X, compute Q, K and V with three matrix multiplications, and get every score at once from Q times K transposed. Each row of the resulting attention matrix belongs to one query, each column to one key, and every row sums to one after softmax. Multiplying that matrix by V yields all n output vectors in one go. This compact formula, softmax of QK-transposed over root d_k, times V, is the heart of every Transformer.
points: X stacks n token vectors (n x d_model)
Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V
Attention matrix: rows = queries, columns = keys
Each row sums to 1
Output has shape n x d_v, all positions in parallel
cards.formula: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. X is n x d_model, Q and K are n x d_k, V is n x d_v, output is n x d_v.
cards.example: Illustrative 4 x 4 weight matrix (rows = queries): [0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1]; [0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1]; [0.1, 0.2, 0.6, 0.1]; [0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5]. Each row sums to 1; row 3 means token 3 takes 60 percent of its new vector from its own value.
cards.say: By stacking all tokens into one matrix, attention for the whole sentence becomes a few matrix multiplications. The attention matrix has one row per query and one column per key, and every row adds up to one.
covers: B3: Scaled dot-product attention and the attention matrix

cards.title: Many Heads in Parallel
cards.text: One attention head compares tokens in just one learned similarity space, yet language holds many relations at once: syntax, meaning, who refers to whom. Multi-head attention therefore runs h heads side by side on the same input, each with its own W_Q, W_K and W_V and each producing its own attention pattern. Heads use a smaller size, d_k = d_v = d_model / h. Their outputs are concatenated along the feature axis and a learned matrix W_O mixes them back into a d_model-sized vector. In the original Transformer, 8 heads of 64 dimensions concatenate to exactly 512 features.
points: Single head = one projection set, one pattern per query
h heads, each with its own projections
d_k = d_v = d_model / h
Concatenate heads, then project with W_O
Original: d_model = 512, h = 8, 8 x 64 = 512
cards.formula: head_i = softmax(Q_i K_i^T / sqrt(d_k)) V_i with Q_i = X W_Q^(i), K_i = X W_K^(i), V_i = X W_V^(i);  MultiHead(X) = Concat(head_1 .. head_h) W_O. W_O has shape (h d_v) x d_model; output is n x d_model.
cards.example: d_model = 512, h = 8 -> d_k = d_v = 512 / 8 = 64 per head; concatenating 8 heads gives 8 x 64 = 512 features per position.
cards.say: Instead of one attention pattern, multi head attention runs several heads in parallel, each with its own projections. In the original model, eight heads of size sixty four are concatenated back to five hundred twelve features and mixed by an output matrix.

cards.title: What Do Heads Learn?
cards.text: Researchers who inspect trained models often find heads with recognizable habits. Some mostly attend to the previous token. Some link adjectives to their nouns, as in 'red car'. Others connect a verb with a distant subject for agreement, resolve 'he' to 'John', relate 'dog' to 'barked', or track order words like 'first', 'next' and 'finally'. It is like reading a sentence with several minds and pooling their notes. But beware: nobody assigns these roles. Heads learn their behaviour during training, can overlap, and many have no clean human interpretation.
points: Positional: attend to the preceding token
Local syntax: 'red' -> 'car'
Long-range: verb to distant subject
Coreference: 'he' -> 'John'; semantic roles: 'dog' -> 'barked'
Roles are learned, not predefined, and may overlap or be unclear
cards.example: Five example head roles: local syntax ('red car'), long-range agreement (verb and distant subject), coreference ('he' to 'John'), semantic roles ('dog' to 'barked'), positional patterns ('first', 'next', 'finally').
cards.say: Inspecting trained heads, we often see patterns: one looks at the previous word, another links he to John, another connects a verb to its subject. But these roles are learned, not assigned, and many heads have no clear meaning.

lessons.title: Position & Masking
lessons.goal: Understand why self-attention is blind to word order, how sinusoidal positional encodings fix this, and how a causal mask lets a decoder train on whole sequences in parallel while still generating one token at a time.

cards.title: Attention Is Order-Blind
cards.text: 'The dog chased the cat' and 'The cat chased the dog' use exactly the same tokens but describe opposite events. Self-attention, however, applies identical Q, K and V projections at every position and only compares vectors with each other. Shuffle the input tokens and the outputs are shuffled in exactly the same way; nothing else changes. Mathematicians call this permutation equivariance. Unlike an RNN, which reads in order, a Transformer processes all tokens in parallel and has no built-in sense of sequence. To understand order, distance and position-dependent relations, it needs extra positional information.
points: Same tokens, different order, different meaning
Same projections are used at every position
Unmasked self-attention is permutation-equivariant
Reordering inputs just reorders outputs
Positional information must be added explicitly
cards.formula: SelfAttn(P X) = P SelfAttn(X) for any permutation matrix P, when no positional information is present.
cards.example: 'The dog chased the cat' vs 'The cat chased the dog'; likewise 'The cat sat on the mat' vs 'The mat sat on the cat'.
cards.say: Self attention treats a sentence like a bag of vectors. If you shuffle the words, the outputs are just shuffled the same way. So the dog chased the cat and the cat chased the dog would look identical without position information.
covers: B3: Why self-attention needs positional information

cards.title: Sinusoidal Position Vectors
cards.text: The original Transformer gives every position its own d_model-sized vector and simply adds it to the token embedding before the first layer. These vectors are built from sine and cosine waves: even dimensions use sine, odd dimensions use cosine, and each pair of dimensions oscillates at its own frequency. Nothing here is learned; the encoding is a fixed, deterministic formula, so it costs no parameters and works for any position. After the addition, each input vector says both which token this is and where it sits.
points: PE(pos) has dimension d_model and is added to the embedding
Even dimensions: sine; odd dimensions: cosine
Each dimension pair has a different frequency
Deterministic, no learned parameters
The sum is the input to the first layer
cards.formula: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model));  PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model));  x_pos = e_token + PE(pos). pos = token position, i = frequency-pair index, d_model = embedding size.
cards.example: Position 0: every sine dimension is sin(0) = 0 and every cosine dimension is cos(0) = 1, so PE(0) = [0, 1, 0, 1, ...].
cards.say: The original Transformer adds a position vector to each token embedding. It is made from sine and cosine waves at many frequencies. Nothing is learned, it is a fixed formula, and the result tells the model both what the token is and where it is.
covers: B3: Sinusoidal positional encoding and its effect on embeddings

cards.title: Fast and Slow Waves
cards.text: Plot the encodings as a heatmap, with position on one axis and dimension on the other, and you see stripes. Low dimension indices hold high-frequency waves that flip quickly from one position to the next, giving fine, local position detail. High dimension indices hold slow waves that change only over long stretches, giving a coarse, global sense of where we are. Together they act a bit like the hands of a clock, combining fast and slow cycles to make every position unique. A neat side effect: similarity between two position vectors falls as their distance grows.
points: Heatmap: position vs dimension shows stripes
Low dimensions = high frequency = fine local position
High dimensions = low frequency = coarse global position
Multiple scales make each position distinguishable
Cosine similarity of PE vectors drops with distance
cards.formula: Wavelength grows with the dimension index: the frequency of pair i is 1 / 10000^(2i / d_model).
cards.example: Dimension pair i = 0 has frequency 1 and repeats roughly every 6.3 positions; the last pairs have frequencies near 1/10000 and barely change across a whole sentence.
cards.say: In a heatmap of positional encodings, the first dimensions wiggle quickly and track fine position, while later dimensions change slowly and track coarse position. Like fast and slow clock hands, together they give every position a unique pattern.
covers: B3: Sinusoidal positional encoding and its effect on embeddings

cards.title: Does Adding Position Hurt Meaning?
cards.text: Adding PE to an embedding nudges the vector: its direction and length both change. Is that a problem? Not really, for two reasons. First, embedding magnitudes are typically much larger than the positional ones, so the vector stays close to its semantic neighbourhood. Second, and more fundamentally, the change is intended. A Transformer needs a word's meaning at a particular place in context, not its isolated dictionary meaning. Each token becomes 'a word at a place', and the projections and later layers learn during training to untangle the 'what' from the 'where'. Preserving the original geometry exactly is not required.
points: x' = x + PE changes direction and magnitude
Embedding norms are usually much larger than PE norms
Change is intentional: token identity plus position
Model needs meaning-in-context, not dictionary meaning
Training learns to separate what from where
cards.formula: x' = x + PE(pos)
cards.say: Adding the position vector slightly shifts the embedding. That is fine, and actually intended. Each token becomes a word at a place, and the network learns during training to separate what the word is from where it appears.
covers: A4: Does positional encoding distort meaning?
B3: Sinusoidal positional encoding and its effect on embeddings

cards.title: Unmasked Encoder Attention
cards.text: In an encoder the whole input is known before processing starts, so there is no notion of a future to hide. Every token may attend to all tokens before and after it; this is bidirectional, unmasked attention. Look at 'The bank raised interest rates'. The row for 'bank' spreads its weight across later words like 'raised', 'interest' and 'rates', exactly the context that tells us this is a financial bank. Every row of the weight matrix still sums to one. This full view is perfect for understanding a sentence, but would be cheating for a model that has to predict the next word.
points: Encoder sees the entire input at once
Each token attends to past and future tokens
Row for 'bank' uses 'raised', 'interest', 'rates'
Every row sums to 1
Ideal for understanding, not for next-word prediction
cards.formula: softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V with no mask (all positions accessible).
cards.say: An encoder knows the whole sentence, so every word may look both backward and forward. In the bank raised interest rates, the word bank gets most of its context from the words that come after it.

cards.title: The Causal Mask
cards.text: A decoder is trained on whole target sentences at once, but it must never peek at words it will not have during generation. The fix is a mask matrix M added to the scores before softmax: zero where a token may look (itself and earlier positions) and minus infinity everywhere to the right. Since exp of minus infinity is zero, future weights vanish and the remaining weights are renormalized, so each row still sums to one. The weight matrix becomes lower-triangular. Compare the tables: 'The' can only attend to itself, while 'bank' splits 0.25 and 0.75 between 'The' and itself.
points: Mask entries: 0 if j <= i, minus infinity if j > i
Applied to scores before softmax
Weight matrix becomes lower-triangular
Rows still sum to 1 after renormalization
Preserves the autoregressive property
cards.formula: MaskedAttention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) + M) V;  M_ij = 0 for j <= i, minus infinity for j > i.
cards.example: Masked weights for 'The bank raised interest rates': The [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]; bank [0.25, 0.75, 0, 0, 0]; raised [0.12, 0.44, 0.44, 0, 0]; interest [0.07, 0.14, 0.43, 0.36, 0]; rates [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.40]. The last row equals the unmasked one because 'rates' has no future.
cards.say: A causal mask hides every future word by adding minus infinity to its score before softmax. Those weights become zero, so each word only attends to itself and earlier words. The weight matrix turns into a lower triangle.

cards.title: Train in Parallel, Generate in Sequence
cards.text: Masking unlocks a powerful asymmetry. During training the complete sentence is available, so one forward pass computes next-token predictions for every position at once, with the mask making sure each prediction only uses its prefix. During inference no future text exists yet: the model predicts one token, appends it, and runs again on the longer prefix. That is why Transformers train efficiently on GPUs yet still write text word by word. Parallel training does not make generation parallel.
points: Training: whole sequence known, mask hides the future
Training: logits for all positions in one pass
Inference: only the prefix exists
Inference: predict, append, repeat
Mask keeps training consistent with inference
cards.example: Training: 'The bank raised interest rates' -> next-token logits at all 5 positions in one pass. Inference: 'The' -> 'The bank' -> 'The bank raised' -> ...
cards.say: Thanks to the mask, training predicts the next word at every position in a single pass. But at inference time the future does not exist yet, so the model must generate one token, append it, and run again.
covers: B3: Parallel training vs. sequential generation

lessons.title: Inside a Transformer Layer
lessons.goal: Assemble a full Transformer: the layer's attention, feed-forward, residual and normalization parts, how layers stack and scale, the three model families, and how the final hidden state becomes next-token logits.

cards.title: Four Parts of a Layer
cards.text: Every Transformer layer combines four parts with distinct jobs. Multi-head self-attention moves information between token positions. The feed-forward network transforms each position on its own. Residual connections give information and gradients a direct path around each sublayer, and layer normalization keeps vector sizes in check. In the original design the order is attention, Add & Norm, FFN, Add & Norm. Zoom out and the full 'Attention Is All You Need' model appears: token IDs from the context window, embeddings plus positional encoding, encoder and decoder stacks (the decoder input shifted right by one), then a linear layer, softmax and a decoding rule such as greedy search.
points: Multi-head attention: exchange across positions
FFN: nonlinear per-position transformation
Residuals: direct path for information and gradients
LayerNorm: stable training
Original order: MHA -> Add & Norm -> FFN -> Add & Norm
Full model: embeddings + PE -> stacks -> linear -> softmax -> next token
cards.formula: H = LayerNorm(X + MHA(X));  Y = LayerNorm(H + FFN(H)). X = layer input, H = intermediate result, Y = layer output.
cards.say: A Transformer layer has four parts. Attention shares information between words, the feed forward network processes each word on its own, and residual connections plus layer normalization keep deep stacks stable. Wrapped with embeddings and an output layer, that is the whole Transformer.
covers: B3: Components of a Transformer layer
A5: Full 'Attention Is All You Need' Architecture

cards.title: The Feed-Forward Network
cards.text: After attention has mixed information across tokens, the feed-forward network works on each token vector separately. It widens the vector from d_model = 512 to d_ff = 2048 in the base model, applies a ReLU nonlinearity, and projects back to 512. The same FFN weights are used at every position within a layer, but each layer has its own. This adds nonlinear feature processing that linear projections alone cannot provide. FFNs are also heavy: in Transformer Base they hold about twice as many weights as the attention block, roughly two thirds of the layer.
points: Applied to each position independently
Expand 512 -> 2048, ReLU, project 2048 -> 512
Shared across positions, different per layer
Attention mixes tokens; FFN transforms features within a token
FFN is about 2/3 of a block's weights in Transformer Base
Wider FFN = more parameters and compute per token
cards.formula: FFN(x) = max(0, x W_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2. W_1 is d_model x d_ff, W_2 is d_ff x d_model. Weights per block: attention 4 d_model^2 (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O); FFN 2 d_model d_ff.
cards.example: Transformer Base: attention 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 (about 1.05M) weights; FFN 2 x 512 x 2048 = 2,097,152 (about 2.10M) weights. Counts exclude biases, normalization, embeddings and the output head.
cards.say: The feed forward network treats every token separately. It widens the vector from five hundred twelve to two thousand forty eight, applies a nonlinearity, and shrinks it back. It holds about two thirds of each layer's weights.
covers: B3: Feed-forward network and parameter count

cards.title: Residual Connections
cards.text: Very deep networks are notoriously hard to train: gradients fade as they travel backwards, early features get overwritten, and convergence is slow. The Transformer borrows a fix from ResNet in computer vision. Each sublayer, attention or FFN, is wrapped in a skip connection, so its output is added to its own input. The sublayer therefore only learns a correction or refinement instead of rebuilding the representation from scratch, the original information survives along the identity path, and gradients can flow straight back through the addition to early layers. Each layer adds understanding rather than starting over.
points: Problems: vanishing gradients, information loss, slow convergence
Output = input + sublayer(input)
Sublayer learns only an update
Identity path preserves information
Gradients flow directly to early layers
Idea comes from ResNet
cards.formula: y = x + Sublayer(x). x = input token vector, Sublayer = attention or FFN.
cards.say: A residual connection adds each sublayer's output back onto its input. The sublayer only needs to learn a small correction, the original information is never lost, and gradients have a highway back to the early layers.
covers: A4: Residual connections and layer normalization (Add & Norm)
B3: Residual connections and layer normalization (Add & Norm, Post-Norm)

cards.title: LayerNorm and Add & Norm
cards.text: Stacking many layers can make activations explode or shrink. Layer normalization rescales each token's vector on its own: compute the mean and variance across its d_model features, subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, then apply a learned scale gamma and shift beta so the model keeps its flexibility. Residual addition followed by LayerNorm forms the Add & Norm step. The original Transformer places it after every attention and every FFN sublayer, a layout called Post-Norm. Very deep models may still need further tricks, which the next lesson on modern variants covers.
points: Statistics per token, across its features
Normalize to zero mean, unit variance
Learned gamma (scale) and beta (shift)
Add & Norm = residual add, then LayerNorm
Original Transformer is Post-Norm: after MHA and FFN
Very deep models may need extra measures
cards.formula: mu = (1/d) sum_k z_k;  sigma^2 = (1/d) sum_k (z_k - mu)^2;  LayerNorm(z) = gamma (z - mu) / sqrt(sigma^2 + epsilon) + beta;  AddNorm(x) = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). d = d_model, epsilon = small constant.
cards.example: Token vector z = [2, 4, 6]: mu = 4, sigma^2 = 8/3, so normalized z is about [-1.22, 0, 1.22] before gamma and beta.
cards.say: Layer normalization rescales each token vector to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a learned scale and shift. Together with the residual addition it forms Add and Norm, which follows every attention and feed forward block in the original Transformer.
covers: A5: Layer Normalization and the Add & Norm Block
A4: Residual connections and layer normalization (Add & Norm)
B3: Residual connections and layer normalization (Add & Norm, Post-Norm)

cards.title: Stacking Layers into Depth
cards.text: A full model chains tokenizer, embeddings plus positional encoding, L identical blocks, and finally a linear layer with softmax. Each block takes the previous block's output and again applies attention, Add & Norm, FFN, Add & Norm. Repeating exchange and nonlinear processing lets later layers build on earlier features. A popular rough picture: early layers (about 1-4) handle token identity and local syntax, middle layers (about 5-20) semantic relations and coreference, deep layers (20+) whole-sentence meaning and multi-step reasoning. Treat this as intuition only: there is no fixed, universal division of labour between layers.
points: Pipeline: tokenizer -> embeddings + PE -> L blocks -> linear -> softmax
Block l takes the output of block l-1
Compositional: later layers reuse earlier features
Rough picture: early = local syntax, middle = relations, deep = meaning
No universal layer-by-layer assignment
cards.formula: H^(0) = Embed(x) + PE;  H^(l) = Block_l(H^(l-1)) for l = 1..L;  P = softmax(H^(L) W_out).
cards.example: 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired': the vector for 'it' starts as token plus position, gathers context from 'animal' and 'street', and deeper layers can support reading 'it' as the animal (illustrative).
cards.say: Stacking many identical layers lets the model refine its understanding step by step. Roughly, early layers handle local grammar and deeper layers handle meaning, for example figuring out that it refers to the animal. But there is no strict rule.

cards.title: Width, Depth and Size
cards.text: Two numbers largely set a Transformer's size. Width, d_model, is the length of every token vector flowing through the network. Depth, L (also written N), is the number of stacked blocks. The original model has L encoder plus L decoder blocks; decoder-only models have just L decoder blocks. Growing either dimension adds capacity, but also parameters and compute, and the counts explode quickly: from 65 million parameters in Transformer Base to 175 billion in GPT-3, which is both far wider and sixteen times deeper.
points: Width = d_model, the token vector size
Depth = L (or N), the number of blocks
Original: L encoder + L decoder blocks
Decoder-only: L decoder blocks
More width/depth = more capacity, parameters, compute
cards.formula: Width = d_model;  Depth = L (N in the original paper).
cards.example: Transformer Base: d_model = 512, L = 6+6, 65M parameters. Transformer Big: d_model = 1024, L = 6+6, 213M parameters. GPT-3: d_model = 12288, L = 96, 175B parameters.
cards.say: A Transformer's size is set mainly by its width, the vector length, and its depth, the number of layers. Transformer Base had sixty five million parameters, while GPT three, much wider and with ninety six layers, has one hundred seventy five billion.
covers: A4: Width and depth: model size parameters

cards.title: Three Transformer Families
cards.text: The original encoder-decoder design split into three families. Encoder-decoder models such as the original Transformer and T5 handle sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation and conditional generation. Encoder-only models such as BERT and RoBERTa use bidirectional attention to build rich representations for classification and extraction, for example deciding if a review is positive or negative. Decoder-only models generate text autoregressively and follow instructions; they power general-purpose language models: GPT-2, GPT-3 and GPT-4 historically, LLaMA, Mistral, and recently Llama 4, Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V3. Today's LLMs are overwhelmingly decoder-only.
points: Encoder-decoder: seq2seq, e.g. translation (Transformer, T5)
Encoder-only: understanding, e.g. sentiment (BERT, RoBERTa)
Decoder-only: autoregressive generation, instruction following
Decoder-only: GPT-2/3/4, LLaMA, Mistral, Llama 4, Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3
Modern LLMs are mostly decoder-only
cards.example: Type | Task | Models: Enc-Dec | text to text (NMT) | Transformer, T5; Enc-only | classification/extraction (sentiment) | BERT, RoBERTa; Dec-only | autoregressive generation | GPT family, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3.
cards.say: There are three Transformer families. Encoder decoder models translate, encoder only models like BERT understand and classify, and decoder only models like GPT, Llama and Qwen generate text. Almost all modern large language models are decoder only.
covers: A4: Three types of Transformer models

cards.title: From Hidden State to Logits
cards.text: The last layer outputs one contextual vector per position, and thanks to the causal mask the vector at position t summarizes only tokens 1 to t. A linear layer, the LM head, maps each d-dimensional vector to V logits, one per vocabulary entry. During training all positions are projected at once, giving a prediction target everywhere. During generation only the final position matters: for the prompt 'The cat sat on', the hidden state of 'on' already contains all available context, so only it is projected and passed through softmax. Earlier positions still contribute, but only through attention.
points: One contextual hidden state per position
Causal: state t sees tokens 1..t
LM head: linear map from d to V logits
Training: logits for all positions in parallel
Generation: only the last position's state is projected
cards.formula: z_t = h_t W_LM (+ b), W_LM is d x V;  Z = H W_LM for all positions (H is n x d);  P(x_(n+1) | x_1..x_n) = softmax(h_n W_LM).
cards.example: Prompt 'The cat sat on': only the state of 'on' is projected to logits; 'The', 'cat' and 'sat' are not needed for this generation step.
cards.say: The LM head is a linear layer that turns each final hidden state into one score per vocabulary token. When generating, only the last position matters. For the cat sat on, only the vector for on is projected to predict the next word.
covers: B4: From Hidden States to Vocabulary Logits (LM Head)
B4: Which Hidden State Predicts the Next Token?
A5: Output Projection and Weight Tying

cards.title: Weight Tying
cards.text: A language model holds two huge vocabulary matrices: the input embedding table E (V x d) and the output projection (d x V). Weight tying reuses the transposed embedding matrix as the output projection, so only one matrix is learned. That halves the parameters spent on these two parts, which for large vocabularies means hundreds of millions of weights. It also tends to help generalization, because the same 'dictionary' is used to read tokens in and write tokens out, giving a pleasing symmetry between encoding and decoding.
points: Without tying: two independent V x d sized matrices
With tying: W_out = E transposed
Halves embedding plus projection parameters
Shared token representation can improve generalization
Same dictionary for input and output
cards.formula: W_LM = E^T, E is V x d. Parameters: 2 V d without tying vs V d with tying.
cards.example: 409.6M embedding plus projection weights without tying vs 204.8M with tying - consistent with, for example, V = 50,000 and d = 4,096, since 50,000 x 4,096 = 204.8M per matrix.
cards.say: Weight tying reuses the input embedding table as the output layer, just transposed. With a large vocabulary that saves hundreds of millions of parameters, for example cutting about four hundred ten million weights down to about two hundred five million.
covers: B4: Weight Tying: Sharing Input and Output Embeddings
A5: Output Projection and Weight Tying

cards.title: Why Transformers Won
cards.text: RNNs read tokens one by one, squeeze history into a single hidden state and suffer vanishing gradients. Transformers process known positions in parallel, connect every position directly to every other, and use residuals, LayerNorm and multi-head attention to train very deep stacks. Within about two years of 2017 they became the default for language, vision, speech and multimodal systems. Five principles summarize the design: contextual exchange through attention, position awareness, complementary attention and FFN, deep composition, and parallel computation, while generation stays sequential. To see it all in real code, nanoGPT implements a GPT in a few hundred readable lines.
points: Parallel processing instead of sequential recurrence
Direct links handle long-range dependencies; no single-state bottleneck
Residuals + LayerNorm + MHA make deep models trainable
Default across modalities within about 2 years of 2017
Five principles: exchange, position, complementarity, depth, parallelism
Transformer = a family of designs, leading to modern variants
cards.example: nanoGPT: a minimal educational GPT in a few hundred lines (github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT); an interactive 3D walkthrough of a nanoGPT-sized model is at bbycroft.net/llm.
cards.say: Transformers replaced recurrent networks because they train in parallel, connect all words directly, and stay stable when very deep. Within two years they took over language, vision and speech. Projects like nano GPT show the whole design in a few hundred lines of code.
covers: B4: Transformer Architecture: Key Design Principles
A5: Why Transformers Replaced RNN Seq2Seq

lessons.title: Modern Transformer Variants
lessons.goal: Explain which components today's LLMs swap into the original Transformer block (Pre-Norm, RMSNorm, RoPE, MQA/GQA, SwiGLU) and why each change helps.

cards.title: Where the Norm Sits: Post-LN vs Pre-LN
cards.text: The 2017 Transformer normalized after the residual addition (Post-LN). That puts LayerNorm right on the skip path: even if a sublayer outputs zero, the block returns LN(x) instead of x, and every backward gradient is rescaled and mixed by each norm it passes. Early in training, gradients near the output can be large, so Post-LN needs warm-up and careful learning rates, and stacks deeper than about 24 layers get hard to train. Pre-LN normalizes only the sublayer's input and adds its output to an untouched residual stream. The skip path becomes a clean identity, which is why 100+ layer models like GPT-3 and LLaMA train stably.
points: Post-LN: y = LN(x + F(x)), the norm sits on the residual path
Post-LN cannot express the identity and distorts gradients block by block
Post-LN usually needs learning-rate warm-up; ~24 layers is a practical limit without tricks
Pre-LN: y = x + F(LN(x)), the skip path stays an identity with a direct gradient route
Pre-LN tolerates larger learning rates and enables 100+ layers
Pre-LN stacks add one final norm before the LM head
cards.formula: Post-LN: y = LayerNorm(x + F(x)); Pre-LN: y = x + F(LayerNorm(x)). x = block input (residual stream), F = sublayer (attention or FFN).
cards.example: Set the sublayer output F to zero: Post-LN returns LayerNorm(x), a changed vector; Pre-LN returns exactly x. A gradient travelling back through 48 blocks is reshaped 48 times in Post-LN but rides the identity line in Pre-LN.
cards.say: Moving one box changes everything. If normalization sits after the residual addition, gradients get reshaped in every block. Put it before the sublayer instead, and the skip connection becomes a clean highway, so very deep models train smoothly.

cards.title: RMSNorm: Normalization Without the Mean
cards.text: LayerNorm subtracts each token's mean and divides by its standard deviation. RMSNorm skips the centering step: it divides the token vector by the root mean square of its features, then multiplies by a learned per-feature weight gamma. A tiny epsilon keeps the division safe when the vector is close to zero. Each token is normalized on its own with a single scale factor. Dropping the mean saves computation, although the real speedup depends on hardware and kernels, while stability and gradient flow stay good. Because only the normalization operation changes, RMSNorm drops straight into a Pre-Norm block, and most modern LLMs use it.
points: No mean subtraction and no bias, only division by the RMS
Learned per-feature weight gamma, applied element-wise
Epsilon prevents division by a value near zero
Cheaper than LayerNorm; actual speedup is implementation dependent
Drop-in replacement inside Pre-Norm blocks; standard in modern LLMs
cards.formula: RMS(x) = sqrt((1/d) * sum_i x_i^2 + eps); RMSNorm(x) = (x / RMS(x)) ⊙ gamma. d = hidden size, gamma = learned feature weights, ⊙ = element-wise product.
cards.example: Shift every entry of a vector by the same constant: LayerNorm's output does not change because it re-centers, but RMSNorm's output does, since it only rescales.
cards.say: RMSNorm is LayerNorm on a diet. It forgets about the mean and simply divides each token vector by its root mean square, then applies a learned weight. Less work, the same stability, and it slots right into a pre norm block.

cards.title: RoPE: Position by Rotation
cards.text: Instead of adding a position vector to the embeddings, Rotary Position Embeddings rotate the query and key vectors. Their features are split into pairs, and each pair is turned like a 2D arrow by an angle proportional to the token's position, with every pair spinning at its own frequency. When a query at position m meets a key at position n, the rotations combine into a single rotation by n minus m, so the attention score depends on content plus relative distance. Rotations keep vector lengths, values are left alone, and no position table is stored. RoPE generalizes better than sinusoidal encodings, though very long contexts still need position scaling and extra training.
points: Rotates Q and K; nothing is added to the embeddings
Feature pairs rotate at different frequencies; the angle grows with position
Score depends on the relative offset n - m plus content
Length-preserving, values unchanged, no learned position table
Better length generalization than sinusoidal PE; standard in decoder-only LLMs
Longer contexts usually need position scaling plus further training
cards.formula: q'_m = R_m q_m, k'_n = R_n k_n; (R_m q_m)^T (R_n k_n) = q_m^T R_(n-m) k_n. R_m = block-diagonal matrix of 2x2 rotations by angle m * theta_i, theta_i = base^(-2i/d) with base usually 10000, d = head dimension.
cards.example: Put a query at position 5 and a key at position 3, then shift both by 100 to positions 105 and 103: the offset is still 2, so the rotated dot product is unchanged.
cards.say: RoPE turns position into rotation. Queries and keys spin by an angle that grows with their position. When two of them meet, only the difference in their angles matters, so attention naturally sees how far apart two tokens are.

cards.title: Multi-Query Attention: One Shared K/V
cards.text: In standard multi-head attention every head owns its query, key and value projections, so generation must store keys and values for every head. Multi-Query Attention keeps one query projection per head but lets all heads share a single key projection and a single value projection. Since keys and values are exactly what gets cached while generating, the cache shrinks by a factor equal to the number of heads. That matters for long windows of 32k, 128k or even 1M tokens and for on-device models. Less data moves through memory, so decoding gets faster, and there are fewer K/V parameters. The price: heads lose diversity, which can hurt quality, especially in smaller models.
points: Queries: one projection per head
Keys and values: one projection shared by all heads
KV cache shrinks by the number of heads h
Faster decoding through less memory movement; fewer K/V parameters
Useful for 32k, 128k, 1M-token contexts and edge devices
Downside: less head diversity, possible quality drop
cards.formula: Number of KV heads: MHA = h, MQA = 1 (h = number of query heads).
cards.example: 8 query heads all read from one shared K/V block, so the stored keys and values are 8 times smaller than with MHA. In the 32-head model of lesson 3.7 the cache drops 32-fold, from 16 GiB to 512 MiB at 32,768 tokens.
cards.say: Multi query attention lets every head ask its own question, but all heads look things up in one shared set of keys and values. The cache becomes tiny and decoding speeds up, though the heads become less diverse.

cards.title: Grouped-Query Attention: The Sweet Spot
cards.text: Grouped-Query Attention sits between the two extremes. The query heads are divided into G groups, and each group shares one key head and one value head. With G groups the KV cache is G/h of the MHA size, because cache memory scales linearly with the number of KV heads. GQA reaches almost MQA-level speed and memory, while the several K/V groups keep much of the flexibility that MQA throws away, which especially helps small and mid-sized models. MHA gives the best quality but is slow and memory hungry; MQA is fastest but riskier. Because G is a tunable knob, GQA became the standard choice in modern LLMs.
points: Queries: one per head; keys/values: one per group
KV heads: MHA = h, GQA = G with 1 < G < h, MQA = 1
KV cache scales linearly with the number of KV heads
Near-MQA speed, much smaller memory than MHA
Quality close to MHA, better than MQA
Eases the memory-bandwidth bottleneck during decoding
cards.formula: KV cache size is proportional to n_kv; GQA uses n_kv = G, so cache(GQA) = (G / h) * cache(MHA).
cards.example: 32 query heads with 8 KV groups: each group of 4 query heads shares one K/V pair, so the cache is 8/32 = 1/4 of MHA, for example 4 GiB instead of 16 GiB at 32,768 tokens.
cards.say: Grouped query attention is the compromise everyone adopted. Query heads form small teams, and each team shares one key and value head. You get most of the memory savings of multi query attention while keeping quality close to full multi head attention.
covers: A5: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and MHA/GQA/MQA Comparison
B4: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and MHA/GQA/MQA Comparison

cards.title: Gates and the Gated Linear Unit
cards.text: The original FFN uses ReLU, which behaves like a light switch: positive values pass unchanged, everything else becomes zero, and there is no setting in between. A gate works more like a valve. A value near 1 lets information through, near 0 blocks it, and anything in between lets part of it flow. A Gated Linear Unit computes two projections of the same input: a main projection carrying the values and a gating projection squashed by a sigmoid. The two are multiplied element by element, and an output projection maps back to model width. Because the sigmoid lives between 0 and 1, this gate is a dimmer that can only weaken signals.
points: ReLU = hard on/off switch, max(0, x)
Gate = valve between 0 (block) and 1 (pass)
GLU = main projection ⊙ sigmoid(gating projection)
An output projection returns to the model dimension
Sigmoid saturates, so the gate can only attenuate
GLU originates from gated convolutional language models
cards.formula: GLU(x) = (x W) ⊙ sigma(x V); FFN_GLU(x) = ((x W) ⊙ sigma(x V)) W_2. W = main projection, V = gating projection, sigma = sigmoid, W_2 = output projection, ⊙ = element-wise product.
cards.say: ReLU is a light switch, either on or off. A gate is a dimmer. In a gated linear unit one projection carries the content, and a second projection, squeezed through a sigmoid, decides how much of each feature passes through.

cards.title: SwiGLU: A Gate That Can Amplify
cards.text: SwiGLU keeps the GLU recipe but swaps the sigmoid gate for SiLU, also called Swish, which is x times sigmoid of x. SiLU is bounded below but unbounded above, so the gate can now boost features as well as dampen them. Multiplying gate and values creates rich feature interactions that tend to be more parameter-efficient. Its derivative is smooth everywhere, avoiding ReLU's hard zeroing and the harsh saturation of a sigmoid, although it cannot guarantee that every unit stays active. SwiGLU gives measurable quality gains in language modelling, replaces the ReLU FFN without other changes, and appears in most modern LLM families.
points: SwiGLU = GLU with a SiLU/Swish gate
SiLU(x) = x * sigma(x): bounded below, unbounded above
Can both suppress and amplify features
Smooth gradients, no harsh saturation, no hard zeroing
Better quality per parameter; drop-in for the ReLU FFN
Used in most modern LLM families
cards.formula: SiLU(x) = x * sigma(x); SwiGLU_FFN(x) = (SiLU(x W_gate) ⊙ (x W_up)) W_down. W_gate = gate projection, W_up = value (feature) projection, W_down = output projection.
cards.example: A feature whose gate input is large and positive gets a SiLU value above 1 and is amplified; one with a strongly negative gate input gets a value near 0 and is suppressed. A sigmoid gate could only ever give values below 1.
cards.say: SwiGLU replaces the sigmoid gate with a smoother function called SiLU. Because it is not capped at one, the gate can turn features up as well as down. It trains smoothly and is the feed forward layer inside most current language models.

cards.title: Assembling a Modern Decoder Block
cards.text: Put the upgrades together and you get the block inside models like Qwen3 and LLaMA. The skeleton is still attention followed by an FFN, each wrapped in a residual connection. First comes RMSNorm, then causal grouped-query attention with RoPE applied to queries and keys, then an output projection whose result is added back to the residual stream. Next comes another RMSNorm, a SwiGLU FFN that transforms each token independently, and a second residual add. To trace a decoder-only model line by line, the compact educational nanoGPT repository, a few hundred readable lines, and its 3D visualisation make great companions.
points: Pre-RMSNorm keeps the direct residual path
RoPE rotates Q and K inside causal attention
GQA: groups of query heads share K/V heads
SwiGLU FFN transforms each token independently
Same attention-then-FFN skeleton with modern parts (e.g. Qwen3)
nanoGPT: a minimal GPT in a few hundred lines; 3D view at bbycroft.net/llm
cards.formula: h = x + GQA_RoPE(RMSNorm(x)); y = h + SwiGLU(RMSNorm(h)). x = block input, h = stream after attention, y = block output.
cards.example: Swap list from original to modern: Post-LayerNorm to Pre-RMSNorm, sinusoidal PE to RoPE, MHA to GQA, ReLU FFN to SwiGLU FFN. Code walkthrough: github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT; visual walkthrough: bbycroft.net/llm.
cards.say: Here is the modern recipe. Normalize with RMSNorm, attend with grouped query attention using rotary positions, add back to the residual stream, normalize again, run a SwiGLU feed forward layer, and add again. Same skeleton, better parts.
covers: B4: A Modern Decoder Block: Pre-RMSNorm + RoPE + GQA + SwiGLU

lessons.title: The KV Cache
lessons.goal: Explain why generation caches keys and values, how prefill and decode differ, and how to size and shrink the KV cache.

cards.title: Why Cache Keys and Values?
cards.text: During generation the model predicts each new token from the prompt plus everything generated so far. Without help it would push this growing prefix through every layer at every step, repeating almost all the work. Causal masking rescues us: earlier tokens never look at later ones, so appending a token leaves their keys and values unchanged. Store those keys and values per attention layer in a KV cache, and each step only processes the single new position, whose query attends to the cached entries plus itself. The trade is simple: a little more memory buys far less computation.
points: Each step conditions on the prompt plus previously generated tokens
Without a cache the whole prefix is recomputed every step
Causal masking keeps earlier keys and values unchanged
The KV cache stores keys and values per attention layer
Each step processes only the new position
Trade-off: more memory, much less compute
cards.example: Generating 'The capital of France is' then ' Paris' then '.' then '<EOS>': without a cache the full prefix is fed through every layer again at each of the three steps.
cards.say: Without a cache the model would reprocess the whole growing prompt at every step. But tokens only look backwards, so the older keys and values never change. We store them, and each step just handles the newest token.
covers: B4: Why a KV Cache? Recomputing the Growing Prefix

cards.title: Prefill and Decode
cards.text: Inference runs in two phases. In prefill the entire prompt is processed once and in parallel within each layer under the causal mask, building the initial KV cache for every layer; the last prompt position's logits give the first output token. In decode each step feeds only the newest token: it computes that token's query, key and value, appends the new key and value to the cache, and the new query attends to all cached positions plus itself. Earlier queries and attention outputs are never recomputed. With RoPE, queries and keys are rotated first, so the rotated keys are what get cached.
points: Prefill: whole prompt in parallel, builds the initial cache per layer
Prefill logits of the last prompt position select the first token
Decode: one new position per step
Decode appends the new key and value to the cache
The new query attends to all earlier positions and itself
With RoPE, the already-rotated keys are cached
cards.formula: Prefill: Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V for all prompt rows; A = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) + M) V with causal mask M. Decode: q_t = x_t W_Q, k_t = x_t W_K, v_t = x_t W_V; append k_t, v_t to K, V; a_t = softmax(q_t K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
cards.say: Think of two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt at once to warm up the cache and produce the first token. Decode then adds one token at a time, reusing everything already stored. That is why the first token feels slower than the rest.

cards.title: Where the Latency Goes
cards.text: Total response time is the prefill time plus one decode step for every further output token. Prefill depends on prompt length, so a long prompt with a short answer can be dominated by prefill. A long answer is dominated instead by the many sequential decode steps, because each token has to wait for the previous one. The practical rule: speeding up per-token decoding pays off most for long responses, while making prefill faster helps short answers. Two metrics capture this, time to first token and time per output token.
points: Prefill runs once and produces the first token
Every later token needs one decode step
Latency depends on both prompt length and output length
Long prompt with short answer: prefill may dominate
Long answer: decode dominates
Faster decoding benefits long responses most
cards.formula: T_total ~= TTFT + (N - 1) * TPOT. TTFT = time to first token, TPOT = average time per output token, N = generated response length.
cards.say: Total latency is the first token plus every token after it. A long prompt with a short answer is dominated by prefill. A long answer is dominated by decode, where each token waits for the last. So faster decoding helps long responses most.

cards.title: Sizing the KV Cache
cards.text: The cache stores, per sequence, per layer and per cached position, one key vector and one value vector for every KV head. Its size is 2 times batch size times cached positions times layers times KV heads times head dimension times bytes per element. Take a model with 32 layers, 32 query heads and head dimension 128 in FP16. Full multi-head attention with 32 KV heads needs 4 GiB at 8,192 tokens and 16 GiB at 32,768. Grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads needs a quarter of that, and multi-query with 1 KV head just a thirty-second: 128 MiB and 512 MiB.
points: Per token, per layer, per sequence: 2 * n_kv * d_head * bytes
Total grows linearly with batch size, positions, layers, KV heads and bytes
Example model: 32 layers, 32 query heads, head dimension 128, FP16
MHA: 4 GiB at 8,192 positions, 16 GiB at 32,768
GQA (8 KV heads): 1 GiB at 8,192, 4 GiB at 32,768
MQA (1 KV head): 128 MiB at 8,192, 512 MiB at 32,768
cards.formula: M = 2 * B * T * L * n_kv * d_head * b. B = batch size, T = cached positions, L = layers, n_kv = KV heads, d_head = head dimension, b = bytes per element; the 2 counts keys and values.
cards.example: GQA at full context: 2 * 1 * 32,768 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 bytes = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB. Per token for GQA: 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB.
cards.say: The cache size is easy to estimate. Two, for keys and values, times batch, positions, layers, KV heads, head size and bytes. In our example model full attention needs sixteen gigabytes at full context. Grouped query attention cuts that to a quarter, and multi query to half a gigabyte.
covers: B4: KV Cache Memory Model and Worked Example

cards.title: Capacity, Quantization and Bandwidth
