cards.text: With everything else fixed, the cache grows with cached positions, concurrent sequences, attention layers, KV heads and bytes per element. A common surprise: quantizing the model weights does not shrink the KV cache at all, because the cache holds activations, not parameters. Only KV-cache quantization reduces the bytes per element, and parameter count alone never determines cache size. As context and users grow, the cache can exhaust memory and trigger out-of-memory errors. Because every decode step reads the cached keys and values, long contexts and many concurrent sequences turn decoding into a memory-bandwidth bottleneck. Fitting the weights is not the same as fitting the workload.
points: Drivers: positions, concurrent sequences, layers, KV heads, bytes per element
Weight quantization alone does not shrink the KV cache
KV-cache quantization reduces bytes per cached element
Parameter count does not determine cache size
A growing cache can cause out-of-memory errors
Every decode step reads the cache, so bandwidth can bottleneck
cards.formula: M is proportional to B * T * L * n_kv * d_head * b.
cards.say: Here is a trap. Quantizing the weights does not shrink the cache, because the cache stores activations, not parameters. Only quantizing the cache itself helps. And since every step reads the cache, long contexts and many users turn decoding into a memory bandwidth problem.
covers: B4: KV Cache Memory Implications: Capacity, Quantization, Bandwidth

cards.title: Batching and Memory Bandwidth
cards.text: A server can batch requests from several users so that each decode step processes one new position per sequence on the same model instance. The weights load once and are shared, which raises total tokens per second across all users. Individual responses do not automatically get faster, and every sequence keeps its own KV cache, so bigger batches need more cache memory. Each step still has to read the weights plus the required cached keys and values; with only a few requests this data movement takes longer than the arithmetic, which is why decode is bandwidth-limited. Batching trades per-user latency for overall throughput.
points: Batching groups several users' sequences into one step
Each decode step processes one new position per sequence
Shared weights raise total throughput
Individual latency is not automatically better
Every sequence keeps its own KV cache
Small batches: memory bandwidth, not compute, limits speed
cards.example: Users A, B and C share one set of model weights; each keeps its own KV cache for its own context, and each decode step processes one position per user.
cards.say: Serving many users, the server groups their requests into a batch and shares the weights. Total throughput rises, but each user still keeps their own cache, and with few requests the bottleneck is moving memory, not doing maths.
covers: B4: Batching and Memory Bandwidth in Decode

cards.title: Levers to Shrink the Cache
cards.text: You can shrink the cache along three axes. Cache fewer positions by using shorter context, truncating history or retrieving only selected passages, but you may drop relevant information. Use fewer KV heads through grouped-query or multi-query attention, though that is an architectural choice fixed at design time, not a runtime switch. Use sliding-window attention so local layers keep only their window, at the cost of direct access to older tokens, since arbitrary eviction under full attention changes the computation. Finally, KV-cache quantization stores keys and values in fewer bits, trading numerical error and overhead for memory.
points: Three axes: positions, KV heads, bytes per element
Shorter context: truncate or retrieve, but may omit relevant info
Fewer KV heads: GQA or MQA, an architectural choice
Sliding-window attention keeps only the local window
Arbitrary eviction under full attention changes results
KV-cache quantization: fewer bits, possible quality and speed cost
cards.say: You can shrink the cache in three ways. Keep fewer positions by shortening context. Use fewer key and value heads with grouped or multi query attention. Or store each entry in fewer bits. Each lever has a cost, usually lost information or some numerical error.
covers: B4: Levers for Reducing KV-Cache Memory

lessons.title: Mixture of Experts
lessons.goal: Explain how a sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer routes each token to a few expert networks, how the router and experts are trained, and what total versus active parameters mean.

cards.title: More Capacity, Same Compute
cards.text: In a dense Transformer the same feed-forward network processes every token in every layer. Making that network's intermediate layer wider adds parameters, but it also enlarges the matrix multiplications, so compute per token grows in step. Four times wider means roughly four times the parameters and four times the per-token cost. The engineering question behind mixture of experts is whether we can add trainable parameters without paying proportionally more computation, so that we get better quality for a fixed training budget.
points: A dense FFN processes every token with the same weights
Widening the intermediate layer adds parameters
In a dense layer, more parameters means proportionally more compute per token
Goal: more parameters without proportionate per-token compute
Aim: better quality for a fixed training-compute budget
cards.formula: Dense FFN cost per token grows with d_model * d_ff; widening d_ff raises parameters and FLOPs together.
cards.example: Original FFN width: 1x parameters and 1x compute per token. Four times wider: about 4x parameters and about 4x compute per token.
cards.say: A dense model runs the same big feed forward layer for every token. Widen it and you add parameters, but you also add work in lock step. Mixture of experts asks a sharp question: can we add parameters without adding proportional compute?
covers: B4: Motivation: More Capacity Without More Compute

cards.title: Conditional Computation: Dense vs Sparse
cards.text: Conditional computation lets a network hold more parameters than it uses for any single input, by choosing which components to run based on that input. In dense execution every input runs the whole computation, so extra parameters raise the cost for everyone. In sparse conditional execution each input uses only a selected subset, so the extra components add capacity without all being evaluated. Here sparse means skipping whole components; the weight matrices inside a selected component can still be fully dense.
points: A network can hold more parameters than it uses per input
The input decides which components execute
Dense: the same full computation for all inputs
Sparse: each input uses a selected subset
Sparse activation skips components; their matrices stay dense
Some designs select one component, others several
cards.example: Input 1 routes to Component A, Input 2 to Component C, Input 3 to Component B: only one component is active per input, while all three are stored.
cards.say: Dense means every input pays for everything. Sparse means each input only visits the parts it needs. The trick is that the network still stores all of it, so capacity grows while the work per input stays small.
covers: B4: Conditional Computation and Sparse Activation

cards.title: Experts, Router, Combination
cards.text: A sparse MoE layer replaces the dense FFN sublayer of a Transformer block with several feed-forward networks, called experts, plus a learned router. For each token the router looks at that token's current representation, selects some experts, and only those experts run; their outputs are then combined into one output vector. Everything else stays exactly the same: attention, normalization, residual connections, embeddings and the output head are untouched. Each MoE layer has its own router and experts, tokens routed to the same expert reuse its weights, and MoE can replace some or all of the FFN sublayers.
points: An MoE layer is several expert FFNs plus a learned router
It replaces only the dense FFN sublayer
The router picks experts per token from its representation
Unselected experts are not evaluated for that token
Selected outputs are combined into one vector
Attention, normalization, residuals, embeddings and the head are unchanged
cards.example: A token representation enters the router, which selects Expert 1 and Expert 3 of 3; Expert 2 is not selected, and the two outputs are combined into one vector.
cards.say: Take the feed forward layer and split it into a team of experts. A small router reads each token and sends it to a couple of them. The rest of the block, the attention and the connections, are completely untouched.
covers: B4: Mixture of Experts Layer: Experts, Router, Combination

cards.title: Top-k Routing per Token and per Layer
cards.text: The router scores every expert from a token's current representation, and top-k routing keeps the k highest-scoring experts. In the running example k equals 2 of 4 experts: the tokens 'The', 'cat' and 'sleeps' each use two experts, experts 1 and 3 each serve two tokens and reuse their weights, and across the whole sequence all four experts see at least one token. Selection happens independently per token and per layer, because each later MoE layer routes again using representations that earlier layers have already updated.
points: The router scores every expert per token
Top-k selects the k highest scores
Example: k equals 2 of 4 experts
Experts are shared across the tokens that pick them
All experts can be used across a sequence
Routing repeats in every MoE layer
cards.example: Tokens 'The', 'cat' and 'sleeps' with k = 2 of 4 experts: experts 1 and 3 each process two tokens, so every token uses two experts and all four experts are used across the sequence.
cards.say: For each token the router scores all the experts and keeps the best few. Two tokens might share an expert, and over a sentence every expert can get some work. Crucially, this choice is repeated again in every MoE layer.
covers: B4: Top-k Routing per Token and per Layer

cards.title: Inside the Router
cards.text: The router multiplies the token representation by a learned router matrix, giving one score per expert. TopKIndices returns the indices of the k largest scores; these decide which experts run, but the raw scores are not yet the combination weights. A softmax is applied over only the selected scores to get positive weights that sum to one, which fix how strongly each expert's output contributes. With scores 2.0, 0.2, 1.0 and -0.5 and k equal to 2, experts 1 and 3 are selected; softmax over 2.0 and 1.0 gives about 0.73 and 0.27. Experts 2 and 4 are excluded.
points: Scores s = x W_r, one per expert
TopKIndices picks the k largest scores
Selection decides which experts run
Softmax over the selected scores gives the combination weights
The weights are positive and sum to one
Unselected experts are excluded from the normalization
cards.formula: s = x W_r, with x the token representation, W_r the router matrix and s one score per expert. S = top-k indices of s; g_i = exp(s_i) / sum over selected j of exp(s_j).
cards.example: Scores expert 1 = 2.0, expert 2 = 0.2, expert 3 = 1.0, expert 4 = -0.5. exp(2.0) = 7.39 and exp(1.0) = 2.72, sum 10.11, so the weights are 7.39/10.11 = 0.73 for expert 1 and 2.72/10.11 = 0.27 for expert 3.
cards.say: The router gives every expert a score. We keep the top few, then run a softmax over just those scores to turn them into weights that add up to one. Here the top two scores give weights of about zero point seven three and zero point two seven.
covers: B4: Inside the Router: Scores, Selection and Softmax Weights

cards.title: Combining Expert Outputs
cards.text: Each selected expert is a separate feed-forward network that receives the same token representation and transforms it with its own weights, so different experts produce different outputs. Each expert output vector is multiplied by its combination weight, and the weighted vectors are summed into a single MoE output that keeps the model dimension of the input. Unselected experts are never evaluated at all. In the example the output is 0.73 times Expert 1's result plus 0.27 times Expert 3's, and experts 2 and 4 are simply not computed.
points: The same input goes to every selected expert
Different FFN weights give different outputs
Scale each output by its combination weight
Sum them into one vector of the model dimension
Unselected experts are never computed
cards.formula: y = sum over selected experts i of g_i * E_i(x), where E_i is expert FFN i, g_i is its combination weight and x is the token representation.
cards.example: y = 0.73 * Expert 1(x) + 0.27 * Expert 3(x); experts 2 and 4 are not evaluated.
cards.say: Every chosen expert reads the same token but transforms it differently. We scale each result by its weight and add them up into one vector. The experts that were not chosen never even run.
covers: B4: Computing and Combining Expert Outputs

cards.title: How Router and Experts Learn
cards.text: Router and experts are trained jointly from the ordinary next-token prediction loss, with no predefined topic labels telling experts what to specialise in. For a given token, gradients reach the selected experts through their output vectors and reach the router through the softmax combination weights. No gradient flows through the discrete top-k selection, and unselected experts get no gradient from that token, though other tokens may select them. As router weights change, later steps may pick different experts, so expert specialisation emerges from learning rather than being assigned by hand.
points: Joint training from the next-token prediction loss
No topic labels are given to the experts
Selected experts get gradients through their outputs
The router gets gradients through the softmax weights
No gradient flows through the discrete top-k selection
Specialisation is learned, not assigned
cards.formula: dL/dW_r flows through the softmax weights g_i over the selected scores; the top-k index selection is non-differentiable.
cards.example: For one token, experts 1 and 3 receive gradients through their output vectors, experts 2 and 4 receive none, and the router receives gradients through the combination weights.
cards.say: Nobody tells the experts what to be good at. They learn from the ordinary next-token loss. The chosen experts get gradients from their outputs, the router gets gradients from the weights, and specialisation just emerges.
covers: B4: How Router and Experts Learn

cards.title: Total vs. Active Parameters
cards.text: MoE models distinguish total parameters, everything that is stored including all experts, from active parameters, the subset that one token's computation actually uses. Model-wide counts also include shared parts such as attention. Adding more experts raises capacity and storage while per-token expert compute can stay fixed; selecting more experts per token raises that compute. With 100M parameters per expert, 4 experts with 2 selected give 400M total and 200M active; 8 experts with 2 selected give 800M total and still 200M active; 8 with 4 selected give 800M total and 400M active.
points: Total parameters = all experts plus shared parts
Active parameters = those used for one token
Adding experts: more capacity and storage, same compute
Selecting more experts per token: more compute per token
Model-wide counts include attention and other shared parts
cards.formula: Total expert parameters = E * P_expert; active expert parameters = k * P_expert, where E is the number of experts, k the number selected per token and P_expert the parameters per expert.
cards.example: 100M per expert: 4 experts, 2 selected, gives 400M total / 200M active; 8 experts, 2 selected, gives 800M total / 200M active; 8 experts, 4 selected, gives 800M total / 400M active.
cards.say: MoE separates two numbers. Total parameters is everything stored, including every expert. Active parameters is what one token actually touches. So you can double the experts, keep the active count the same, and only spend more memory.

cards.title: Load Balancing
cards.text: Routers can fall into favouring the same few experts, leaving the others underused. Rarely chosen experts receive fewer training signals and may stay undertrained, and when experts live on different devices an overloaded expert delays the whole computation. A common remedy is an auxiliary loss, an extra training objective added to the main loss that encourages balanced expert usage; perfect equality in every batch is not required. In the example, 100 tokens with 2 experts each give 200 assignments; a skewed router might split them 90, 70, 30 and 10, while balanced usage would be about 50 each.
points: The router may favour a few experts
Underused experts get few training signals
An overloaded device delays the whole step
An auxiliary loss encourages balanced utilisation
Exact equality per batch is not required
cards.formula: A Switch-style auxiliary loss L_aux = alpha * E * sum_i f_i * P_i, with f_i the fraction of tokens routed to expert i, P_i the mean router probability for expert i and E the number of experts.
cards.example: 100 tokens with 2 experts each give 200 assignments; a skewed router routes 90, 70, 30 and 10 to the four experts, while a balanced reference would route about 50 to each.
cards.say: Left alone, a router can dump most tokens on a few favourite experts and starve the rest. We add a small auxiliary loss during training to spread the load. It does not need perfect balance, just enough to keep every expert learning.

cards.title: Shared and Fine-Grained Experts
cards.text: Two design choices refine the basic MoE layer. Fine-grained experts split the same expert budget into more, smaller feed-forward networks with narrower intermediate width and select more of them, which gives more flexible combinations at similar compute. Shared experts are always active and process every token alongside the routed experts, aiming to learn common transformations and reduce duplication among the routed ones. Both shared and selected routed experts count toward per-token compute. For example, 8 experts at full width with 2 selected and 32 quarter-width experts with 8 selected have about the same total expert parameters and selected compute.
points: Fine-grained: more, smaller experts; select more of them
More flexible combinations at similar compute
Shared experts process every token
Routed experts are selected per token
Shared experts capture common knowledge and reduce duplication
Both shared and routed experts count toward compute
cards.example: Larger experts: 8 experts at 1x width, 2 selected. Fine-grained: 32 experts at 1/4 width, 8 selected. Both use about the same total expert parameters and selected compute.
cards.say: You can slice the expert budget two ways. Fine-grained gives you many small experts and picks more of them for flexibility. A shared expert always runs for every token to soak up common knowledge, so the routed experts do not duplicate it.

cards.title: Efficiency: Compute, Memory, Latency
cards.text: Sparse activation affects resources differently. Compute drops because only the selected experts run, but routing and regrouping tokens add overhead. Weight memory does not drop, because all experts must stay stored and available. Latency can improve from the reduced arithmetic, but small per-expert batches, uneven loads and data transfers limit the speedup. In training, extra capacity can improve quality for the same compute budget, though storing and updating more parameters still costs resources; at inference, larger batches keep experts efficiently utilised.
points: Compute: only selected experts execute, plus routing overhead
Weight memory: all experts must still be stored
Latency: less arithmetic, limited by small batches, imbalance and transfers
Training: better quality per unit of compute
Inference: batch size matters for expert utilisation
cards.say: Sparse experts cut compute but not memory, because every expert must stay stored. Latency improves, though small batches and uneven loads eat into the gain. At inference, batching helps keep all those experts busy.
covers: B4: MoE Efficiency: Compute, Memory, Latency

cards.title: MoE in Practice
cards.text: Publicly documented models use MoE in different ways. gpt-oss-120b has about 117B total and 5.1B active parameters, selecting 4 of 128 experts per layer with a softmax over the selected scores, exactly like the lecture example. DeepSeek-V4-Pro has about 1.6T total and 49B active, selecting 6 of 384 routed experts plus 1 shared, and it uses token-ID-based selection in its first three layers. Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B has about 2.4T total and 95B active, selects 10 of 512 routed experts plus 1 shared, and combines MoE with attention and Gated DeltaNet layers. Counting conventions vary between developers.
points: gpt-oss-120b: about 117B total / 5.1B active, 4 of 128 experts
DeepSeek-V4-Pro: about 1.6T total / 49B active, 6 of 384 routed plus 1 shared
DeepSeek-V4-Pro: first 3 layers use token-ID-based routing
Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B: about 2.4T total / 95B active, 10 of 512 routed plus 1 shared
Qwen3.8 mixes MoE with attention and Gated DeltaNet layers
Expert counts are per MoE layer
cards.example: gpt-oss-120b is about 117B total / 5.1B active (about 4.4% active); DeepSeek-V4-Pro about 1.6T / 49B (about 3%); Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B about 2.4T / 95B (about 4%).
cards.say: Real models show the idea in action. One has a hundred and seventeen billion total parameters but activates only about five billion per token, picking four of a hundred and twenty eight experts. Others scale that up to trillions of stored parameters while activating a few percent.
covers: B4: MoE in Practice: Current Models

lessons.title: Beyond Transformers
lessons.goal: Survey the model families that replace or complement self-attention (state space models, Mamba, xLSTM, linear attention, Gated DeltaNet, looped and hybrid models) and what each trades away.

cards.title: Why Look Beyond Attention
cards.text: Self-attention lets every token look back at all earlier tokens, but that explicit access is expensive: the KV cache grows with the sequence and each new token must attend to more and more positions. Several alternative families carry information forward more cheaply: state-space and recurrent models, linear attention, looped models and hybrids. They all keep the same overall language-model pipeline of token embedding, a stack of processing blocks and a vocabulary prediction head. What changes is mainly the sequence-mixing part of each block, how information flows across tokens, and how blocks combine projections, gating, memory and feed-forward layers.
points: KV cache memory grows linearly with sequence length in standard attention
Per-token decode compute grows as each token attends to all previous positions
Two flows: across layers (depth) and across tokens (sequence mixing)
Alternatives replace or complement attention with recurrent or state-space mixing
Sequence memory can be a KV cache, a recurrent state, or both
Embeddings, stacked blocks and next-token prediction stay the same
cards.example: Four alternative ideas: state-space and recurrent models, linear attention, looped LLMs, and hybrid architectures.
cards.say: Attention is powerful but its memory keeps growing with the context. So researchers built other ways to carry information forward: state space models, linear attention, looped blocks and hybrids. The pipeline stays the same, only the way tokens talk to each other changes.

cards.title: State Space Models
cards.text: A state space model summarises everything seen so far in a compact, fixed-size state vector. For every new token the state is updated by combining the old state with the new input through learned linear maps, and an output is read from the updated state. The learned parameters A, B and C are fixed after training and shared across positions, while the state itself changes with every token. Because the update is linear, with no nonlinearity between steps, many steps can be composed mathematically, which allows a known input sequence to be processed in parallel during training or prefill.
points: State is a fixed-size summary of previous tokens and changes every token
Parameters A, B, C are learned and shared across positions
Like an RNN, but the state update is linear (no nonlinear activation)
Linear updates compose across positions, so known sequences can be processed in parallel
State size never grows with sequence length
cards.formula: h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t (state update); y_t = C h_t (readout). h = state, x = input token representation, A and B write the state, C reads it.
cards.say: A state space model keeps one fixed-size summary of everything so far. Each new token updates that state with simple linear maps. Because the update is linear, a whole known sequence can be crunched in parallel. The state never grows.

cards.title: Mamba: Selective State Spaces
cards.text: A basic SSM applies the same update and readout rules to every token, so it cannot decide from content what to remember. Mamba makes some SSM parameters depend on the current input, so the model can choose, per token, how strongly to retain the old state and how much new information to write. This selectivity lets it keep important information, let irrelevant details fade, and learn to retrieve earlier facts in context. The cost is the usual fixed-state trade-off: there is no growing KV cache, but the model cannot look up every earlier token exactly.
points: Basic SSM: same parameters at every position, content-independent
Mamba computes selected parameters from the input (selective SSM)
Enables content-dependent retain and write decisions
Supports in-context retrieval when trained to keep useful information
Fixed-size state avoids KV-cache growth but loses direct access to every past token
cards.formula: h_t = A(x_t) h_{t-1} + B(x_t) x_t; y_t = C(x_t) h_t (conceptual: the controls depend on the current input x_t).
cards.say: Mamba makes the state space model selective. Instead of fixed rules, the current word decides how strongly to keep the old state and how much to write. Important words get remembered, filler fades, but there is no cache to look up every past token exactly.

cards.title: LSTM: Gated Memory
cards.text: Long Short-Term Memory networks add a separate cell state that acts as memory next to the hidden state that serves as output. Three gates, each producing values between 0 and 1 from the current input and the previous hidden state, regulate the flow: the forget gate decides how much old memory to keep, the input gate how much new candidate content to write, and the output gate how much of the transformed memory to expose as hidden output. This gating lets recurrent networks keep information over much longer spans than plain RNNs.
points: Plain RNNs use one hidden state for both memory and output
LSTM adds a separate cell state that carries information across tokens
Forget gate: how much previous cell memory is retained
Input gate: how much newly computed content is written
Output gate: how much transformed cell memory becomes the hidden output
Gate values come from the current input and previous hidden state
cards.formula: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * c~_t (f = forget gate, i = input gate, c~ = candidate content); h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t) (o = output gate). All products are element-wise.
cards.say: The LSTM adds a memory pipe next to its output. Three valves, driven by the current input and the previous hidden state, decide what to forget, what to write and what to show. That is how recurrent nets remember over long stretches.

cards.title: xLSTM: Scalar and Matrix Memory
cards.text: xLSTM modernises the LSTM to compete with Transformers. It replaces the usual sigmoid gates with exponential gating, which can weight memory updates much more strongly relative to each other, and uses normalisation to stay numerically stable. It offers two cell types: sLSTM keeps a vector of scalar memory cells and still has hidden-state recurrence, while mLSTM stores a fixed-size matrix of key-value associations read with a query and drops hidden-state recurrence, which makes it parallelisable.
points: Classic LSTM: vector memory with gates that depend on the previous hidden state, so sequential
Exponential gating with normalisation keeps it numerically stable
sLSTM: scalar memory cells, exponential gating, hidden-state recurrence
mLSTM: matrix memory of key-value associations with query-based retrieval
mLSTM has no hidden-state recurrence, so known sequences can be processed in parallel
cards.example: sLSTM is shown as a vector of scalar cells c1..c4; mLSTM is shown as an associative matrix memory written by key-value outer products and read by a query.
cards.say: xLSTM gives the old LSTM a modern engine. It swaps sigmoid gates for exponential ones and adds normalisation. One cell type keeps a vector of scalar memories. The other keeps a matrix of key-value pairs that can be read in parallel.
covers: B5: xLSTM: scalar and matrix memory

cards.title: Recurrence Without Sequential Training
cards.text: Recurrent models pass information from one token to the next, which seems to force strictly sequential computation. For the classic RNN, LSTM and sLSTM this is true, because each gate depends on the previous hidden state. In Mamba and mLSTM, however, the update parameters depend only on the known input tokens and the updates can be combined algebraically, so a whole known sequence can be processed in parallel during training and prefill. During autoregressive generation tokens are still produced one after another, because each new token depends on the previous output.
points: RNN, LSTM and sLSTM: each update waits for the previous hidden state
Mamba and mLSTM: token-specific updates are prepared in parallel, then combined
Possible because updates depend only on inputs and are composable
Prefill and training can use parallel algorithms
Autoregressive decoding is still sequential, token by token
cards.example: Tokens t1..t4: a sequential chain for the RNN, LSTM and sLSTM, versus parallel preparation followed by a combine step for Mamba and mLSTM.
cards.say: Recurrent sounds sequential, and for the old models it is. But in Mamba and mLSTM the update only depends on the input tokens, so a whole known passage can be processed at once. Generation is still one token at a time, because each output feeds the next.

cards.title: Linear Attention
cards.text: Standard attention keeps one key and one value per previous token, so memory grows with context. Linear attention replaces the softmax similarity with a feature map, a kernel, so that by the associativity of matrix multiplication the keys and values can be combined first into one matrix S whose size does not depend on sequence length. Writing adds the outer product of the transformed key and the value to S; reading multiplies the transformed query by S, weighting stored contributions by query-key similarity. Cost becomes linear in sequence length, but individual past pairs are no longer separately accessible and associations can interfere.
points: Standard attention: the KV cache grows by one key-value pair per token
Linear attention uses a kernel feature map instead of softmax
Associativity lets keys and values be combined before the query is applied
Write: add the outer product of transformed key and value to matrix memory S
Read: output = transformed query times S
Memory size is independent of sequence length but past pairs are not individually accessible
cards.formula: S_t = S_{t-1} + phi(k_t) v_t^T (write); o_t = phi(q_t)^T S_t (read). S = matrix memory, phi = feature map, k = key, v = value, q = query.
cards.example: Write a fact like 'Alice lives in Berlin' into S, then a later query 'Alice lives in ...' reads back 'Berlin', because the query matches the stored key.
cards.say: Linear attention folds all the past keys and values into a single matrix that does not grow. Writing adds an outer product; reading multiplies the query by that matrix. Memory stays fixed, but old pairs blur together and can interfere.
covers: B5: Linear attention: fixed-size matrix memory

cards.title: Gated DeltaNet: Correcting Memory
cards.text: Plain linear attention only ever adds associations, so outdated facts stay in memory and conflict with new ones. Gated DeltaNet first applies a learned gate that decides how much of the existing memory to keep, so it can forget selectively. It then uses the incoming key to read what the memory currently predicts, compares that with the new value, and writes only the difference, the delta, back. This error-driven update corrects stale associations instead of piling new ones on top.
points: Accumulating is not updating: plain linear attention just adds
Retain: a learned gate scales how much existing memory is preserved
Compare: the incoming key retrieves the currently stored value
Correct: write the difference between the new and the predicted value
Combines selective forgetting with error-based updates of fixed-size memory
cards.formula: S_t = alpha_t * S_{t-1} + beta_t * k_t (v_t - S_{t-1}^T k_t)^T. alpha = retention gate, beta = write strength; the transposition convention varies between papers.
cards.example: Memory holds 'customer lives in Berlin'. New info 'customer moved to Munich': plain linear attention adds a second association and both interfere, while Gated DeltaNet corrects the association toward Munich.
cards.say: Plain linear attention only piles new facts on top of old ones. Gated DeltaNet first decides how much to keep, then compares the new value with what memory predicts and writes only the difference. Stale facts get corrected instead of stacking up.

cards.title: Looped LLMs
cards.text: Standard Transformers apply a fixed sequence of layers with different weights, so adding depth adds parameters. Looped models instead apply the same block with shared weights several times, feeding the refined representations back in before the final next-token prediction. This yields more processing steps without more parameters, but every loop costs compute and latency, and reusing weights does not automatically improve predictions.
points: Standard: different weights per layer, so more depth means more parameters
Looped: the same block applied repeatedly with shared weights
The final loop output is used for next-token prediction
Benefit: extra computation without extra parameters
Cost: more compute and inference latency per loop
No guarantee of better predictions
cards.say: Instead of stacking many different layers, a looped model runs one shared block again and again. You get more thinking steps without adding parameters. But every loop costs time, and looping does not promise a better answer.

cards.title: Hybrid: Nemotron 3 Nano
cards.text: Real models increasingly mix mechanisms. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Nano, with 30B total parameters and about 3B active, interleaves Mamba-2 layers for efficient sequence processing with self-attention in selected layers for direct access to earlier tokens, and uses Mixture-of-Experts layers to increase capacity while activating only some experts per token. The combination balances model capacity, inference efficiency and retrieval ability.
points: Mamba-2: compact recurrent state for efficient sequence processing
Self-attention only in selected layers: direct access to previous tokens
MoE: large total capacity, only a subset of experts active per token
A hybrid is an engineering compromise between efficiency and capability
cards.example: Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B: about 30B total parameters and about 3B active per token.
cards.say: Real designs mix the ideas. One model stacks Mamba layers for speed, adds attention in a few layers for exact recall, and uses experts for extra capacity. Each mechanism covers for the weaknesses of the others.
covers: B5: Hybrid example: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano

lessons.title: Choosing an Architecture
lessons.goal: Compare how architectures scale with context length, what Big-O hides, and how to pick a model that meets accuracy within the latency and memory budget.

cards.title: How Cost Scales with Context
cards.text: Big-O notation describes how compute and memory grow with the number of tokens N, while model dimensions, layer count and batch size are fixed. Full attention needs quadratic prefill compute, linear decode compute per token, and a KV cache that grows linearly. Recurrent and linear-attention models, such as Mamba, xLSTM and Gated DeltaNet, need linear prefill and constant per-token decode cost and state memory. Hybrids with at least one global attention layer inherit attention's scaling plus a recurrent state. Remember that O(1) means independent of context length, not free.
points: Full attention MHA: prefill O(N^2), decode O(N) per token, memory O(N)
GQA and MQA: same Big-O but a smaller KV cache
Mamba, xLSTM, linear attention and Gated DeltaNet: prefill O(N), decode O(1), state O(1)
Hybrid with a global attention layer: O(N^2), O(N), O(N) plus a recurrent state
O(1) means independent of context length, not free
The comparison ignores weights, feed-forward compute and temporary buffers
cards.example: Big-O by architecture. Full attention MHA: O(N^2) / O(N) / O(N). GQA and MQA: O(N^2) / O(N) / O(N) with a smaller cache. Mamba, xLSTM and Gated DeltaNet: O(N) / O(1) / O(1). Attention-recurrent hybrid: O(N^2) / O(N) / O(N) plus a recurrent state.
cards.say: Big-O tells you how cost grows with context. Full attention is quadratic to prefill and keeps a growing cache. State space and linear models do linear prefill and constant decode. A hybrid pays attention's cost plus a recurrent state.

cards.title: What Big-O Hides
cards.text: Two models with the same Big-O can perform very differently on real hardware. GQA and MQA shrink the KV cache and memory traffic without changing the quadratic complexity; Mamba relies on specialised parallel-scan kernels for fast prefill; LSTM-style recurrence can block parallel execution; and matrix-state models avoid growing caches but may still need a lot of memory. Actual speed depends on GPU utilisation, memory bandwidth and kernel quality, so the complexity class alone never tells you which model is fastest.
points: Complexity is not speed: kernels, bandwidth and utilisation decide runtime
Fixed-size is not small: a constant-size state can still be large
Linear is not parallel: linear work may still run sequentially
GQA and MQA reduce memory traffic, not the complexity class
Big-O shows how cost scales, not which model is fastest
cards.say: Same Big-O does not mean same speed. Kernels, bandwidth and how well the GPU is used decide the real runtime. Grouped query attention cuts traffic without changing the complexity class, and a linear model can still run slowly if it cannot parallelise.
covers: B5: What complexity does not tell you

cards.title: What Fixed-Size Memory Gives Up
cards.text: Full attention keeps token-specific keys and values, so a later question can directly attend to an earlier detail, although correct retrieval is still not guaranteed. Fixed-state recurrent models must squeeze everything into their state, which can lose specific details over long contexts. Exact recall tasks, like finding one phone number among hundreds of records, expose the difference. Given hundreds of customer records including 'Mira Chen -> 0531 / 482-7319', a later question 'What is Mira Chen's phone number?' is exactly where a growing cache helps and a small state can blur the digits.
points: Full attention gives direct access to cached token representations
Fixed-state models must preserve information inside the evolving state
Long-context exact recall is harder for fixed-state models
Direct access does not guarantee correct retrieval either
cards.example: Hundreds of customer records include 'Mira Chen -> 0531 / 482-7319'; the later question 'What is Mira Chen's phone number?' tests exact recall, where a fixed state can lose the specific digits.
cards.say: Full attention can point straight at an earlier detail. A fixed state has to carry everything inside one small vector, so exact facts can blur over a long context. Asking for one phone number among hundreds of records is where that difference shows.
covers: B5: What fixed-size memory gives up

cards.title: Prefill vs Decode Performance
cards.text: Inference has two phases with different bottlenecks. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is often compute-bound; decode generates one token at a time and is often limited by memory bandwidth, especially at small batch sizes. Full attention does quadratic prefill work, which optimised kernels such as FlashAttention ease by reducing memory traffic, and reads a growing KV cache while decoding; recurrent and linear models do linear prefill work and constant-size state updates. Engineers should measure time to first token, time per output token and throughput under realistic conditions.
points: Prefill is often compute-intensive
Decode is often memory-bandwidth-limited, especially at low batch sizes
TTFT (time to first token) is sensitive to prefill
TPOT (time per output token) is sensitive to decode
Throughput (tokens per second) is overall capacity under concurrent requests
Benchmark at representative context lengths, batch sizes and hardware
cards.say: Prefill is usually limited by compute, and decode by memory bandwidth, especially with small batches. So time to first token tracks prefill, and time per token tracks decode. Always benchmark both on the hardware and context length you actually expect.

cards.title: Ways to Spend the Model Budget
cards.text: Architects trade capacity, active computation, memory and information access in different ways. Mixture of Experts increases total parameters while each token uses only a few experts, at the price of storing more weights and paying routing and communication overhead. Looped models reuse parameters for extra steps but pay in compute and latency. Attention-recurrent hybrids combine direct access with efficient recurrence but must maintain both KV caches and recurrent states. Improving one dimension does not automatically improve the others, so every gain has a matching cost somewhere.
points: MoE: more capacity with few active experts; cost is weight storage, routing and communication
Looped models: shared parameters reused; cost is compute and latency per iteration
Hybrids: direct access plus efficiency; cost is both a KV cache and a recurrent state
Improving one dimension does not automatically improve the others
cards.say: Every architecture spends its budget differently. Experts buy capacity but need storage and routing. Loops buy extra steps but cost latency. Hybrids get the best of both, but must carry both a cache and a recurrent state. There is no free lunch.
covers: B5: Ways to spend the model budget

cards.title: Choosing an Architecture
cards.text: There is no universally best architecture; the choice follows application requirements. Accurate long-document retrieval favours full attention or hybrids, but retrieval accuracy still has to be tested. Many concurrent users favour GQA or MQA, or fixed-state models that cut per-request memory. Small devices require checking the weights plus the KV cache plus the state size. Low latency requires benchmarking both prefill and decode on the target hardware. A documentation assistant, for example, would compare candidate models on answer accuracy, time to first token, time per output token, throughput and peak GPU memory, then pick the one that meets quality within budget.
points: Long-document retrieval: full attention or hybrids, verify retrieval accuracy
Many users: GQA or MQA and fixed-state models reduce per-request memory
Limited device memory: account for weights plus KV cache plus recurrent state
Low latency: benchmark prefill and decode on the target hardware
Pick the available model that meets quality within the latency and memory budget
cards.example: A documentation assistant compares a full-attention Transformer, an attention-recurrent hybrid and a recurrent model on answer accuracy, TTFT, TPOT, throughput and peak GPU memory.
cards.say: There is no best model, only the best fit. Long document retrieval points to attention or a hybrid. Many users point to grouped query attention. Small devices need every memory cost counted. Then measure, and pick the model that meets quality inside your budget.

lessons.title: Training Data
lessons.goal: Understand where LLM training text comes from, how raw web crawls are turned into clean, well-mixed corpora, and how data choices shape model quality and bias.

cards.title: Data Becomes Weights
cards.text: Pretraining has exactly one goal: guess the next token. Yet chasing that goal across trillions of tokens forces the model to soak up grammar, facts about the world, tone and style, reasoning habits and recurring task formats such as translation. All of it ends up stored as statistical regularities in the weights. The catch is that a model can only generalize from what its data actually contains. A language or domain that is rare or missing leaves a blind spot, so data quality, scale and diversity effectively cap how good the model can become. Garbage in, garbage out.
points: One objective (next-token prediction), many learned skills
Learned: syntax, world knowledge, style, reasoning cues, pragmatics, task templates
Weights store the statistical regularities of the corpus
Rare or missing languages and domains perform poorly
Generalization must be checked on unseen, representative tasks
cards.example: 'She writes a letter' vs 'They write letters' teaches subject-verb agreement; 'Paris is the capital of France' teaches a fact; 'Hey, can you help me?' vs 'Could you please assist me?' teaches style; 'Translate house into German: Haus' teaches a task pattern. A model that never saw Thai text cannot handle Thai.
cards.say: Pretraining only asks the model to guess the next word, but to do that well it has to absorb grammar, facts, style and even task formats. Whatever the data lacks, the model lacks too.
covers: B5: What models learn from data

cards.title: Where the Text Comes From
cards.text: Training corpora are stitched together from several kinds of text. Wikipedia supplies curated reference knowledge, BooksCorpus and Project Gutenberg give long-form prose, GitHub contributes code, and arXiv and PubMed add scientific writing. By far the largest ingredient is the open web, mostly through Common Crawl, a nonprofit that regularly archives billions of public pages and publishes them for free. That scale comes with a price: ads, duplicates, spam and broken fragments are everywhere, and the content is heavily tilted toward English. Raw crawls are therefore a starting point that needs serious cleaning, never a finished dataset.
points: Sources: Wikipedia, books, GitHub code, arXiv/PubMed papers, web pages
Common Crawl: nonprofit, periodic public web archives
August 2025 crawl: about 2.44 billion pages, roughly 47 TB
Parts of Common Crawl fed GPT-3 and Gemini
English is about 46% of Common Crawl; many languages are scarce
cards.example: Common Crawl CC-MAIN-2025-33 (August 2025): 2.44 billion pages, about 47 TB. Language shares: English 45.88%, Russian 5.97%, German 5.88%, Chinese 4.87%, Japanese 4.79%, French 4.73%, Spanish 4.47%, Italian 2.57%, Dutch 2.06%, Polish 1.66%, Portuguese 1.15%, Vietnamese 1.03%.
cards.say: Models read encyclopedias, books, code and research papers, but the biggest slice is the open web, mainly Common Crawl. One recent crawl held about two and a half billion pages, nearly half of them in English.
covers: B5: Training data sources and transparency

cards.title: Crawlers, Licenses and Black Boxes
cards.text: AI companies also run their own crawlers, such as OpenAI's GPTBot and Anthropic's ClaudeBot, which fetch web pages that may end up in training sets. What exactly was collected, how it was mixed and how it was filtered usually stays secret: the GPT-4 report only mentions publicly available and licensed data. Without that information nobody can reconstruct or audit the corpus. For engineers building their own datasets, the lesson is to document provenance carefully, recording sources, collection dates and versions, and to check licenses and personal data, because being reachable on the internet does not make text legal to train on.
points: Industry crawlers: GPTBot (OpenAI), ClaudeBot (Anthropic)
Commercial corpora (e.g. GPT-4) are not disclosed in detail
Opacity blocks reproduction and independent analysis
Track provenance: source, date, version
Publicly accessible does not mean legally usable
cards.example: GPT-4's report describes its data only as 'publicly available and licensed data'; the exact documents, mixture and filters are unknown.
cards.say: Big labs send out their own crawler bots, but they rarely reveal what they collected. If you build a dataset, record where every piece came from, and check licenses and privacy before training.
covers: A2: Industry crawlers and data opacity
B5: Training data sources and transparency

cards.title: FineWeb: An Open Recipe
cards.text: FineWeb, released by Hugging Face in May 2024, is an answer to that secrecy. It processes 96 Common Crawl snapshots from 2013 to 2024 into about 44 TB of English text with a fully documented, reproducible pipeline. The goals were open research, imitating the kind of pipelines behind closed models, and measuring how each processing choice affects data quality. The outcome is roughly 52 billion records. Every record keeps its text together with metadata like an id, the crawl dump and the source URL, so its origin can always be traced. Before training, the text still has to be tokenized.
points: Hugging Face, May 2024, fully documented pipeline
Built from 96 Common Crawl snapshots (2013-2024)
About 44 TB of English text
52,453,695,892 rows, roughly 52 billion records
Each record = text + metadata (id, dump, url) for provenance
cards.example: 96 snapshots -> ~44 TB -> 52,453,695,892 documents, each stored with id, crawl dump and URL.
cards.say: FineWeb is an open dataset from Hugging Face that shows every cleaning step. It turned ninety six web crawls into about forty four terabytes of English text, around fifty two billion documents.
covers: B5: FineWeb pipeline and text extraction

cards.title: From Raw HTML to Clean Text
cards.text: The FineWeb pipeline works like a factory line. First, extraction pulls the main article out of each HTML page in reading order, keeping headings and paragraphs while throwing away menus, navigation bars and footers; sloppy extraction either adds noise or loses content. Second, URLs are checked against a blocklist of malware, adult, gambling, spam, fake-news and similar sites. Third, a language filter keeps only English, a deliberate design choice. Fourth, exact and near-duplicate documents are removed. Finally, heuristic quality rules discard text that looks like navigation, keyword spam or tag lists. Each stage shrinks and reshapes what the model will see.
points: 1 Extract main text, drop boilerplate (nav, menus, footers)
2 URL blocklist (malware, adult, gambling, spam, misleading content...)
3 Language filter: English only (design choice)
4 Remove exact and near-duplicates
5 Heuristic quality filters for non-prose text
cards.example: A Wikipedia page on Barack Obama: the nav 'Contents | Languages' and footer 'Privacy | About' are dropped; the heading and the paragraph about the 44th president (2009-2017) survive. Heuristics reject 'Home > Products > Contact > FAQ' (few lines end with punctuation), 'Buy now! Buy now! free download free download' (many repeated characters) and 'AI; ML; Deep Learning; NLP; Robotics' (mostly short lines).
cards.say: Cleaning happens in stages: pull out the real article text, block bad websites, keep one language, remove duplicates, and finally drop pages that look like menus, spam or keyword lists.
covers: B5: FineWeb pipeline and text extraction

cards.title: Every Filter Has a Price
cards.text: Filters do not just remove junk; each one changes the distribution the model learns from. URL filters catch known spam domains but miss new ones. Language filters sharpen focus on one language at the expense of all others. Quality filters cut noise yet may also delete useful structured content such as tables or lists. Deduplication matters because repeated documents push the model toward memorizing and regurgitating text word for word; fewer copies reduce memorization and make training more efficient. Finally, always check that evaluation questions did not leak into the training set, since such contamination quietly inflates benchmark scores.
points: URL filter: removes known spam, some still slips through
Language filter: focus gained, other languages lost
Quality filter: less noise, possibly less useful structure
Duplicates raise memorization and verbatim output
Higher average quality can cost coverage
Check train/test overlap to avoid contaminated benchmarks
cards.example: The same news article mirrored on three websites is kept in fewer copies, so the model does not overweight and memorize it.
cards.say: Each filter is a trade off. Removing duplicates reduces memorization, but strict quality or language filters can also throw away useful text. And always make sure test questions never sneak into training data.

cards.title: FineWeb-Edu: Better Beats Bigger
cards.text: FineWeb-Edu asks a simple question: what if we keep only text that actually teaches something? Llama 3 rated around 460,000 FineWeb records (often rounded to half a million) for educational value on a 0 to 5 scale. A small embedding-based classifier learned to imitate those ratings and scored the whole corpus, and documents with a rounded score of 3 or more were kept, about 1.3 trillion tokens. With the same 1.71B model and 350B training tokens, MMLU accuracy rose from 33% to 37%. Comparable results needed roughly ten times less data. Filtering also shifted topics toward education and history.
points: An LLM (Llama 3) acts as annotator, scoring 0-5
A small classifier extends the scores to all documents
Keep score >= 3: about 1.3T tokens
Same model and token budget: MMLU 33% -> 37%
About 10x less data for comparable or better results
Topic mix shifts: more education/history, less business/entertainment
cards.formula: keep document d if classifier_score(d) >= 3, where scores range from 0 (no educational value) to 5 (highly educational)
cards.example: 1.71B-parameter model, 350B tokens on each dataset: FineWeb 33% vs FineWeb-Edu 37% on MMLU, a gain of 4 percentage points from data selection alone.
cards.say: FineWeb Edu used a large model to grade pages for teaching value, then trained a small classifier to grade everything. Keeping only good pages lifted a benchmark score from thirty three to thirty seven percent.

cards.title: Mixing the Ingredients
cards.text: Having lots of web text does not mean the model should read mostly web text. The data mixture sets which share of training tokens comes from each source, regardless of how much is available. Valuable but small sources like books, code or math can be upsampled, meaning they are sampled more often and may even be repeated; dominant sources like general web pages are downsampled. Because the total token budget is fixed, every extra percent for one domain is a percent taken from another. Note that mixture percentages always refer to tokens, not to documents.
points: Mixture need not mirror availability
Upsampling: sample a source more often, possibly repeating it
Downsampling: shrink dominant sources like web text
Fixed token budget means domains compete
Shares are measured in tokens, not documents
cards.formula: Mixture weights w_i sum to 1; tokens drawn from source i = w_i x D_total, where D_total is the total token budget
cards.example: Illustrative mix: web 70% of available data -> 40% of training (down), books 15% -> 20% (up), code 10% -> 25% (up), math 5% -> 15% (up). Math at 15% of tokens from 5% of data means each math document is seen about three times.
cards.say: A data mixture decides how many training tokens come from each source. Small valuable sources such as code or math get boosted, while the huge pile of web text gets turned down.

cards.title: Synthetic Textbooks: Phi-1
cards.text: Sometimes the best data has to be written on purpose. Microsoft's Phi-1 (2023) is a 1.3B-parameter model for Python code. Its creators picked useful existing code, defined topics and target audiences, and asked GPT-3.5 to generate textbook-style explanations with annotated examples. The model was pretrained on this blend of filtered real and synthetic material, then finetuned on generated exercises with solutions. In a controlled 350M-parameter test, adding the synthetic textbooks raised the share of solutions passing unit tests from 17.7% to 20.1%, without more parameters. The takeaway: data is an engineering design choice, though synthetic data is not automatically superior.
points: Phi-1: Microsoft 2023, 1.3B parameters, Python code
GPT-3.5 writes textbook-style lessons and examples
Pretrain on real + synthetic, finetune on generated exercises
350M test: pass rate 17.7% -> 20.1% (+2.4 pp)
Does not prove synthetic data always wins
cards.example: A synthetic lesson on filtering even numbers: keep n when n % 2 == 0, so [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] becomes [2, 4, 6]. Pass rate (350M model): filtered web plus code 17.7%, plus synthetic textbooks 20.1%.
cards.say: Phi one was trained partly on textbooks written by another language model. In a small controlled test, those synthetic lessons raised the share of correct code solutions from about eighteen to twenty percent.

cards.title: Bias Lives in the Data
cards.text: A language model is rewarded for predicting text well, not for being right or fair. It therefore copies whatever correlations its corpus contains, including unfair ones. Web text mirrors human behavior and media production, and some groups, regions and viewpoints are far louder online than others, so predictions tend to favor the overrepresented. Worse, training can amplify small asymmetries: if men appear only slightly more often than women in leadership contexts, the model may form a strong, systematic association. Bias is thus best understood as a property of the data distribution, which itself reflects value-laden human choices.
points: Objective rewards likely text, not true or fair text
Models replicate correlations, including harmful ones
Web corpora overrepresent some voices
Training can amplify small skews into systematic patterns
Bias is a property of the data distribution
cards.example: Slight data skew: men mentioned a bit more often than women in leadership sentences -> the model links leadership with men much more strongly in its outputs.
cards.say: Models learn correlations, not truth. If the data slightly favors one group, the trained model can turn that small tilt into a strong and systematic bias.

cards.title: The Language Gap
cards.text: Language bias is easy to measure. For the GPT-4 report, the MMLU benchmark of multiple-choice questions across many subjects was translated into numerous languages and the same model was tested on each. English scored highest at 85.5%, while Telugu reached only 62.0%, and low-resource languages generally lagged. A likely main cause is that English dominates the training data. Other contributors may be less efficient tokenization, which spends more tokens per sentence on some scripts, translation quality of the test, and some languages simply being harder to model. Careful: the scores show the gap but do not by themselves prove which cause matters most.
points: MMLU translated into many languages, same model (GPT-4)
English 85.5% vs Telugu 62.0%
Low-resource languages score lower
Likely causes: data imbalance, tokenization, translation effects
A measured gap does not prove its cause
cards.example: GPT-4 on translated MMLU: English 85.5% (best) vs Telugu 62.0%, a gap of 23.5 percentage points, compared with English making up about 46% of Common Crawl.
cards.say: When GPT four took the same exam in different languages, it scored eighty five and a half percent in English but only sixty two percent in Telugu, largely because English dominates its training data.

lessons.title: Pretraining: Objective & Compute
lessons.goal: Understand the self-supervised next-token objective and its cross-entropy loss, how the learning rate and batches are scheduled, and how FLOPs and GPU hardware set the cost of pretraining.

cards.title: The Pretraining Objective
cards.text: Pretraining teaches an LLM with one simple self-supervised task: given all previous tokens, predict the next one. Raw text supplies its own labels, because the target sequence is just the input shifted right by one position. In each forward pass the model turns every position into a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and causal masking stops a position from peeking at future tokens. That lets all positions of a sequence be trained at once. The result is a language model that has absorbed grammar, facts and style purely from predicting text.
points: Objective: maximize p(next token | all previous tokens)
Self-supervised: the raw text is its own label
Target = input sequence shifted right by one position
Causal masking blocks future tokens, so all positions train in parallel
cards.formula: p_theta(x_{t+1} | x_<=t) = probability of the next token given all previous tokens; theta = model parameters
cards.example: Input 'The cat sat on the', target 'mat'; the model scores every word in its vocabulary, and the true next word gets one probability.
cards.say: Pretraining uses a single task: guess the next word. The text itself provides the answers, because the target is just the input shifted by one. Causal masking keeps the model honest by hiding future words.
covers: B6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss
A6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss

cards.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
cards.text: The training signal is cross-entropy loss: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the correct next token. A confident correct answer gives a small loss, while a low probability gives a large one. The loss is averaged over every position and billions of tokens, backpropagation computes its gradient with respect to all parameters, and an optimizer nudges the weights to raise the probability of what actually came next. Minimizing cross-entropy is exactly maximizing the likelihood of the training text.
points: Loss = -log p(correct next token)
Low target probability -> high loss
Averaged over all positions and billions of tokens
Backpropagation gives gradients; the optimizer updates weights
Minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing data likelihood
cards.formula: L(theta) = -(1/T) * sum_t log P_theta(x_t | x_<t); single position L = -log p(target)
cards.example: For 'The cat sat on the mat.' the model gives p('mat') = 0.10, so the loss is -ln(0.10) ≈ 2.30. Raising that probability to 0.9 drops the loss to about 0.11.
cards.say: Cross entropy just measures how much probability the model gave the right word. A low probability means a big loss, so training pushes that probability up until the loss for the right word is tiny.
covers: B6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss
A6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss

cards.title: Warm-Up and Cosine Decay
cards.text: Training is very sensitive to the learning rate, so it follows a schedule. It begins with a linear warm-up, rising from near zero to a peak, because early on the weights are random and Adam's running estimates of the gradient mean and variance are still unreliable; large steps there could destabilize training. After the peak a cosine curve decays the rate smoothly to a small minimum, giving finer updates near the end and avoiding loss spikes. Linear warm-up plus cosine decay is the standard recipe behind models such as GPT-3 and Llama 2/3.
points: Adam scales each step by the gradient mean over its root-mean-square
Warm-up: linear ramp from ~0 to the peak learning rate
Protects Adam's still-unreliable moment estimates early on
Cosine decay: smooth drop to a small final learning rate
Warm-up is usually 1k-10k steps; decay spans millions
Used in GPT-3 and Llama 2/3
cards.formula: Warm-up: eta(t) = eta_max * t / T_warmup; Cosine: eta(t) = eta_min + 0.5(eta_max - eta_min)(1 + cos(pi (t - T_warmup)/(T_total - T_warmup)))
cards.example: Peak learning rate is reached after a warm-up of about 1,000-10,000 steps, then decayed along a cosine curve to a small final value across millions of optimizer steps.
cards.say: Training starts with a gentle warm up, because Adam needs time to trust its own estimates. Then the learning rate glides down along a cosine curve, so the model settles smoothly instead of overshooting at the end.
covers: B6: Learning-rate schedules: warm-up and cosine decay
A6: Learning rate schedules: warm-up, cosine decay and Adam

cards.title: Batches and Optimizer Steps
cards.text: A batch is the set of examples whose gradients are combined into a single optimizer update. Each example is a token sequence of length L, so a batch of B sequences holds B times L tokens; only after the whole batch is processed does the loss, the gradients and one weight update happen. Small batches give noisy, unstable gradients, while large batches give smoother ones and better hardware use, though not automatically faster convergence. Modern LLM pretraining uses very large effective batches, often millions of tokens per step.
points: Batch = examples contributing to one optimizer update
Tokens per batch = B (sequences) x L (sequence length)
One batch: compute loss, compute gradients, then one update
Small batch: noisy, unstable gradients
Large batch: smoother gradients, better efficiency
LLM batches reach millions of tokens per step
cards.formula: T_batch = B * L  (tokens per batch; B = sequences per batch, L = sequence length)
cards.example: A batch of 2,048 sequences of length 4,096 tokens holds about 8.4 million tokens, all contributing to a single optimizer update.
cards.say: A batch is everything the optimizer sees before one update. Big batches give steadier gradients and are more efficient on hardware, and large models use batches of millions of tokens per step.

cards.title: FLOPs and the Cost of Training
cards.text: A FLOP is one floating-point operation, and a fused multiply-add counts as two. Transformers are dominated by huge matrix multiplications, so the FLOP count sets the compute, cost and time of a training run. A standard rule of thumb is about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token: two for the forward pass and four for the backward pass, ignoring attention overhead. Compute then grows linearly with parameters and tokens, while the attention part grows quadratically with sequence length. Training time is roughly total FLOPs divided by achieved FLOP/s.
points: FLOP = one floating-point operation; FMA = 2 FLOPs
FLOPs = total work; FLOP/s = hardware speed
~6 FLOPs per parameter per token (2 forward, 4 backward)
Compute scales linearly with parameters and tokens per step
Attention scales quadratically with sequence length
Depth is cheaper than width
cards.formula: C_train ~ 6 * N_params * T_batch  (FLOPs per optimizer step); Training time ~ total FLOPs / achieved FLOP/s
cards.example: With 2,048 tokens per step: a 7B model needs 6 * 7e9 * 2048 ≈ 8.6e13 FLOPs per step, while a 70B model needs ≈ 8.6e14 FLOPs, roughly ten times more.
cards.say: Every training step costs about six operations per parameter per token, two going forward and four coming back. That is trillions of operations per step, and the compute scales up with both the model and the batch.
covers: A6: FLOPs and the compute cost of training

cards.title: Why GPUs: The H100
cards.text: CPUs have a few powerful general cores; GPUs have thousands of parallel units built for the matrix math that dominates training. They also add Tensor Cores for low-precision multiply-accumulate, very high memory bandwidth for moving weights and activations, and fast interconnects such as NVLink for multi-GPU work. Because training is often memory-bound, bandwidth matters as much as raw compute. The NVIDIA H100 shows the scale: 80 GB of HBM3, 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, NVLink up to 900 GB/s, support from FP32 down to FP8, and up to 700 W.
points: CPU: few versatile cores; GPU: thousands of parallel units
Tensor Cores accelerate low-precision matrix math
Training is often memory-bound, so bandwidth matters
H100: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, NVLink 900 GB/s, up to 700 W
Memory limits model, batch and context size per GPU
An H100 cost around 35,000 EUR in late 2025
cards.example: A CPU reaches about 0.5-2 TFLOP/s and 50-100 GB/s of bandwidth, while a GPU offers thousands of TFLOP/s and multiple TB/s, turning training from years on CPUs into days or weeks on GPU clusters.
cards.say: Training runs on GPUs because they do thousands of matrix operations at once and move data incredibly fast. A single H100 packs eighty gigabytes of memory and more than three terabytes per second of bandwidth.
covers: B6: GPUs for LLM training (NVIDIA H100)
A6: Hardware: CPU vs. GPU and the NVIDIA H100

lessons.title: Numbers & Parallelism
lessons.goal: Understand how numeric precision, memory limits and the four families of parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline and 3D with ZeRO) let training scale beyond one GPU, and what a finished base model looks like.

cards.title: Numeric Precision Formats
cards.text: Every weight, activation, gradient and optimizer state is stored in a numeric format, and that choice affects stability, memory, speed, bandwidth and how big a model or batch fits. In floating point, exponent bits set the representable range and fraction bits set precision. FP16 is more accurate than BF16 near 1.0 but has a tiny range and needs loss scaling. BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits with only 7 fraction bits, so it is stable, half the size, and the standard for training. FP8 speeds up supported GPUs; INT8 and INT4 serve inference and QLoRA.
points: Format affects stability, memory, speed, bandwidth and model size
Exponent bits set range; fraction bits set precision
FP32: 1+8+23 bits, used for optimizer states and high precision
FP16: 1+5+10, precise but small range, needs loss scaling
BF16: 1+8+7, FP32-like range at half the size, standard for training
FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) speeds training; INT8/INT4 for inference and QLoRA
cards.formula: Value = (-1)^sign * 1.fraction * 2^(exponent - bias); integer quantization w ~ s * q (s = scaling factor)
cards.example: FP32 is 32 bits (1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 fraction); FP16 is 16 bits (1+5+10); BF16 is 16 bits (1+8+7); FP8 E4M3 is 8 bits (4 exponent, 3 fraction). Lower precision halves or quarters memory, allowing larger batches and longer context.
cards.say: Every number in training has a format. Floating point spends some bits on range and some on precision, and the sweet spot for training is BF sixteen, which keeps a wide range at half the size of full precision.

cards.title: Why One GPU Is Not Enough
cards.text: A large model simply does not fit on one GPU. A 70B-parameter model needs about 140 GB just for its 16-bit weights, well over the 80 GB of an H100. Gradients, optimizer states and activations add much more memory on top, and activations explode with longer sequences and deeper stacks. The raw compute and the large effective batches needed for stable training would also keep a single GPU busy far too long. The answer is to spread training across many GPUs.
points: 70B params x 2 bytes (BF16) ≈ 140 GB > 80 GB of an H100
Gradients, optimizer states and activations add much more
Activation memory grows with sequence length, depth and width
Total FLOPs too large for one GPU in reasonable time
Solution: distributed training across many GPUs
cards.formula: Weight memory ~ N_params * bytes_per_value  (2 bytes for BF16)
cards.example: 70B parameters at 2 bytes each ≈ 140 GB, versus an H100's 80 GB, so even the weights alone do not fit on one device.
cards.say: A seventy billion parameter model takes about a hundred and forty gigabytes just for its weights in half precision, and one H100 only has eighty. Add gradients and optimizer states and it is hopeless, so training must be spread across many GPUs.
covers: B6: Why single-GPU training is impractical
A6: Why one GPU is not enough and gradient accumulation

cards.title: Gradient Accumulation
cards.text: Gradient accumulation fakes a large batch when memory only fits a small one. The batch is split into N micro-batches; each gets its own forward and backward pass, and the resulting gradients are summed without touching the weights. Only after all N micro-batches is the averaged gradient applied in a single optimizer step, and the gradient buffer is reset. This keeps peak activation memory low and gives the effect of the full large batch, but because the micro-batches run one after another it does not make training faster.
points: Split a batch into N micro-batches
Forward + backward per micro-batch, accumulate gradients, no update
After N: average gradients, one optimizer step, reset
Enables large effective batches with limited memory
Lowers peak activation memory
Does not speed up training by itself
cards.formula: g_accum = (1/N) * sum_{i=1..N} g_i ; B_eff = N * B_micro
cards.example: N = 8 micro-batches of 256 sequences behave like one batch of 2,048 sequences for the optimizer step, while only 256 sequences ever sit in memory at once.
cards.say: Gradient accumulation lets a small GPU pretend to use a big batch. Each mini batch adds to a running gradient, and only after several of them does the optimizer actually take a step.
covers: A6: Why one GPU is not enough and gradient accumulation

cards.title: Data Parallelism
cards.text: In data parallelism every GPU keeps a full copy of the model but processes different micro-batches. After the forward and backward passes, gradients are averaged across GPUs so all copies take the same optimizer step and stay identical. It raises throughput and combines naturally with gradient accumulation. The limitation is memory: because parameters, gradients and optimizer states are replicated on every GPU, the model must still fit on a single device, so data parallelism scales speed but not model size.
points: Each GPU holds the full model
Each GPU processes different data
Gradients averaged across GPUs (all-reduce)
Same update on every replica, keeping them in sync
Benefit: higher throughput
Limitation: full model and training states replicated per GPU
cards.formula: B_eff = D * N * B_micro  (D = data-parallel GPUs, N = accumulation steps, B_micro = micro-batch size)
cards.example: With two GPUs, GPU1 processes micro-batches 1 and 3 while GPU2 processes 2 and 4, both holding the full model; their gradients are averaged before both update.
cards.say: Data parallelism gives every GPU the whole model but a different slice of the data. The GPUs average their gradients, so they all update identically and train faster together.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

cards.title: Tensor Parallelism
cards.text: Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. A large matrix might be cut into columns, with each GPU multiplying the same input by its own shard to produce a partial output; the partials are then concatenated for an expansion layer or summed for an attention projection. This is applied inside the attention and feed-forward layers when a single layer is too big for one GPU. The price is heavy communication, because the shards exchange partial results frequently during every forward and backward pass.
points: Shard large weight matrices across devices
Each GPU computes a partial result for the same input
Column split -> concatenate; row split -> sum
Applied to attention and feed-forward layers
Handles layers too big for one GPU
Requires frequent, fast GPU-to-GPU communication
cards.formula: Column sharding: W = [W1, W2]; Y = X W = [X W1, X W2], each GPU i computes X Wi
cards.example: A feed-forward weight matrix is split by columns so GPU1 and GPU2 each hold a shard and both process the same micro-batch, then their partial outputs are combined.
cards.say: Tensor parallelism chops a single big weight matrix into pieces across GPUs. Each GPU does only its part, then the pieces are stitched back together. It is powerful but needs constant talking between GPUs.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

cards.title: Pipeline Parallelism
cards.text: Pipeline parallelism gives different GPUs different groups of consecutive layers, called stages. A micro-batch flows through the stages in order, and several micro-batches can be in flight at once so the stages all stay busy. This lowers the model memory each GPU must hold and combines well with the other strategies. Its drawbacks are pipeline bubbles, the idle gaps while the pipeline fills and drains, the cost of shipping activations and gradients between stages, and the tricky scheduling of overlapping forward and backward passes.
points: Consecutive layers split into stages on different GPUs
Micro-batches flow through stages, overlapping in time
Reduces model memory per GPU
Combinable with data and tensor parallelism
Pipeline bubbles: idle time during fill and drain
Needs inter-stage communication and careful scheduling
cards.example: GPU1 holds layers 0-3 and GPU2 holds layers 4-6; a micro-batch finishes on GPU1 then moves to GPU2 while the next micro-batch enters GPU1.
cards.say: Pipeline parallelism assigns groups of layers to different GPUs, like stations on an assembly line. Micro batches keep every stage busy, though the first and last stages always waste a little time.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

cards.title: 3D Parallelism and ZeRO
cards.text: Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism can be stacked into 3D parallelism. But plain data parallelism wastefully replicates parameters, gradients and optimizer states on every GPU, and Adam's two moment states alone take several times the parameter memory. ZeRO removes that redundancy by sharding the training states across data-parallel GPUs: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters. It works with all three parallelism types and slashes memory at the cost of more communication. PyTorch's FSDP implements this ZeRO-style sharding, gathering parameters only when needed.
points: 3D parallelism = data + tensor + pipeline together
Plain DP replicates parameters, gradients and optimizer states
Adam stores two moment states, several times the model size
ZeRO stage 1: optimizer states; stage 2: + gradients; stage 3: + parameters
Works with DP, TP, PP; trades memory for communication
PyTorch FSDP: gathers parameters only when needed
cards.formula: Without ZeRO, per GPU ~ (2 + 2 + K) * Psi bytes; ZeRO stage 3 over N_d GPUs ~ (2 + 2 + K) * Psi / N_d
cards.example: ZeRO paper example: a 7.5B model on 64 GPUs (K = 12) drops from a 120 GB per-GPU baseline to 31.4 GB (stage 1), 16.6 GB (stage 2) and just 1.9 GB (stage 3).
cards.say: Plain data parallelism copies the same optimizer states onto every GPU, which is a huge waste. Zero shards those states across GPUs, stage by stage, so memory falls dramatically, from a hundred and twenty gigabytes down to under two.

cards.title: Choosing a Strategy
cards.text: Each distributed technique fixes a different bottleneck and brings its own cost. Gradient accumulation buys larger effective batches but lengthens each step.
