Data parallelism raises throughput but replicates the training states. Tensor parallelism splits oversized layers but communicates constantly. Pipeline parallelism spreads layers across GPUs but creates idle bubbles. ZeRO removes redundant memory but adds coordination. There is no single best choice: large training runs combine several of them to balance memory, speed and communication against the hardware actually available.
points: Larger batches -> gradient accumulation and data parallelism
Layers too large -> tensor parallelism
Model too deep to fit -> pipeline parallelism
Training states too large -> ZeRO
No universally optimal strategy; combine techniques
cards.example: Gradient accumulation trades longer steps for bigger batches; DP trades replicated memory for throughput; TP trades communication for splitting huge layers; PP trades bubbles for less per-GPU memory; ZeRO trades communication for memory.
cards.say: Every strategy solves a different problem and charges a different price. Real training systems mix them together, trading memory, speed and communication to fit the hardware they have.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

cards.title: The Base Model: Llama 3.1 8B
cards.text: The finished product of pretraining is a base model: a network that continues text fluently but has not yet been aligned to follow instructions. Llama 3.1 8B (base) is a decoder-only causal Transformer with about 8 billion parameters, 32 blocks, 4096-dimensional hidden states and 32 attention heads, with a feed-forward size of roughly 14,336 and a context of up to 128k tokens. It was trained by self-supervised next-token prediction on a large multilingual corpus. Its size is set by depth (blocks), width (hidden size), heads and the feed-forward dimension.
points: Pretraining output = base model, not yet instruction-following
Decoder-only causal Transformer
~8B parameters, 32 blocks, hidden size 4096, 32 heads
MLP intermediate size ~14,336
Context up to 128k tokens
Self-supervised next-token prediction on multilingual data
cards.example: Llama 3.1 8B: 32 blocks, d_model 4096, 32 heads, FFN 14,336, 128k context.
cards.say: Pretraining ends with a base model that can continue text well but does not yet follow instructions. Llama three point one eight billion is a decoder only transformer with thirty two layers and a hundred and twenty eight thousand token context.
covers: A6: Result of pretraining: the base model (Llama 3.1 8B)

lessons.title: Training Recipes
lessons.goal: Understand how training recipes schedule data over time and shape capabilities, through multi-stage midtraining, progressive context extension and late-stage domain upsampling.

cards.title: Training Recipes and Scheduling
cards.text: Give two runs the same model, data, token count and compute and they can still end up with different abilities, because how the data is exposed over time matters. A training recipe coordinates the data mixture, the data schedule and the optimization settings across phases. The mixture sets which fraction of tokens comes from each domain; the schedule decides when they appear. The same 30% code share can be spread evenly, concentrated at the start or saved for the end, and each choice hands later gradients a different starting point. Curriculum learning, easy examples first, is a deliberate special case.
points: Same ingredients, different decisions -> different capabilities
Recipe = data schedule plus optimization settings and phases
Mixture = token proportion per domain
Schedule = timing and ordering of data
Order matters: gradients depend on the current weights
Curriculum learning = deliberate easy-to-hard progression
cards.example: Three schedules all use 30% code overall: uniform (30% throughout), early (60% in the first half, 0% after) and late (0% first, then 60% in the second half). Same budget, different skills.
cards.say: Two runs can share the same data and budget yet end up different, because when the model sees each domain matters. A recipe decides the mixture and the timing of everything the model reads.
covers: B6: Training recipes and data scheduling

cards.title: OLMo 2: Multi-Stage Training
cards.text: OLMo 2 7B shows how recipes work in stages. Stage 1 is broad pretraining on about 4 trillion tokens. Stage 2, called midtraining, continues next-token prediction for 50 billion tokens on Dolmino Mix, a curated blend of high-quality web, math and question-answering data. This is repeated three times from the same checkpoint with different data shuffles, and the three resulting models are averaged element-wise. The learning rate warms up and decays during broad pretraining, then gets a final annealing on the targeted data, letting the model refine itself without overwriting earlier skills. Weight averaging adds stability at no extra inference cost.
points: Multi-stage: successive phases with different data or settings
Midtraining = continued pretraining with the same objective
Stage 1: ~4T tokens of broad pretraining
Stage 2: 3 x 50B tokens on Dolmino Mix, different shuffles
Final model = element-wise average of the three runs
High-quality data paired with decreasing LR (final annealing)
cards.formula: theta_final = (theta_A + theta_B + theta_C) / 3  (element-wise weight averaging)
cards.example: OLMo 2 7B: stage 1 about 4T tokens, then three continuations of 50B tokens each (shuffles A, B, C), averaged into one final model.
cards.say: OLMo two trains in stages. It first reads four trillion tokens broadly, then does a targeted midtraining pass on curated math and question answering, three times over, and averages the three results into one stronger model.
covers: B6: OLMo 2: multi-stage training and weight averaging

cards.title: Extending the Context (Llama 3)
cards.text: Llama 3 was first pretrained with an 8K-token context window, then stretched to 128K tokens in six progressive stages of continued next-token prediction using about 800 billion extra tokens. Long sequences are added late because attention compute grows quadratically with length, so short-context training is far cheaper. The model only moves to the next length after it recovers its short-context performance and passes needle-in-a-haystack tests, which check that it can still find a fact buried in a long document. The objective never changes; only the sequence length does.
points: Start: 8K context; target: 128K context
Six progressive stages of increasing sequence length
~800B additional tokens for the extension
Same next-token objective on longer sequences
Long sequences come late because attention cost is quadratic
Advance only when short-context and needle tests pass
cards.example: 8K -> 128K context in six stages using roughly 800B extra tokens, each stage gated by short-context recovery and needle-in-a-haystack checks.
cards.say: Llama three started with an eight thousand token context and grew it to a hundred and twenty eight thousand in six stages, adding about eight hundred billion tokens. Long sequences come last because attention gets expensive fast.

cards.title: Late-Stage Domain Upsampling
cards.text: Domain upsampling raises the sampling probability of chosen domains above their original share. In a controlled test with a 7B model and 1 trillion tokens, upsampling selected domains during only the final 20% of training improved math and code benchmarks over the original mixture, without adding any tokens. The gains were not free everywhere: MMLU rose from 35.69 to 42.59, GSM8K from 14.71 to 22.97 and HumanEval from 17.23 to 23.40, while a language-understanding score slipped slightly from 61.52 to 60.08. Changing the schedule shifts capabilities rather than lifting everything.
points: Domain upsampling: raise the sampling probability of chosen domains
Setup: 7B model, 1T tokens, same budget
Upsampling only in the final 20% of training
Math (GSM8K) and code (HumanEval) improve clearly
Language understanding drops slightly
Capabilities shift without more tokens
cards.example: No upsampling vs final-20% upsampling: MMLU 35.69 -> 42.59, GSM8K 14.71 -> 22.97, HumanEval 17.23 -> 23.40, while language understanding eased from 61.52 to 60.08.
cards.say: If you feed more math and code in the last fifth of training, the model gets much better at those, with no extra tokens. But language understanding dips a little, so you are trading skills, not adding them for free.

lessons.title: Scaling Laws
lessons.goal: Understand how held-out loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute, and how scaling laws guide budget, allocation and deployment choices.

cards.title: What Scaling Laws Are
cards.text: Scaling laws are empirical formulas describing how a model's held-out prediction loss changes with its size, its training data and its training compute. They turn a fixed budget into a plan: build a bigger model on fewer tokens, or a smaller model on more tokens? In practice, larger and better-trained models reach lower loss, but with diminishing returns. Each multiplicative step in scale buys a roughly constant percentage improvement rather than a fixed amount. Because the pattern is smooth, small runs let you forecast large ones, but only inside the range you actually measured.
points: Resources: model size N, training tokens D, compute C, held-out loss L
Goal: find the allocation that minimizes loss for a budget
Larger, sufficiently trained models reach lower held-out loss
Diminishing returns: a constant relative gain per scaling step
Power law: constant percentage improvement per multiplicative scale-up
Fits are reliable only within the range of conditions measured
cards.formula: L(X) ~ (X_c / X)^alpha  (X = size, tokens or compute; X_c and alpha are fitted constants)
cards.example: Training runs of many sizes fall on a straight line on a log-log plot of loss against scale. Extrapolating that line forecasts the loss of a model far larger than any you actually trained.
cards.say: Scaling laws say that as you grow a model, its data or its compute, the prediction error falls smoothly and predictably, following a power law. That lets engineers forecast how a large model will do before paying to train it.
covers: A7: What scaling laws are and why they matter

cards.title: Kaplan's Power Law
cards.text: In 2020 Kaplan and colleagues measured held-out loss for language models of many sizes and found that, for sufficiently trained models, loss follows a power law in the number of non-embedding parameters. The exponent is small, about 0.076, so doubling the model multiplies loss by roughly 0.949, about five percent lower. Loss bends toward an irreducible floor, the entropy of natural language, that no model can beat. Such tiny exponents mean returns diminish, yet improvement persists across many orders of magnitude. But Kaplan used fixed data and training settings, which overestimated how large models should be.
points: Loss vs non-embedding parameter count follows a power law
Exponent alpha_N estimated at about 0.076
Doubling model size -> multiply loss by 2^-0.076 ~ 0.949 (~5.1% lower)
Irreducible loss floor = entropy of natural language
Exponents around 0.05-0.1: diminishing but persistent returns
Flaw: fixed settings overestimated the optimal model size
cards.example: Doubling model size cuts loss by about 5.1%. Kaplan's implied recipe grew the model about 5.5x and the data only about 1.8x for 10x compute, which later turned out to starve big models of tokens.
cards.say: Kaplan's team found that bigger models lose error following a power law with a small exponent, so doubling the size cuts loss by only about five percent. Their fit assumed fixed data, which later turned out to overestimate how big models should be.

cards.title: Training Compute C = 6ND
cards.text: For a dense Transformer, where every parameter is used for every token, the total training compute is approximately six times the number of parameters times the number of training tokens. The factor six comes from about two floating-point operations per parameter per token in the forward pass and about four in the backward pass, ignoring extra costs such as attention overhead. The formula makes budget trade-offs concrete: doubling the tokens at a fixed size doubles compute, while halving the model and doubling the tokens leaves compute unchanged. Under a fixed budget, a larger model must therefore see fewer tokens.
points: Dense Transformers use all parameters for every token
Training compute C ~ 6 N D
About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward, about 4 backward
Excludes extra operations such as attention overhead
Fixed C: a bigger model N must take smaller D
cards.formula: C ~ 6 N D  (C = training FLOPs, N = parameters, D = training tokens)
cards.example: N = 2B parameters on D = 40B tokens is 1x compute; 2B on 80B tokens is 2x; 1B on 80B tokens is back to 1x. Halving the model and doubling the tokens keeps the training budget constant.
cards.say: Total training compute is about six times the parameter count times the token count, roughly two operations per parameter per token forward and four backward. So with a fixed budget, a bigger model can only see fewer tokens.

cards.title: Chinchilla: Scale Both Equally
cards.text: DeepMind's Chinchilla study re-examined scaling by training more than 400 models from 70M to 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens, matching the learning-rate schedule to each run length. Plotting loss against model size at a fixed compute budget gives a U-shaped IsoFLOP curve: left of the minimum the model is too small, right of it the model is too large and undertrained. Joining the minima shows that parameters and tokens should grow roughly equally with compute. This corrected Kaplan's advice and revealed that many earlier large models carried too many parameters for their token count.
points: IsoFLOP curve: loss vs model size at constant compute
Left of the minimum: too small; right: too few tokens
Optimum shifts to larger models and lower loss as compute grows
N_opt ~ C^0.49, D_opt ~ C^0.51: scale both about equally
Kaplan grew parameters much faster than tokens
Many earlier models were undertrained for their size
cards.formula: N_opt ~ C^0.49 ; D_opt ~ C^0.51
cards.example: For 10x compute, Chinchilla grows the model 3.09x and the tokens 3.24x, while Kaplan's older fit grew the model 5.37x but the tokens only 1.86x. GPT-3 (175B parameters, ~300B tokens) was undertrained and should have seen 3-4 trillion tokens.
cards.say: Chinchilla trained hundreds of models and found that parameters and data should grow together: ten times the compute means about three times the model and three times the data. That showed earlier giants like GPT-3 were starved of tokens.

cards.title: ~20 Tokens per Parameter
cards.text: Chinchilla itself, with 70 billion parameters trained on about 1.4 trillion tokens, illustrates a handy rule of thumb: about twenty training tokens per parameter is compute-optimal. Its predecessor Gopher had 280 billion parameters but only about 300 billion tokens, roughly one token per parameter, and was heavily undertrained for its size. At roughly the same training compute, Chinchilla used four times fewer parameters and about 4.7 times more tokens, and it outperformed Gopher on a wide range of downstream evaluations.
points: Compute-optimal is roughly 20 training tokens per parameter
Chinchilla: 70B parameters, 1.4T tokens
Gopher: 280B parameters, ~300B tokens (~1.1 tokens/parameter)
Same compute; Chinchilla scored better on many evaluations
4x fewer parameters, about 4.7x more tokens
cards.formula: D_opt ~ 20 * N  (rule of thumb)
cards.example: Gopher (2021): 280B parameters on ~300B tokens, about 1.1 tokens per parameter. Chinchilla (2022): 70B parameters on 1,400B tokens, 20 tokens per parameter. About equal compute, but Chinchilla won on many benchmarks.
cards.say: The rule of thumb from Chinchilla is about twenty training tokens for every parameter. Chinchilla had seventy billion parameters and far more tokens than the much larger Gopher, yet it scored better at similar compute.
covers: B6: Chinchilla rule of thumb: ~20 tokens per parameter

cards.title: Overtraining & Deploy-Optimal
cards.text: Compute-optimal training minimizes loss for a fixed training budget, but a deployed model also pays for every request it serves. Overtraining means training a model on more tokens than the Chinchilla-optimal amount for its size, spending more on training so that a smaller, cheaper model reaches the required quality. This differs from overfitting: with overtraining, held-out loss can keep improving. A simple lifetime-cost model adds the one-time training cost to the number of requests times the per-request inference cost, and the break-even point decides which model is cheaper in the end.
points: Compute-optimal: minimize loss per training budget
Deployment-optimal: meet quality at minimum lifetime cost
Overtraining = more tokens than compute-optimal for its size
Smaller model means lower inference memory and cost
Overtraining is not overfitting
The cheaper model depends on the number of requests
cards.formula: C_total = C_train + R * c_inf  (C_train = one-time training cost, R = requests, c_inf = cost per request); break-even R* = (C_train,B - C_train,A) / (c_inf,A - c_inf,B)
cards.example: Model A (larger): training EUR 200,000, inference EUR 0.002 per request. Model B (smaller, overtrained): EUR 300,000, EUR 0.001 per request. At 100M requests they tie; below that A is cheaper, above it B wins - at 200M, A costs EUR 600,000 versus B's EUR 500,000.
cards.say: Deployed models cost money on every request, so it often pays to overtrain a smaller model: spend more once so each answer is cheaper forever. Whether that wins depends on how many requests you actually serve.

cards.title: Limits & Practical Use
cards.text: Scaling laws are fitted to specific experiments and can fail when conditions change. Better data quality can lower loss without adding tokens, repeated data counts toward compute but brings little new information, mixture-of-experts and other architectures follow different curves, and optimizer or schedule choices shift the observed loss. Extrapolating far beyond the fitted range is risky. In practice engineers run small experiments, fit a scaling relation, validate it with a larger pilot run, then choose the deployed model on task quality, memory, latency and lifetime cost - not on training loss alone.
points: Data quality and repetition change the relationship
Dense and mixture-of-experts models scale differently
The training recipe affects the observed loss
Extrapolation becomes unreliable far from the fitted range
Workflow: small runs -> fit -> pilot validation -> deployment choice
Final choice uses quality, memory, latency and lifetime cost
cards.example: A law fitted on dense Transformers cannot be trusted to predict a mixture-of-experts model trained on heavily repeated data.
cards.say: Scaling laws are only as good as the experiments behind them. Better data, repeated tokens, new architectures and different recipes all break the fit, so engineers run small tests, then a pilot, and pick the deployed model on task quality and cost.
covers: B6: Limits and practical use of scaling laws

lessons.title: In-Context Learning
lessons.goal: Understand how a model learns tasks from prompt examples without weight updates, why that ability emerges from pretraining, and where it breaks down.

cards.title: In-Context Learning
cards.text: In-context learning is the model's ability to pick up a new task at inference time from examples written in the prompt, with no change to its weights. It emerges naturally from large-scale next-token training: the model spots the pattern in the input and adapts its internal hidden states to match it. Because nothing is learned permanently, the same model can switch between translation, sorting or classification just by being shown the right examples. This is what lets a single model serve countless tasks without ever being retrained.
points: ICL: learn a task from prompt examples with no parameter updates
Emerges from next-token prediction at scale
Model adapts its hidden-state dynamics to the pattern
Works for translation, sorting, classification and more
Nothing is stored in the weights; the task lives in the context
cards.example: Show the model 'English: cat -> German: Katze' and it can translate a new word it was never explicitly trained to translate, simply by following the pattern in the prompt.
cards.say: In-context learning is the model picking up a new task just from examples in the prompt, without changing any weights. It comes out of large-scale next-token training, and it lets one model do many tasks on demand.
covers: A6: What in-context learning is and base-model behaviour

cards.title: Base Models Just Continue
cards.text: A base model - the raw result of pretraining - has no instruction-following behavior; it only continues text in a statistically likely way. Ask it to plan a Paris trip and it rambles on with an invented itinerary full of blog-style sections rather than answering. Type 'translate Blume from German to English' and it echoes the phrase and lists related compound words instead of giving a translation. This continuation habit is why bare base models feel unusable as assistants, and why alignment matters.
points: A base model continues text, it does not answer questions
Paris prompt -> long invented travel narrative with blog-style sections
'translate Blume' -> repeats the phrase and related compound words
It imitates the expected genre, not the user's intent
A direct consequence of next-token training on raw web text
cards.example: Prompt 'I am going to have breakfast at' -> an invented travel story full of made-up facts. Prompt 'translate Blume from German to English' -> 'translate blume into english...', Blumensprudler, Blumenkistchen.
cards.say: A base model does not answer you, it just continues whatever you type. Ask it about Paris and it writes an invented blog post; ask it to translate a word and it echoes the prompt and lists related words.
covers: A6: What in-context learning is and base-model behaviour

cards.title: Few-Shot Prompting
cards.text: When the prompt contains a clear pattern of examples, a base model can produce exactly the output you want. Listing German-to-English word pairs and ending with 'Blume ->' makes the model output just 'flower', because every example ended with a single English word and nothing else. Two input/output examples of turning key-value text into JSON lead it to format a third correctly. The model is not following instructions like a human; it predicts the most probable continuation of the pattern, so the example format constrains the answer's format.
points: Consistent example pairs define the task
The example format constrains the output format
Strong structural cues give clean, minimal answers
The same mechanism produces structured output like JSON
It is pattern continuation, not true instruction following
cards.example: Milch -> milk, Butter -> butter, Fenster -> window, Blume -> flower. Or: 'name=Clara, age=32, city=Hamburg' -> {"name": "Clara", "age": 32, "city": "Hamburg"} after two similar examples.
cards.say: Give the model a few clean examples and it copies the pattern exactly. A list of German words with English translations makes it answer with one English word, and two JSON examples make it format a third correctly.
covers: A6: Few-shot prompting examples: translation and JSON

cards.title: Algorithmic vs Semantic ICL
cards.text: Researchers split in-context learning into two modes. Algorithmic ICL covers mechanical skills such as copying, sorting or completing a repeated sequence; it comes from the structure of self-attention plus large-scale training. Semantic ICL uses the model's stored world knowledge to infer what a task means, such as working out that a set of examples describes English-to-German translation. Together the two modes enable few-shot and zero-shot behaviour. The distinction matters because algorithmic skills are about pattern-matching inside the prompt, while semantic skills lean on knowledge baked into the weights.
points: Algorithmic ICL: copying, sorting, repeating patterns, matching prefixes
Semantic ICL: task inference using latent world knowledge
Algorithmic comes from self-attention and scale
Semantic uses knowledge stored during pretraining
Together they enable few-shot and zero-shot learning
cards.example: Algorithmic: 'A B C ... A B ?' -> C. Semantic: 'English cat -> German Katze; dog -> Hund' lets the model infer the translation task and handle a new word.
cards.say: In-context learning has two flavours. Algorithmic learning handles mechanical patterns like copying or completing a sequence, while semantic learning figures out the task from stored knowledge, like realising a list of word pairs is a translation task.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

cards.title: Induction Heads
cards.text: In-context learning emerges because training text is full of example-solution and question-answer patterns, so the model implicitly learns to learn. At scale, specific attention circuits called induction heads appear: they look back for an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy whatever followed it. That is the mechanism behind algorithmic ICL - completing 'A B C ... A B' with 'C' because the head finds the earlier 'A B' and copies its successor. Self-attention and positional encodings let the model locate such patterns inside the prompt.
points: Training text is full of example-answer patterns
The model implicitly learns to learn from them
Induction heads form at scale and drive algorithmic ICL
They find an earlier match and copy the token that followed
Self-attention plus positional encoding make this possible
cards.example: Given 'A B C A B ?', an induction head notices the earlier 'A B' and copies the token that came after it, 'C'.
cards.say: The ability to learn from examples emerges because training text is full of patterns. At scale the model grows induction heads, attention circuits that find an earlier match and copy whatever came next, which is how it completes sequences.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

cards.title: Limits of ICL
cards.text: In-context learning is still statistical continuation, not reasoning with guarantees. It is sensitive to the format, order and quality of the examples: the same task can succeed or fail depending on how the prompt is laid out, and a bad example can mislead the model. It offers no guarantee of correctness or safety, and a model may simply ignore the instructions or examples and follow a more familiar pattern from its training. So ICL is powerful and cheap, but it must be measured and checked rather than trusted blindly.
points: ICL is statistical continuation, not guaranteed reasoning
Sensitive to formatting, ordering and example quality
A misleading example can steer the answer wrong
No guarantee of correctness or safety
The model may ignore the prompt and follow a training pattern
cards.example: The same word-pair task gives a clean one-word answer with tidy examples but rambling text when the examples are inconsistent or their order confuses the pattern.
cards.say: In-context learning is still just pattern continuation. It is picky about formatting and example quality, gives no guarantee of being correct or safe, and the model may even ignore your prompt and follow a habit from training.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

lessons.title: Alignment: SFT
lessons.goal: Understand why models are post-trained after pretraining, how supervised fine-tuning turns a base model into an assistant, and where imitation alone falls short.

cards.title: Pretraining then Post-Training
cards.text: Modern LLMs are trained in two stages. Pretraining gives the model broad knowledge of language, facts and reasoning patterns from huge text corpora, producing a capable base model that is not yet aligned with human intentions. Post-training then shapes that raw ability into helpful, instruction-following, safe behavior that reflects human preferences. The stages are kept separate because pretraining is extremely expensive and done once, while alignment is cheap enough to iterate and gives clearer control without destroying the pretrained knowledge.
points: Stage 1 pretraining: grammar, semantics, world knowledge, general representations
Result: a powerful base model that is not aligned or instruction-following
Stage 2 post-training: follow instructions, behave helpfully and appropriately
Post-training reduces harmful, biased or unsafe behaviour and encodes preferences
Pretraining is expensive and done once; alignment is cheaper and iterated
The split avoids catastrophic deviation from pretrained knowledge
cards.example: A base model that knows grammar and world facts will still ramble; post-training turns the same weights into an assistant that answers, summarises and refuses unsafe requests.
cards.say: Models are built in two stages. Pretraining soaks up language and knowledge from huge text corpora and leaves a capable but unruly base model; post-training then shapes that raw ability into a helpful, safe assistant. The split keeps the expensive step fixed while alignment stays cheap to iterate.

cards.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning
cards.text: Supervised fine-tuning continues training the pretrained model with the same next-token loss, but on high-quality human-written instruction-response pairs instead of raw web text. A pair like 'Summarize this text' with a clean summary teaches the model to follow instructions and answer in the right shape. Public datasets include Google's FLAN collection and Alpaca, Dolly and OIG, though many industrial datasets stay private. The key lesson from this work is that data quality matters more than quantity: a small set of well-written examples can outperform a much larger noisy one.
points: SFT = continued training with the next-token loss on instruction-response pairs
Example: 'Summarize this text' -> a clean summary
Data sources: FLAN (Google), Alpaca/Dolly/OIG; many datasets are private
Teaches instruction following, structured answers and safe refusals
Data quality matters more than quantity
cards.formula: Same loss as pretraining: L = - sum_t log p_theta(y_t | prompt, y_<t), applied to curated responses
cards.example: A pair 'Summarize this paragraph' followed by a two-sentence summary trains compression rather than rambling. Data guidelines: clear, concise, correct, polite and safe.
cards.say: Supervised fine-tuning keeps the same next-token loss but feeds it human-written instruction and response pairs. That is what teaches a base model to follow instructions and answer cleanly, and the quality of the examples matters far more than their number.
covers: A6: Supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) and InstructGPT

cards.title: InstructGPT: 13k Examples
cards.text: OpenAI's InstructGPT work combined supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from human feedback and marked the shift from base models to assistant models, enabling the conversational behavior seen in ChatGPT. Its striking finding was that data quality beats quantity: about 40 trained annotators wrote roughly 13,000 instruction-response examples following strict style guidelines. These covered summarization, closed-book question answering, reasoning explanations, creative writing, coding and safe refusals. Even a relatively small but well-curated set like this made the model markedly more helpful and better aligned.
points: InstructGPT: SFT plus RLHF, turning a base LM into an assistant LM
Enabled ChatGPT-style conversational behaviour
About 40 trained annotators wrote ~13,000 examples
Strict style guidelines: clear, concise, correct, polite, safe
Tasks: summarization, closed-book QA, reasoning, creative writing, coding, refusals
Data quality mattered more than quantity
cards.example: Roughly 13,000 human-written pairs from about 40 annotators produced a model that humans preferred to a much larger, unaligned baseline - a small, careful dataset with an outsized effect.
cards.say: InstructGPT showed that a small, carefully written dataset can do a lot. About forty trained annotators wrote around thirteen thousand instruction and response examples under strict guidelines, and combining fine-tuning with human feedback turned a base model into a genuine assistant.
covers: A6: Supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) and InstructGPT

cards.title: ChatGPT = FM + Alignment
cards.text: ChatGPT is a product built on top of a foundation model, not a foundation model itself. The underlying model is aligned with instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback so it follows what the user wants, and an interface layer then adds the chat system, memory, safety filters and user experience. Successive ChatGPT versions have used newer foundation models: the 2022 launch used GPT-3.5, the 2023 release moved to GPT-4, and later versions use newer models still. Alignment is the layer that turns raw capability into usable, well-behaved conversation.
points: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface
Alignment: instruction tuning plus RLHF so the model follows human intent
Interface: chat system, memory, safety filters and user experience
ChatGPT uses a foundation model but is not one itself
2022 -> GPT-3.5, 2023 -> GPT-4, later -> newer models
cards.example: ChatGPT (Nov 2022) -> GPT-3.5; ChatGPT-4 (Mar 2023) -> GPT-4; ChatGPT 5 (2025) -> GPT-5. The foundation model changes while the alignment and interface layers keep the product consistent.
cards.say: ChatGPT itself is a product: a foundation model, plus an alignment layer of instruction tuning and human feedback, plus the chat interface with memory and safety filters. Remove any of those layers and the experience falls apart.
covers: A1: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface (1.4)

cards.title: Limits of SFT
cards.text: SFT only teaches imitation: the model copies human demonstrations without learning which answers are better or worse. Because every training example counts as correct, there is no negative feedback to penalize bad or unsafe answers. The next-token loss rewards fluent text rather than accurate text, so hallucinations can persist. SFT models also struggle with ambiguous, open-ended or multi-turn requests and can overfit to a verbose, overly polite assistant tone. These weaknesses motivate preference-based methods such as RLHF, covered next.
points: Imitation only: no notion of better versus worse
No negative feedback: cannot penalize bad or unsafe responses
No truthfulness guarantee: the loss rewards fluency, so hallucinations persist
Limited safety: it shows safe answers but cannot punish unsafe ones
Poor handling of ambiguity, multi-turn or conflicting instructions
Style overfitting: verbose, overly polite, generic tone
cards.example: An SFT model may answer a factual question with a fluent but wrong paragraph, because the loss rewarded how the sentence read, not whether it was true.
cards.say: Fine-tuning by imitation has a ceiling. The model never learns which answers are better or worse, has no way to penalise bad or unsafe ones, and can drift into a wordy, over-polite tone. That is exactly why preference-based methods come next.

lessons.title: Alignment: Human Preferences
lessons.goal: Understand why aligning to human preferences is hard, how preference data is collected, and how RLHF and DPO turn those preferences into a better model.

cards.title: Why Preferences Are Hard
cards.text: For tasks like math or factual questions it is clear what a good answer looks like, but many real questions touch topics where people deeply disagree. Culture, politics, religion, income and identity all shape what someone expects from an AI. A model that answers frankly may upset some users, while one that refuses everything becomes useless, and companies fear offensive or legally risky outputs. Preference fine-tuning tries to shape behavior according to human values, yet there is no single universal preference, and encoding values into a model is extremely difficult.
points: Clear-cut tasks (math, summarization, factual QA) have an obvious target
Controversial topics (e.g., abortion, immigration) have no globally accepted answer
Disagreement stems from culture, politics, socioeconomics, identity, religion
Trade-off: frank answers can offend; refusing everything makes a model useless
Companies worry about offence, legal risk and reputation
Preferences are multiple, conflicting, dynamic and context-dependent
cards.example: Ask about abortion or immigration policy and there is no answer that satisfies everyone: a frank reply upsets one group, a refusal disappoints another.
cards.say: For many questions there is simply no correct answer that everyone agrees on. Culture, politics and identity shape what people want from an AI, so a frank answer offends some users while refusing everything makes the model useless. That tension is what makes alignment hard.
covers: A7: Why human preference is hard to align to

cards.title: Absolute vs Relative Ratings
cards.text: One idea is to let humans score the SFT model's answers, then use those scores to update its parameters. Absolute scores, for example 1 to 7, are noisy: annotators disagree, drift stricter or more lenient over time, scores do not transfer between task types, and models learn to game superficial traits such as length or politeness. So absolute ratings are not used for preference alignment. Instead humans compare or rank answers, which is more reliable, avoids calibration problems and is cognitively easier, because 'A beats B' stays stable even when a scale would shift.
points: Step 1: humans judge SFT answers; step 2: judgments update the model
Absolute ratings (1-7) are inconsistent across annotators and uncalibrated
Baseline drift: annotators become stricter or more lenient over time
Numeric scales do not generalize across task types (poems vs proofs)
Scale hacking: models mimic high-score traits like verbosity or politeness
Relative (pairwise/ranking) judgments are more stable, faster and less noisy
cards.example: On a 1-7 scale the same Rayleigh-scattering answer gets a wide spread of scores, but faced with two answers most people agree on which is better.
cards.say: Scoring answers from one to seven sounds simple but is noisy. Different annotators disagree, they drift over time, and models learn to fake high-scoring traits like length and politeness. So instead we ask people to compare answers, which is far more stable.
covers: A7: Collecting human preferences: absolute vs. relative ratings

cards.title: Building Preference Data
cards.text: Collection starts with a diverse prompt dataset covering QA, summarization, math, coding, safety-critical, creative and multi-turn tasks. For each prompt several candidate answers are sampled, mostly from the SFT model and sometimes from other models, with different decoding settings for diversity. Annotators then rank the answers, and each ranking is broken into pairwise comparisons such as best versus second-best and best versus third-best. The result is a dataset of triples: a prompt, a preferred answer and a less preferred answer, following the InstructGPT recipe.
points: Use a diverse prompt set (QA, summarization, math, coding, safety, creative, multi-turn)
Sample several candidates per prompt, often from the SFT model, with varied decoding
Humans rank the candidates given the prompt
A ranking of K answers becomes up to K(K-1)/2 pairwise comparisons
Each entry is (x, y_w, y_l): prompt, preferred answer, less preferred answer
cards.formula: D = {(x, y_w, y_l)}; candidates y_1..y_K ~ pi_SFT(y|x); pairs from a full ranking of K = K(K-1)/2
cards.example: Ranking A > B > C > D expands into pairs (A,B), (A,C), (A,D), (B,C), (B,D), (C,D) - six preference pairs from four answers.
cards.say: To collect preferences we gather many prompts, let the model generate several answers each, and ask people to rank them. Each ranking is then split into simple winner-versus-loser pairs, giving the prompt, chosen answer and rejected answer triples that training needs.
covers: A7: Building the human preference dataset

cards.title: Reinforcement Learning Basics
cards.text: Reinforcement learning is a paradigm in which an agent learns a sequence of decisions by acting in an environment and receiving rewards; over time it does rewarded actions more often, much like training an animal, without anyone telling it the exact right action. In RLHF the agent is the LLM, the state is the prompt or conversation history, and the action is generating text, token by token or as a full answer. The reward is a score from a reward model that represents human preferences, and the policy is the model's probability distribution over answers.
points: RL: agent acts, environment reacts, agent gets reward; higher-reward actions grow more frequent
Nobody tells the agent the exact right action; it discovers a strategy
Agent = the LLM; state = prompt or dialogue context
Action = generating text, token by token or as a full answer
Reward = a reward-model score representing human preference
Policy pi_theta(y|x) is the probability of answer y; the objective maximizes expected reward
cards.formula: theta* = argmax_theta E_{x~D, y~pi_theta(.|x)} [ r(x, y) ]
cards.example: An analogy is training an animal or teaching a child: good behavior is rewarded, bad behavior is not, and the learner discovers a strategy instead of being handed the answer.
cards.say: Reinforcement learning is learning by trial and reward, not by being shown the right answer. In RLHF the AI is the agent, the prompt is its situation, the generated text is its action, and a reward-model score is how good that action was.
covers: A7: Reinforcement learning basics and RLHF core concepts

cards.title: The Reward Model
cards.text: The reward model is usually the same transformer architecture as the base model, but its output head produces a single scalar score instead of next-token probabilities. It never generates text; it only scores a prompt-answer pair, with a higher score meaning better according to humans. It is trained on preference pairs so the preferred answer scores higher than the rejected one, using the Bradley-Terry logistic loss on the score difference. Once trained it can score any answer, identify good versus bad completions, reject harmful outputs and guide policy optimization.
points: Same transformer architecture as the base LLM, but outputs a scalar score
Learns relative quality, not absolute ratings
Captures correctness, helpfulness, clarity, safety, refusal quality, conciseness
Does not generate text; it is trained so r(x, y_w) > r(x, y_l)
Loss is near zero when the preferred answer scores much higher, large when the order is wrong
Used to rank answers, reject harmful completions and guide PPO
cards.formula: P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l)); L_RM = - E[ log sigma( r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l) ) ]
cards.example: If the chosen answer scores 2.0 and the rejected one 0.5, the difference of 1.5 gives a tiny loss; if the rejected answer scores higher, the loss grows and the model is corrected.
cards.say: The reward model is the base model with a single-number output head. It never writes text, it only scores how good an answer is. Trained on winner-loser pairs with a logistic loss, it learns to give preferred answers higher scores than rejected ones.
covers: A7: Reward model and Bradley-Terry training

cards.title: RLHF: Two Routes
cards.text: After collecting preference data there are two routes. GPT-3 (2020) was a pure pretrained model; InstructGPT (2022) added SFT and RLHF; ChatGPT (late 2022) applied the same recipe to GPT-3.5; and in 2023 DPO appeared as a simpler alternative. The RLHF route trains a separate reward model on the comparisons and then optimizes the SFT model with the PPO reinforcement-learning algorithm. The DPO route instead uses the preference pairs directly with a closed-form loss and needs neither a reward model nor reinforcement learning.
points: 2020: GPT-3 (pretrained only)
2022: InstructGPT = GPT-3 + SFT + RLHF
Late 2022: ChatGPT = GPT-3.5 + SFT + RLHF
2023: DPO introduced
RLHF/PPO: train a reward model, then optimize the SFT model with PPO
DPO: use preference pairs directly, no reward model and no RL
cards.example: GPT-3 2020 (pretrained), InstructGPT 2022 (SFT + RLHF), ChatGPT late 2022 (same recipe on GPT-3.5), DPO 2023 (direct preference optimization).
cards.say: Once you have preference data there are two ways forward. RLHF trains a separate reward model and then tunes the model with reinforcement learning, while DPO skips both and learns directly from the winner-loser pairs. The field moved from plain pretraining to these methods in just a few years.
covers: A7: Timeline and two routes: RLHF with PPO vs. DPO

cards.title: RLHF with PPO and KL
cards.text: The RLHF objective takes prompts, samples answers from the policy being trained (initialized from the SFT model), and maximizes the average reward-model score of those answers. A KL-divergence penalty, weighted by beta, keeps the new policy from drifting too far from the reference SFT model, which prevents reward hacking and keeps language fluent. PPO is the reinforcement-learning algorithm used to optimize this objective stably. In the InstructGPT paper humans preferred RLHF models over much larger baselines: even a 1.3B PPO model beat all non-RLHF models, including the 175B GPT-3.
points: Policy pi_theta starts from the SFT model and generates candidate answers
Reward term: how much humans like the answer, via the reward model
KL penalty: do not drift too far from the SFT reference model
beta controls how strongly drift from SFT is penalized
PPO optimizes this objective stably
A 1.3B PPO model beats 175B non-RLHF models in human evaluation
cards.formula: max_theta E[ r_phi(x, y) ] - beta * D_KL( pi_theta(y|x) || pi_ref(y|x) )
cards.example: In human comparisons a 1.3B-parameter PPO model was judged better than the 175B GPT-3, showing that alignment, not just size, drives preference.
cards.say: RLHF trains the model to earn higher reward scores, but with a leash: a penalty keeps it close to the original fine-tuned model so it cannot game the reward and become incoherent. With this setup even a small aligned model can beat a much larger unaligned one.
covers: A7: RLHF objective with PPO and KL penalty; InstructGPT results

cards.title: Direct Preference Optimization
cards.text: Direct Preference Optimization optimizes the LLM directly on preference pairs, without training a separate reward model and without PPO. It is supervised learning, but not standard SFT: its special loss is mathematically derived from the RLHF objective, with the policy's log-probability ratio to the reference model acting as an implicit reward. The loss pushes the model to increase the relative likelihood of the preferred answer over the rejected one compared to the reference model. This yields RLHF-quality alignment with more stable optimization and much cheaper compute, which is why DPO is widely adopted.
points: No reward model and no RL/PPO needed
Supervised learning on preference pairs with a loss derived from RLHF
Raises the probability of the chosen answer relative to the rejected one, against the reference model
beta plays the same role as the KL weight in RLHF
RLHF-quality alignment, more stable, much cheaper compute
Introduced 2023 and widely adopted
cards.formula: L_DPO = - E[ log sigma( beta*log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta*log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) ) ]; implicit reward r(x,y) = beta*log(pi_theta(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x))
cards.example: DPO treats the language model itself as a hidden reward model: the log-ratio of its probabilities to the reference model stands in for the reward, so no separate scorer is trained.
cards.say: DPO reaches the same goal far more directly. Instead of training a reward model and running reinforcement learning, it applies a special loss straight to the winner-loser pairs, nudging chosen answers up and rejected ones down relative to the reference model.

lessons.title: Decoding & Sampling
lessons.goal: Explain how a model's next-token probabilities are turned into actual text, and how greedy, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p trade determinism against creativity.

cards.title: Why Decoding Matters
cards.text: For every next token the model outputs a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary, and that distribution is long-tailed: a few likely tokens, many medium ones, and a huge tail of unlikely ones. Decoding is the rule that turns these probabilities into an actual token choice. That single choice strongly controls how deterministic or creative the text is, its safety and factual accuracy, its diversity and style, and the risk of repetition or hallucination. Different tasks want different decoding, so it is one of the most important engineering knobs in an AI system.
points: Next-token distribution is long-tailed: few high, many medium, huge low tail
Decoding = the rule that picks a token from the distribution
Controls determinism versus creativity
Affects safety, factuality, diversity and style
Affects the risk of repetition and hallucination
cards.say: For each next word the model produces a probability distribution, and it is very long-tailed, with a few likely words and a huge tail of unlikely ones. Decoding is simply how we pick from that list, and that choice controls how creative, safe and repeatable the output is.

cards.title: Stable Softmax (Log-Sum-Exp)
cards.text: Softmax turns the model's raw scores, called logits, into probabilities by exponentiating them and dividing by their sum. Inside an LLM logits can be large, for example 50, 80 or 200, and exponentiating such values overflows 32-bit floating point to infinity or NaN, breaking the distribution. The fix is to subtract the largest logit from all logits before exponentiating: the biggest term becomes e to the power zero, which is one, and every other term stays at most one, so nothing overflows. The resulting probabilities are mathematically identical, only safer to compute.
points: Softmax converts logits into probabilities summing to 1
Big logits (50, 80, 200) overflow to inf or NaN
Subtract the maximum logit m first
Largest term becomes e^0 = 1, others stay <= 1
Probabilities are unchanged, just numerically stable
cards.formula: p_i = exp(z_i - m) / sum_j(exp(z_j - m)), with m = max_j z_j (z: logits)
cards.example: Logits [200, 198, 150]: naive softmax overflows to NaN because e^200 exceeds the float32 range, but subtracting the max gives e^0, e^-2 and e^-50 and correct probabilities.
cards.say: Softmax turns raw scores into probabilities, but very large scores overflow the computer and produce errors. The trick is to subtract the biggest score first, which keeps every value small while leaving the probabilities exactly the same.

cards.title: Greedy Decoding
cards.text: Greedy decoding always picks the single most probable next token: the argmax at every step. It is deterministic, simple and fast, and usually produces fluent text. But it makes only locally optimal choices with no look-ahead, so one early mistake can snowball through a long sequence. It always outputs the same text, ignores most of the distribution, tends to fall into repetition loops, and picks safe but dull continuations. That makes it weak for creative tasks but fine for translation and factual question answering.
points: Pick the argmax at every step
Deterministic, simple, fast, usually fluent
Locally optimal but globally suboptimal
No diversity, repetition loops, error snowballing
Ignores alternatives; weak on creative tasks
cards.formula: y_t = argmax_w P(w | y_<t)
cards.example: Prompt 'Yesterday I went to the ___' with candidates store 0.30, restaurant 0.20, park 0.15, cinema 0.10, gym 0.08, beach 0.06, doctor 0.04, bank 0.03, concert 0.02, office 0.02. Greedy always outputs 'store' (0.30).
cards.say: Greedy decoding just takes the most likely next word every time. It is fast and repeatable, but it never explores alternatives, so it gets stuck in loops and can derail if it makes one bad choice early on.

cards.title: Random Sampling
cards.text: Random sampling draws the next token at random in proportion to its probability instead of always taking the top one. In practice tokens are sorted by probability, their cumulative sum is computed, a uniform random number r between zero and one is drawn, and the first token whose cumulative probability crosses r is chosen. This adds variability and creativity, avoids repetitive output and reflects the whole distribution, which is what open-ended generation needs. The downside is that rare long-tail tokens can occasionally be chosen, producing nonsense.
points: Sample a token according to its probability
Sort tokens, then compute cumulative probabilities
Draw a uniform random number r in [0,1]
Pick the first token whose cumulative probability exceeds r
Adds creativity and diversity; can pick tail tokens
cards.formula: choose token i where C_(i-1) <= r < C_i, C_i = sum over j<=i of p_j, r ~ Uniform(0,1)
cards.example: Sorted store 0.30, restaurant 0.20, park 0.15, cinema 0.10, gym 0.08, beach 0.06, doctor 0.04, bank 0.03, concert 0.02, office 0.02; cumulative 0.30, 0.50, 0.65, 0.75, 0.83, 0.89, 0.93, 0.96, 0.98, 1.00. A draw with r between 0.65 and 0.75 selects 'cinema'.
cards.say: Random sampling picks the next word at random, weighted by how likely it is. We sort the words, add up their probabilities, and drop a random point on that scale to choose one, so the output varies and feels more creative.
covers: A5: Random Sampling via Cumulative Probabilities

cards.title: Temperature
cards.text: Temperature rescales the logits before softmax to control how sharp the distribution is. Dividing the logits by a value T below one sharpens the distribution, making the model more confident and deterministic; T above one flattens it, making the output more random and exploratory; T equal to one keeps the original distribution. Moderate values increase diversity and reduce repetition, but too low gives boring, deterministic text and too high produces incoherent noise. As T approaches zero, temperature sampling converges to greedy decoding.
points: Divide the logits by temperature T before softmax
T = 1 keeps the original distribution
T < 1: sharper, more deterministic (T -> 0 approaches greedy)
T > 1: flatter, more random
Tunable creativity; too low is boring, too high is incoherent
cards.formula: p_i(T) = exp(z_i / T) / sum_j(exp(z_j / T)); T > 0 (z: logits, T: temperature)
cards.example: From the store distribution [0.30, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, ...], T = 0.5 sharpens it to about [0.51, 0.23, 0.13, ...], while T = 2 flattens it to about [0.19, 0.155, 0.13, 0.11, 0.10, ...].
cards.say: Temperature stretches or squeezes the probabilities. A low temperature makes the model pick its favourite word almost every time, a high temperature flattens the choices so the output wanders, and one keeps the original balance.

cards.title: Top-k Sampling
cards.text: Top-k sampling keeps only the k most probable tokens, discards the rest, renormalizes the kept probabilities so they sum to one, and samples from that smaller set. This removes the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping diversity among good candidates, and it is simple and fast. Its weakness is the fixed k: when the distribution is flat, k can be too restrictive and cut off good options, and when the model is very confident, k can be too permissive and let in bad ones.
points: Sort tokens and keep only the top k
Renormalize the kept probabilities to sum to 1
Sample from the reduced distribution
Removes the long tail, keeps plausible options, fast
Fixed k is too restrictive for flat, too permissive for peaked distributions
cards.formula: p'_i = p_i / sum over j in TopK of p_j, for i in TopK, else 0
cards.example: k = 3 keeps store 0.30, restaurant 0.20, park 0.15 (sum 0.65); renormalized they become 0.46, 0.31 and 0.23, and sampling then picks among these three.
cards.say: Top-k keeps only the k most likely words and throws away the rest, then renormalizes and samples among them. It trims the nonsense, but a fixed k is clumsy because the right number of candidates changes from step to step.

cards.title: Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
cards.text: Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of most probable tokens whose cumulative probability reaches at least p, renormalizes within this set and samples from it. Unlike top-k, the size of the set adapts to the distribution: few tokens when the model is confident, many when it is uncertain. This removes long-tail noise and tends to give more natural text than top-k. It needs sorting, so it costs slightly more compute, and it can keep many tokens when the distribution is flat.
points: Sort descending and compute cumulative probabilities
Keep the smallest set with cumulative probability >= p
Renormalize within the nucleus and sample
Set size adapts to the shape of the distribution
Reduces tail noise; more natural than top-k; small sorting cost
cards.formula: Nucleus V_p = smallest set with sum of p_i over V_p >= p; p'_i = p_i / sum over V_p of p_j
cards.example: With p = 0.8 and cumulative 0.30, 0.50, 0.65, 0.75, 0.83, the nucleus is the top 5 tokens (mass 0.83); renormalized they become 0.36, 0.24, 0.18, 0.12, 0.10, and a draw selects 'restaurant'.
cards.say: Top-p keeps the smallest group of likely words whose probabilities add up to at least p, then samples inside that group. Because the group grows or shrinks with the model's confidence, it adapts better than a fixed top-k and usually reads more naturally.

cards.title: Comparing Strategies
cards.text: The strategies differ in determinism, diversity, risk of nonsense and typical use. Greedy is highly deterministic with no diversity and low risk, good for translation and factual question answering. Temperature gives tunable diversity and risk, suited to creative writing. Top-k is medium on every axis and fits constrained generation. Top-p gives high diversity with low-to-medium risk and suits most open-ended tasks. In short, decoding is a control knob on the model's personality: more deterministic is safer and factual, more stochastic is more creative but riskier.
points: Greedy: high determinism, no diversity, low risk -> translation, factual QA
Temperature: tunable diversity and risk -> creative writing
Top-k: medium on all axes -> constrained generation
Top-p: medium determinism, high diversity, low-to-medium risk -> most open-ended tasks
Deterministic = safer and factual; stochastic = creative but riskier
cards.example: Table (Determinism / Diversity / Risk / Best use): Greedy High/None/Low/translation and factual QA; Temperature Medium/Tunable/Tunable/creative writing; Top-k Medium/Medium/Medium/constrained generation; Top-p Medium/High/Low-Medium/most open-ended tasks.
cards.say: Each strategy is a different setting on one dial. Greedy is safe and repeatable, temperature trades some safety for variety, top-k and top-p trim the tail, and the right choice depends on whether you want factual or creative output.

lessons.title: Measuring Models
lessons.goal: Show why and how language models are evaluated, and how perplexity, accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE and pass@k each measure a different kind of quality.

cards.title: Why and How We Evaluate
cards.text: Language models are powerful but unpredictable: they give plausible but wrong answers, fail silently, and can behave very differently after small changes in data mix, sampling or loss. So engineers evaluate them continuously, not once, to track quality, reliability and safety, to compare architectures, scaling and alignment methods, and to check generalization and real-world fit. The practical questions are whether a model can reliably automate a workflow, call tools correctly, avoid hallucination and follow multi-turn instructions. Evaluation works at three levels: intrinsic, task-level and practical capability.
points: LLMs give plausible but wrong answers and can fail silently
Small changes in data, sampling or loss can shift behaviour a lot
Evaluate continuously: quality, reliability, safety, training progress, comparison, fit
Engineer questions: workflow reliability, tool calls, hallucination, multi-turn, domain fit
Three levels: intrinsic, task-level, practical capability
Not covered here: efficiency, economic and robustness/adversarial evaluation
cards.example: Practical capability areas the course checks: multi-turn instructions, tool use, long-horizon reasoning, factuality and hallucination, and domain or modality-specific performance.
cards.say: Models look confident even when they are wrong, and small training changes can shift how they behave. So we test them again and again on three levels: how well they predict text, how well they do on standard tasks, and how well they handle real practical jobs.
covers: A7: Why and how LLMs are evaluated

cards.title: Perplexity
cards.text: Perplexity is the core metric for pretraining and measures how well a model predicts the next token in held-out text. It is the exponential of the average negative log-probability the model gives to each correct next token, so it is directly tied to cross-entropy loss. Intuitively it is the model's average uncertainty: a perplexity of ten means the model is about as unsure as choosing uniformly among ten tokens. Lower is better, but perplexity only reflects token prediction and says nothing about reasoning, instruction following, tool use, factuality or safety.
points: Measures next-token prediction quality; lower is better
Uses the probabilities assigned to the correct next tokens
Equals the exponential of the cross-entropy loss
Interpretable as average uncertainty (effective number of choices)
PPL = 1 is perfect; PPL = k is like a uniform choice among k tokens
Does not measure reasoning, instruction following, tool use, factuality or safety
cards.formula: PPL = exp( -(1/T) * sum over t=1..T of log p(x_t | x_<t) ) = exp(cross-entropy loss); T = number of tokens, x_t = correct token, p = model probability
cards.example: PPL = 1 means perfect prediction; a perplexity of 10 means the model is about as uncertain as guessing uniformly among 10 tokens. A low-perplexity model can still fail badly on real tasks.
cards.say: Perplexity is how surprised the model is by the real next word. It is the exponential of the average loss, so a perplexity of ten is like being unsure among ten choices. Lower is better, but it only measures next-word prediction, not reasoning or usefulness.

cards.title: Accuracy, BLEU and ROUGE
cards.text: Task-level metrics score models on specific NLP tasks and still matter for fine-tuning. Accuracy is the share of correct predictions in classification tasks like sentiment analysis; it is simple and fits single-label decisions. BLEU, used for machine translation, is precision-oriented: of the n-grams the model produced, how many appear in the reference, plus a brevity penalty so short outputs cannot cheat. ROUGE, used for summarisation, is recall-oriented: of the n-grams in the reference, how many the model included; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence, which respects word order.
points: Accuracy = correct predictions / all predictions; simple, single-label
BLEU: n-gram precision against reference translations + brevity penalty
BLEU scale 0-100; 30-40 is decent MT, 50+ is strong MT
ROUGE: n-gram recall against the reference summary
ROUGE-1 unigram, ROUGE-2 bigram, ROUGE-L longest common subsequence
BLEU asks 'how much of my output is correct?'; ROUGE asks 'how much of the reference did I cover?'
cards.formula: BLEU n-gram precision p_n = matching n-grams / candidate n-grams; brevity penalty BP = 1 if c > r else exp(1 - r/c). ROUGE-N = matching n-grams / reference n-grams; ROUGE-L = LCS length / reference length. Accuracy = correct / total.
cards.example: BLEU reference 'the cat is on the mat' vs candidate 'the cat sat on the': 1-gram 4/5, 2-gram 2/4, with a brevity penalty since the candidate is shorter. ROUGE reference 'cats sit on warm mats in the sun' vs candidate 'cats sit on mats': ROUGE-1 = 4/8, ROUGE-2 = 2/7, ROUGE-L = 4/8.
cards.say: Accuracy is simply the share it gets right. BLEU checks how much of the model's translation matches the reference, while ROUGE checks how much of the reference summary the model covered. Each asks a different question about the output.
covers: A7: Task-level metrics: accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE

cards.title: Pass@k for Code Generation
cards.text: Pass@k is the standard metric for code generation: it estimates the probability that at least one of k generated solutions passes the unit tests. To estimate it without bias, the model generates n samples and c of them are correct, and the formula computes the chance that a random subset of k samples contains at least one correct one. It measures how robust and reliable code generation is across attempts. Larger k always gives a higher pass@k, and pass@1 is simply the fraction of correct samples c over n.
points: Used in code-generation benchmarks such as HumanEval
Probability that at least one of k samples is correct
Unbiased estimator uses n generated samples with c correct
pass@1 equals the fraction c/n
Larger k gives a higher pass@k
Measures robustness and reliability of code generation
cards.formula: pass@k = E_tasks[ 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k) ]; n = samples generated, c = correct samples, k = samples allowed, C = binomial coefficient
cards.example: Prompt: write add(a, b) returning the sum of two integers. With n = 10 samples and c = 3 correct, pass@1 = 1 - C(7,1)/C(10,1) = 0.30, so it solves it 30% of the time on the first try; pass@5 = 1 - C(7,5)/C(10,5) = 1 - 21/252 = about 0.917, a 91.7% chance that at least one of five tries is correct.
cards.say: Pass at k measures the chance that at least one of k code attempts passes the hidden tests. If the model generates ten solutions and three are correct, the first attempt works thirty percent of the time, but any of five attempts works about ninety-two percent of the time.

lessons.title: Benchmarks
lessons.goal: Survey the standard benchmarks that score knowledge, reasoning, coding, safety and agentic capability, and why no single score captures a model's true quality.

cards.title: MMLU Knowledge Benchmark
cards.text: A benchmark is a standardized test suite that scores every model the same way. MMLU, the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark, tests broad knowledge and reasoning over 57 subjects, from STEM through humanities and social sciences to law, medicine and professional exams. Every question is multiple choice with four options and the score is accuracy, so random guessing gives 25%. Rough bands help interpret scores: below 50% is under undergraduate level, top frontier models reach 85-90% or more, and around 95% counts as expert level. Questions test subject knowledge, basic reasoning and formula understanding.
points: Benchmark = a fixed, comparably scored test suite
MMLU covers 57 subjects: STEM, humanities, social sciences, law, medicine, professions
Multiple choice (A-D), scored by accuracy; guessing baseline 25%
Below 50% is under undergraduate; 50-70% a strong base model
70-85% instruct-tuned quality; 85-90%+ frontier; about 95% expert
Tests subject knowledge, reasoning, formula understanding, professional competency
cards.formula: Example physics: t = v / a = (30 m/s) / (3 m/s^2) = 10 s
cards.example: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s^2 to 30 m/s; options 5 s, 8 s, 10 s, 12 s, correct answer C (10 s). Random guessing across four options would score 25%.
cards.say: MMLU is a standard knowledge test covering fifty-seven subjects, all multiple choice with four options and scored as accuracy. Below fifty percent is under undergraduate level, while top models score in the high eighties and expert level is around ninety-five percent.

cards.title: BIG-Bench: Beyond Standard NLP
cards.text: BIG-Bench, short for Beyond the Imitation Game, is a large community benchmark of about 200 tasks contributed by more than 450 researchers. It probes human-like thinking rather than textbook knowledge, covering logic, math puzzles, symbolic manipulation, common sense, ethics, creativity, multilingual and deliberately weird off-distribution problems, in many formats with task-specific metrics, so there is no single score. It revealed emergent abilities that appear only at certain model scales and exposes weaknesses outside the training distribution. Two famous examples are emoji arithmetic and reversing a string.
points: About 200 tasks contributed by 450+ researchers
Covers logic, math puzzles, symbolic manipulation, common sense, ethics, creativity, multilingual, off-distribution tasks
Many formats and metrics; no single score, it is a suite
Reveals emergent abilities that appear only above a certain scale
Example emoji arithmetic: models ignore the given symbol-to-number mapping and invent a story
Example reverse string 'hello' -> 'olleh': needs exact symbolic manipulation that breaks autoregressive token patterns
cards.example: Emoji arithmetic gives a mapping such as one emoji = 2 and another = 5 and asks for a sum; LLMs treat it as a story, ignore the mapping and hallucinate meaning. Reversing 'hello' to 'olleh' is hard because text is split into tokens, not characters.
cards.say: BIG-Bench is a huge community test suite of around two hundred unusual tasks, from logic puzzles to reversing a string. It shows abilities that only appear once a model is large enough, and it exposes failures on problems far outside ordinary training data.

cards.title: HumanEval Coding Benchmark
cards.text: HumanEval is the standard benchmark for coding models, made of 164 hand-written Python tasks. Each task gives a natural-language description and a function signature, and the model must write an executable function that passes hidden unit tests. Grading is objective pass or fail: if all tests pass the solution is correct, if any fails it is wrong, and results are reported as pass@k. It tests understanding, reasoning, planning and correctness, and it correlates strongly with real-world coding performance.
points: 164 hand-written Python programming tasks
Model must write an executable function passing hidden unit tests
Metric: pass@k
Objective pass/fail: all tests pass = correct, any failure = wrong
Tests reasoning, planning, algorithmic thinking and correctness
Strongly correlated with real-world coding performance
cards.example: Task add(a, b) should return 'def add(a, b): return a + b'; hidden tests include add(2, 3) == 5, add(-1, 4) == 3 and add(0, 0) == 0.
cards.say: HumanEval gives a model one hundred sixty-four small Python problems and runs hidden tests on the code it writes. If every test passes the solution counts as correct, and the score is the pass-at-k rate, which lines up well with real coding skill.

cards.title: Long-Horizon Reasoning
cards.text: Long-horizon reasoning tests whether a model can carry out long multi-step tasks where later steps depend on earlier ones. It needs planning, breaking a problem into parts, holding constraints in mind, and catching its own intermediate mistakes. Coding benchmarks are typical because fixing a real bug takes many dependent steps: SWE-bench checks bug fixing in real repositories and Aider Polyglot checks multi-language coding. Scores are task pass rates from 0 to 100%, and they cannot be predicted from classical metrics such as MMLU. This capability is critical for agents.
points: Multi-step, dependency-heavy tasks
Needs planning, decomposition, constraint tracking, error detection and correction
Examples: data transformations, code repair, multi-part problems, agentic loops
Benchmarks: SWE-bench (bug fixing), Aider Polyglot (multi-language code)
Scale: task pass rate 0-100%
Critical for agents; not predictable from MMLU
cards.example: SWE-bench gives a real repository bug and grades whether the model's patch makes the failing tests pass; Aider Polyglot repeats this across many programming languages. Both report a task pass rate from 0 to 100%.
cards.say: Long-horizon tasks are long chains of steps where each depends on the last, like fixing a real bug in a codebase. The model must plan, keep track and catch its own errors, and the score is the share of whole tasks it completes.

cards.title: Safety, Factuality & Deception
cards.text: Safety evaluation checks whether a model can cause harm. Toxicity tests detect offensive or hateful language, and bias tests look for discrimination by gender, race or age. Harmful-instruction tests, including jailbreaks with adversarial prompts, check whether the model can be tricked into giving dangerous advice, while privacy tests probe whether it leaks user data or memorised training text. A related dimension is factuality and deception: whether the model invents facts, states wrong things confidently, misreports success such as claiming it fixed a bug when it did not, or fails to retract errors. These are essential for trust.
points: Toxicity: offensive or hateful language (RealToxicityPrompts, ToxiGen)
Bias and fairness: discrimination by gender, race, age (BiasBench, CrowS-Pairs)
Harmful instruction following incl. jailbreak testing with adversarial prompts
Privacy and data leakage: repeating user data or memorised training text
Factuality and deception: invented facts, confidently wrong claims, misreported success, no retraction
Benchmarks: FActScore, LongFact, deception evals; hallucination and deception rate lower is better
cards.example: FActScore splits an answer into atomic claims and checks each against a reference to compute a factuality score from 0 to 1; a deception test catches a model that says it fixed the bug when it did not.
cards.say: Safety evaluation asks whether a model can cause harm, checking toxicity, bias, jailbreak resistance and privacy. It also tests factuality, whether the model invents facts, sounds confident about wrong answers, or claims success it did not achieve.

cards.title: Multi-Turn Instruction Following
cards.text: Multi-turn instruction following checks whether a model keeps following instructions as a conversation evolves over many turns. A good assistant remembers earlier constraints, revises its work when asked, and fixes mistakes the user points out without drifting off task. It is usually scored by human preference or task completion rate, and constraints should hold across five to ten turns. Interestingly, this ability does not correlate with classical scores like perplexity or MMLU; it is shaped mostly by alignment training such as SFT, RLHF and DPO. Benchmarks include MultiChallenge and COLLIE.
points: Tests following complex, evolving instructions across many turns
Maintain constraints over 5-10 turns, self-correct when an error is pointed out
Handle clarifications, revisions, contradictions; keep task memory without drift
Benchmarks: MultiChallenge, COLLIE
Scored by human preference or task completion rate
Required for assistants and agents; shaped by SFT/RLHF/DPO; not correlated with perplexity or MMLU
cards.example: Turn 1: 'Write a short story about a dragon.' Turn 2: 'Rewrite it in the style of Shakespeare, same plot.' Turn 3: 'Shorten it to 50 words while keeping the tone.' A good model keeps all three constraints at once.
cards.say: Multi-turn instruction following tests whether a model remembers what you asked earlier. If you first ask for a dragon story, then for a Shakespeare style, then for fifty words, a good model keeps all of those rules at once, and this skill comes mostly from alignment training.

cards.title: Tool Use & Tau-2 Bench
cards.text: Tool use evaluation asks whether a model can produce tool or function calls that are both schema-correct and meaningful: picking the right tool, filling arguments with the correct types per the JSON schema, and knowing when to start or stop calling tools. Because tools do the actual work in AI systems, most real-world failures come from bad tool calls rather than bad reasoning. Tau-2 Bench is the flagship example, testing agents across retail, airline and telecom: the model must call the right sequence of APIs, read the results and adapt. In its dual-control setting the simulated user can also act through tools, as in the 'No Service' example.
points: Measures schema-correct, meaningful tool and function calls
Correct arguments respecting JSON schemas and type constraints
Metrics: tool-call success 0-100%, schema compliance 0-100%, hallucinated calls (lower is better)
Tau-2 Bench: multi-step tool use across Retail, Airline and Telecom
Model must call the right API sequence, adapt to tool output, and let the final answer reflect the outcome
Dual-control: agent and simulated user both act via tools
cards.example: Tau-2 'No Service': the phone starts with turn_airplane_mode_on() and unseat_sim_card(); the agent calls get_customer_by_phone('555-123-2002'), checks check_network_status() (Airplane Mode on), toggles it (still no signal), reads get_sim_status() (SIM invalid), reseats the SIM, and reaches 'Excellent signal | 5G'.
cards.say: Tool use is about calling functions correctly, not just talking. The model must choose the right tool and fill its arguments exactly, and Tau-2 Bench tests full agent behaviour, like guiding a customer from no phone service back to a working five-G signal step by step.
covers: A8: Tool Use & API Calling Reliability
A8: Tau-2 Bench: Evaluating Agents with Tools

cards.title: Modality & Domain Evaluation
cards.text: Modality-specific evaluation checks how well a model handles non-text inputs: grounding text in images, reasoning over images, OCR, video, and matching captions to charts or diagrams, using benchmarks such as VQA, ChartQA, DocVQA and VideoMME. Domain-specific evaluation tests high-stakes fields like health, finance, law, education, science and coding, with benchmarks such as HealthBench, FinBen/FLUE, LegalEval and GSM8K/MATH. A model that shines on general benchmarks can still fail badly in a specialised domain, so these tests matter before deployment.
points: Modalities: text-image grounding, image reasoning, OCR, video, multimodal alignment
Multimodal benchmarks: VQA, ChartQA, DocVQA, VideoMME (accuracy 0-100%)
Real apps rely on screenshots, PDFs, charts, tables, product images, videos
Domains: health, finance, law, education, engineering and science, coding
Domain benchmarks: HealthBench, FinBen/FLUE, LegalEval, GSM8K/MATH, CodeContests/HumanEval
General success does not guarantee domain quality
cards.example: A model can top general leaderboards yet collapse on a clinical-reasoning test such as HealthBench, which is why a high-stakes app needs its own domain benchmark before deployment.
cards.say: Some tests check other kinds of input, like images, documents and video, while others check a specialised field such as medicine or law. A model can look great on general tests and still fail badly in your specific domain, so you test it there too.

cards.title: Benchmark Limitations
cards.text: Traditional benchmarks have real weaknesses. Test sets often leak into training data, so scores can overestimate true ability, and benchmarks like MMLU are saturated above 90%, so they barely separate models anymore. Good MMLU or perplexity says little about domain tasks, long instructions, precise tool calls, or user-experience qualities like helpfulness, which need human evaluation.
