The takeaway: no single number captures model quality, so combine intrinsic, task-level and capability tests in your real domain and workflow. Practical capability evaluation often predicts product success better than classical metrics.
points: Contamination and memorisation: benchmarks in training data inflate results
Saturation: MMLU scores above 90% lose discriminative power
Poor predictor of product performance (domain tasks, long instructions, tool calls, reasoning chains)
User experience (helpfulness, politeness, stability, interpretability) needs human evaluation
No single number summarizes LLM quality; evaluation must be multi-dimensional
Combine intrinsic, task-level and capability tests in the real domain and workflow
cards.example: Because MMLU scores now exceed 90%, a two-point gap no longer proves one model is better; a task-specific tool-call test often predicts real product success far better.
cards.say: Benchmarks have blind spots. Questions leak into training data and inflate scores, and tests like MMLU are now so easy that top models all score above ninety percent. No single number captures quality, so test many dimensions in your own domain.

lessons.title: Roles: System, User, Assistant
lessons.goal: Understand what prompt engineering is and how system, user and assistant roles shape a chat model's behaviour.

cards.title: What Is Prompt Engineering?
cards.text: Prompt engineering is the easiest way to adapt a large language model: you change its behaviour through the input text alone, without touching any weights. Its goal is to express human intent clearly enough that the model reliably interprets and carries out the task. Many capabilities such as classification, reasoning, planning and extraction can be unlocked by prompting by itself, and small wording changes can cause surprisingly large behaviour changes. It is the foundation for chat apps, agents and retrieval systems, and it is fast, cheap and reversible.
points: Change model behaviour through the input text only, no weight updates
Goal: translate human intent so the model reliably executes it
Classification, reasoning, planning and extraction emerge from prompting alone
Small prompt changes can cause large behaviour changes
Fastest, cheapest and fully reversible way to adapt an LLM
Cornerstone for applications, agents and RAG systems
cards.example: A single instruction plus a 'Respond in JSON' rule turns a general chat model into a data-extraction component.
cards.say: Prompt engineering means steering a model with words instead of retraining it. You write instructions so the model understands your intent, and because prompting is fast and reversible, it is always the first tool you reach for.

cards.title: Prompt First, Then Finetune
cards.text: Prompting sits at the bottom of an adaptation ladder: it is cheap, fast and reversible, while few-shot examples, retrieval and finetuning sit higher and cost more. The engineering principle is to first get as far as possible with prompts, and only move up a rung when a task clearly still fails at the current level. This keeps development quick, lets you iterate on wording long before any costly training, and avoids retraining a model for something a clearer instruction could have fixed.
points: Prompting is the cheapest, fastest, most reversible rung of the ladder
Few-shot, retrieval and finetuning sit above it
Principle: maximize prompting first, then finetune or post-train if a gap remains
Prompt changes are instant and easy to undo
Avoids expensive training when wording alone can solve the task
cards.example: Try a clearer instruction or a couple of examples first; only finetune when accuracy still falls short after prompting.
cards.say: Think of prompting as the first rung of a ladder. It is cheap and reversible, so you push it as far as you can and only climb to retrieval or finetuning when a task genuinely keeps failing.

cards.title: System, User and Assistant Roles
cards.text: Chat models split their input into roles marked by special tokens: system, user and assistant. The system prompt holds global rules, persona, tone and constraints and has the highest priority; it sets the rules. The user prompt carries the actual request, questions and data, and specifies the task. Assistant messages are the model's own earlier replies; they build the running conversation history - the ongoing context - and strongly influence later output through recency bias, so in multi-turn apps they need careful management.
points: Input is split into system, user and assistant roles using special tokens
System prompt: global rules, persona, tone and constraints, highest priority
User prompt: the actual task, questions and data
Assistant prompt: the model's previous replies, forming the conversation history
Assistant history strongly influences output via recency bias
Multi-turn history must be managed carefully
cards.example: System: 'You are a careful data extraction assistant. Always answer in JSON.' User: 'Extract name and age from: Alice is 29.'
cards.say: A chat model sees three roles. The system prompt sets the rules and persona, the user prompt carries the task, and the assistant messages are the model's earlier answers that keep the conversation going. System rules win when they conflict.
covers: A8: System, User and Assistant Roles

cards.title: Role Priority and the Medical Example
cards.text: Modern chat models resolve conflicting instructions with a strict priority: system first, then user, then assistant history. This hierarchy is not part of the transformer architecture; it is taught during post-training and alignment, and it is what makes systems safe and consistent, enforces tool use and structured output, and keeps multi-turn agents reliable. In the lecture example a user asks for a diagnosis, but the system prompt demands short bullets and general guidance only, so the model refuses to diagnose and advises seeking professional care.
points: Priority order: system > user > assistant history
The hierarchy is learned during post-training and alignment, not built into the architecture
Needed for safety, consistent behaviour, tool use and structured output
Response is shaped by both system constraints and the user request
Basis for multi-turn reliability in agents
cards.example: System: 'You are a concise, safety-focused medical assistant... provide general guidance only.' User: 'I have chest pain. What disease do I have?' The model refuses to diagnose and advises seeking care.
cards.say: When instructions clash, the system prompt wins, then the user, then the history. That order is learned during alignment, and it is exactly what stops the model diagnosing a patient when the system tells it to give general guidance only.

lessons.title: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot & Chain-of-Thought
lessons.goal: Understand zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting: what each is, when it works and how they combine.

cards.title: Zero-Shot Prompting
cards.text: In zero-shot prompting the model receives only an instruction, with no worked examples. It relies entirely on world knowledge learned during pretraining plus the instruction-following skills gained during alignment. Because foundation models encode huge amounts of knowledge and generalise well, zero-shot already handles summarisation, classification, rewriting, explanation, extraction and simple reasoning. It is usually the very first and simplest way to test whether a model can do a task at all.
points: Only an instruction, no examples
Relies entirely on pretrained knowledge plus alignment
Handles summarisation, classification, rewriting, explanation and extraction
Foundation models generalise well across tasks
Often the first and simplest test of a capability
cards.example: 'Summarize this paragraph in one sentence: ...' or 'Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, neutral, or negative.'
cards.say: Zero-shot means you give the model just an instruction and no examples. It leans on what it learned in pretraining and alignment, and it is a great first test of whether the model can do your task.
covers: A8: Zero-Shot Prompting: Concept and Examples

cards.title: Zero-Shot: Strengths and Limits
cards.text: Zero-shot is fast, simple and needs no special expertise, and it is often surprisingly strong thanks to emergent capabilities, which makes it a solid baseline. It struggles on specialised or ambiguous tasks, where the model may need clarification, extra constraints, examples or more structured instructions. Use it for simple tasks and when latency matters, and always measure it as a baseline before investing effort in few-shot or more advanced prompting techniques.
points: Strengths: fast, simple, no expertise needed, good baseline
Often surprisingly strong because of emergent capabilities
Fails on specialised or ambiguous tasks
May need clarification, constraints, examples or structure
Best for simple, latency-critical tasks and as a baseline
cards.example: A bare classifier works on clear reviews but drifts on vague ones, so you add a fixed label list or a few examples.
cards.say: Zero-shot is fast and often surprisingly good, which makes it the go-to baseline. But it struggles on specialised or unclear tasks, where you have to add constraints or examples to get reliable results.
covers: A8: Zero-Shot: Strengths, Limitations, When to Use

cards.title: Few-Shot Prompting
cards.text: Few-shot prompting places a handful of solved examples of the task directly in the prompt; with exactly one example it is called one-shot. The model infers the input-output pattern from these demonstrations and applies it to a new input - an ability called in-context learning - with no weight updates. Examples clarify what the human means and lock the model into the correct format, style or reasoning pattern, which often improves accuracy noticeably over zero-shot.
points: A few solved examples placed inside the prompt
One example is called one-shot
Model infers the pattern and applies it to new input (in-context learning)
Examples clarify intent and fix format, style or reasoning pattern
Usually noticeably better accuracy than zero-shot
cards.example: 'The service was outstanding...' -> positive; 'The meal was okay...' -> neutral; 'I waited an hour...' -> negative. Query 'The pasta was tasty but small' -> neutral.
cards.say: Few-shot prompting shows the model a few solved examples before the real task. It picks up the pattern from them, which is in-context learning, and this usually locks in the right format and lifts accuracy above zero-shot.
covers: A8: Few-Shot Prompting: Concept and Why It Works

cards.title: Few-Shot: Tips and Limitations
cards.text: Few-shot helps with classification, extracting entities or dates, reasoning tasks, style transfer and formatting, and it reduces hallucination by anchoring the output structure. Good examples are short, representative, consistently formatted and unambiguous, and their order matters, with the most relevant or cleanest ones first. The downsides: examples consume context space, poor examples cause poor results, and the model may simply copy examples instead of generalising. Reach for few-shot when zero-shot fails or is inconsistent, when the format must be controlled, or for pattern-recognition tasks.
points: Helps classification, extraction, reasoning, style transfer and formatting
Anchors structure and reduces hallucination
Examples should be short, representative, consistent and unambiguous
Order matters: cleanest and most relevant examples first
Costs context space; bad examples hurt; risk of copying instead of generalising
cards.example: Reordering or cleaning the example set can flip a shaky classification into a stable, reliable one.
cards.say: Few-shot shines for classification, extraction and formatting, and it curbs hallucination because the examples fix the structure. But examples eat context and poor ones mislead, so keep them clean and well ordered.
covers: A8: Few-Shot: Use Cases, Design Tips, Limitations

cards.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
cards.text: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to work through a problem step by step, writing intermediate reasoning in natural language before giving the final answer. It is used for maths, logic, planning and explanations. Simple trigger phrases such as 'Let's think step by step' or 'Explain your reasoning' activate reasoning behaviour the model learned in training, and aligned models expand their answer into a structured reasoning trace before delivering a result.
points: Encourages step-by-step problem solving
Used for maths, logic, reasoning, planning and explanations
Intermediate steps written in natural language before the final answer
Triggers: 'Let's think step by step', 'Explain your reasoning'
Aligned models expand into a structured reasoning trace
cards.example: 'What is 18 x 12? Let's think step by step.' -> 18 x 10 = 180; 18 x 2 = 36; 180 + 36 = 216. Answer: 216.
cards.say: Chain-of-thought means asking the model to reason aloud step by step before answering. A simple phrase like let's think step by step triggers it, and the intermediate steps make hard maths and logic problems far more reliable.

cards.title: CoT as an Emergent Ability
cards.text: The research paper by Wei et al. showed that chain-of-thought prompting unlocks reasoning ability that is latent in large language models, using only simple natural-language cues. The effect appears strongly only once models are large; small models gain little or even get worse, which is taken as evidence for emergent abilities. Few-shot chain-of-thought, which includes worked reasoning examples, clearly beats zero-shot chain-of-thought, producing large accuracy jumps on maths benchmarks.
points: CoT unlocks latent reasoning in large LLMs
Simple natural-language cues elicit step-by-step explanations
Strong effect only in large models, evidence for emergent abilities
Few-shot CoT significantly outperforms zero-shot CoT
Large accuracy gains on maths benchmarks as scale grows
cards.example: Wei et al. Figure 4: standard prompting vs CoT accuracy on maths evaluations, the curves separating only past a certain model size.
cards.say: Wei and colleagues found that chain-of-thought only unlocks reasoning once models are large enough. Small models barely gain, but big ones jump ahead, and worked few-shot reasoning examples beat a bare step-by-step instruction.
covers: A8: Wei et al.: CoT as an Emergent Ability

cards.title: CoT: Properties and Limits
cards.text: Chain-of-thought happens inside one normal inference run: the reasoning steps are just tokens generated autoregressively, one after another. There is no internal planner, loop or multi-pass process, and the model does not solve subtasks separately - it imitates human-like reasoning patterns learned in pretraining and alignment. Writing steps out improves accuracy on multi-step tasks and makes behaviour easier to interpret and debug, but it costs extra tokens and latency, some platforms hide the reasoning, and hard tasks may still need few-shot chain-of-thought.
points: Produced in a single autoregressive pass, token by token
No internal planner, loop or independent subtask solving
Imitates human-like reasoning learned in pretraining and alignment
Strengths: higher multi-step accuracy, interpretability, easier debugging
Limits: extra tokens and latency; some platforms hide reasoning; hard tasks need few-shot CoT
cards.example: The same model produces the reasoning trace and the final answer in one stream of tokens; it is not calling any hidden tool or planner.
cards.say: Chain-of-thought is just one pass: the steps are ordinary tokens generated in order, not a hidden planner. It improves multi-step accuracy and makes the model easier to debug, but it adds latency and is not real subtask execution.

lessons.title: Managing the Context
lessons.goal: Understand how to decide what enters the context window and how its layout affects accuracy and reliability.

cards.title: What Context Management Is
cards.text: Context management means deciding exactly what information goes into the context window and how it is structured so the model can reason well. The window holds the system prompt, user instructions, assistant history, few-shot examples, retrieved documents from retrieval-augmented generation, and summaries or state from earlier turns. Because transformers attend to every token, irrelevant or noisy content lowers accuracy, and important facts can get lost in long chats. Recency bias and poor structure cause hallucination or inconsistency, so prompt engineering really spans the whole context window.
points: Deciding what enters the context window and how it is arranged
Contents: system prompt, user instructions, history, examples, retrieved documents, summaries
Transformers attend to all tokens, so noise reduces accuracy
Important information can be lost in long conversations
Recency bias and poor structure cause hallucination or inconsistency
cards.example: A long chat full of greetings and stale questions dilutes the key instruction that is buried in the middle.
cards.say: Context management is deciding what actually goes into the model's window and how it is laid out. Because the model reads every token, noisy or irrelevant content hurts accuracy, so prompt engineering really covers the whole context window.
covers: A8: What Context Management Is and Why It Matters

cards.title: Primacy, Recency and the Middle
cards.text: Transformers do not weigh all positions equally. Tokens at the start of the prompt get extra influence (primacy bias), and tokens at the end most strongly affect the next generated token (recency bias), while the middle of a long context becomes an attention 'dead zone' - the 'lost in the middle' effect shown by Liu et al. In practice, put the system prompt and key framing at the start, then put format requirements and few-shot examples right before the query at the end, because later instructions override earlier ones.
points: Primacy bias: the beginning gets more influence than the middle
Recency bias: the end most strongly influences the next token
The middle is an attention 'dead zone' (U-shaped performance)
Put the system prompt and key framing at the start
Put format rules and few-shot examples right before the query at the end
cards.example: Liu et al. Figure 1: accuracy is highest when the relevant document sits at the very start or end, and lowest in the middle.
cards.say: Models pay most attention to the start and the end of their context. The middle is a dead zone, so put your system prompt and framing first, and your format rules and examples last, right before the question.
covers: A8: Primacy Bias, Recency Bias and 'Lost in the Middle'

cards.title: Chunking and Summarization
cards.text: Long documents and long chats do not fit neatly into the context window, and dumping everything in confuses the model. Chunking splits a document into coherent, labelled pieces at natural boundaries so only relevant pieces are fed in - never cut mid-sentence or mid-concept, and give each chunk a title such as 'Chunk 2: Liability Clause'. Summarisation compresses a long conversation history into a short, task-focused summary that keeps the important constraints, decisions and preferences. Together they keep inputs clean and preserve state without overflowing the window.
points: Split documents into coherent, labelled sections
Never split mid-sentence or mid-concept; give chunks a title
Feed only the chunks relevant to the task
Cleaner input means better comprehension and fewer hallucinations
Summaries preserve constraints, decisions and user preferences
cards.example: Chunk label: 'Chunk 2: Liability Clause'. Summary: 'User is planning a 5-day Japan trip in April with a 2000 EUR budget.'
cards.say: Chunking cuts long documents at natural boundaries and labels the pieces, while summarization squeezes a long chat into a short task-focused note. Both keep the input clean and keep your important constraints within the window.

cards.title: Pruning and Instruction Reiteration
cards.text: Message pruning removes conversation turns that no longer help - greetings, acknowledgements, outdated details or obsolete assistant answers - keeping only the essential information, which makes generation more stable and predictable. Instruction reiteration exploits recency bias: critical rules, especially output-format requirements, are repeated at the very end of the context so they are not forgotten in long sessions. A simple reminder such as 'Respond in valid JSON' appended last keeps rule-following reliable.
points: Remove greetings, acknowledgements and outdated details
Drop assistant replies that no longer matter
Keep only the minimum essential information
Less noise means more stable, predictable generation
Repeat critical rules, especially formats, at the end (recency bias)
cards.example: Reminder appended at the end: 'Reminder: Respond in valid JSON'.
cards.say: Pruning deletes turns that no longer matter, like greetings and stale answers, so the model stays stable. And because the end of the context is weighted heavily, repeating a critical rule like respond in valid JSON at the bottom keeps it from being forgotten.
covers: A8: Message Pruning and Instruction Reiteration

cards.title: Ordering and Formatting Anchors
cards.text: Because transformers weight the beginning and the end of the context most strongly, the order of prompt parts matters. The recommended order is: global rules (system prompt) first, then task instructions, then examples or schemas, then supporting context, and finally the user's immediate task last. Formatting anchors are consistent output templates - such as JSON, tables or bullet structures - backed by examples and repeated schemas, that make the output format stable and predictable.
points: Beginning and end of the context are weighted most strongly
Order: system rules, task instructions, examples/schemas, supporting context, user task last
Good ordering means clearer, more deterministic behaviour
Use consistent templates: JSON, tables or bullets
Provide examples and repeat schemas when reliability matters
cards.example: A five-block prompt ending with the user's question matches the attention profile best and yields more stable output.
cards.say: Order matters because the model weights the start and end of the context. Put global rules first, then instructions, examples and context, and finally the user's actual task last. Consistent templates keep the output format stable.
covers: A8: Ordering, Structure and Formatting Anchors

cards.title: Challenges and When to Use It
cards.text: Context management is needed because context windows are limited, latency grows with longer inputs, and a model's behaviour can change once examples scroll out of the window. Keeping state across many turns is hard without an external memory, a problem addressed later with agents. These techniques matter most in long conversations, document-heavy tasks, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, multi-step agent workflows, and any production setting that needs consistent behaviour.
points: Limited context window sizes
Latency grows with longer contexts
Behaviour can change when examples scroll out of the window
Long multi-turn state needs external memory (agents)
Use for long chats, document tasks, RAG pipelines and agents
cards.example: As early few-shot examples slide out of a scrolling window, the model's output style visibly drifts.
cards.say: We manage context because windows are finite, latency grows with length, and behaviour can shift once examples scroll out of view. It matters most for long chats, document tasks, retrieval pipelines and multi-step agents.
covers: A8: Challenges and When to Use Context Management

lessons.title: Prompt Patterns
lessons.goal: Learn the reusable prompt patterns that shape instruction, reasoning, quality, decomposition, style and safety.

cards.title: Instruction and Persona Patterns
cards.text: The instruction pattern is simply a direct, explicit command that describes the task; it works best for simple, generalisable, low-risk tasks. The persona pattern assigns the model a role, which shifts its tone, assumed expertise and style. Personas are useful for setting domain expertise, adjusting formality, and in teaching or coaching scenarios. Both are lightweight patterns that stack easily with the other patterns in this chapter.
points: Instruction pattern: a direct, explicit task command
Best for simple, generalisable, low-risk tasks
Persona pattern: assign a role to influence tone, expertise or style
Personas set domain expertise and adjust formality
Personas suit teaching and coaching
cards.example: Instruction: 'Summarize the following text in three bullet points.' Persona: 'You are a senior cloud architect. Explain Kubernetes to a beginner.'
cards.say: The instruction pattern is just a direct command, best for simple tasks. The persona pattern gives the model a role, which changes its tone and expertise, and it is great for teaching or coaching.

cards.title: Example and Chain-of-Thought Patterns
cards.text: The example, or few-shot, pattern shows the model a few input-output demonstrations before the real task so it can copy the mapping, structure and style; it is especially helpful for extraction tasks. The chain-of-thought pattern asks the model to reason step by step, which helps with maths, logic, planning, debugging reasoning and breaking down complex problems.
points: Few-shot: demonstrations of the desired input-output mapping
Used for pattern learning and to control structure or style
Improves accuracy for extraction tasks
Chain-of-thought elicits structured step-by-step reasoning
CoT helps with maths, logic, planning and decomposition
cards.example: Input -> Output example pairs placed before the task; CoT trigger: 'Let's think it through step by step'.
cards.say: The example pattern drops a few input-output pairs before the task to steer the mapping, which is great for extraction. The chain-of-thought pattern asks for step-by-step reasoning and helps with maths, logic and planning.
covers: A8: Few-Shot Example and Chain-of-Thought Patterns

cards.title: Critique-and-Refine and Self-Check
cards.text: In the critique-and-refine pattern the model first evaluates its own draft for weaknesses and then produces an improved version - useful for writing, code review and refactoring. The self-check or verification pattern makes the model give an answer and then check it for mistakes and correct them. Self-checking reduces errors and is valuable in safety-sensitive tasks and for numerical or logical consistency.
points: Critique-and-refine: critique your own output first, then improve it
Used for quality, writing, code review and refactoring
Self-check: answer, then verify and correct
Used for error reduction
Valuable in safety-sensitive tasks and for numeric or logical consistency
cards.example: 'Evaluate the draft above for clarity and correctness, then provide an improved version.' 'Provide an answer, then check for mistakes and correct them.'
cards.say: Critique-and-refine has the model judge its own draft and then rewrite it, which is handy for writing and code review. Self-check has it verify its answer and fix mistakes, which reduces errors in safety-critical or numerical tasks.

cards.title: Decomposition Patterns
cards.text: Decomposition patterns break a hard task into smaller parts. Step-by-step breakdown solves a problem sequentially. Subtask separation splits it into distinct modules, for example extract facts, then infer, then decide. Role decomposition lets the model analyse a problem from several expert viewpoints and merge them, which suits multi-domain reasoning. Program-like decomposition turns the task into pseudo-code steps such as defining variables and computing intermediate values, which suits maths, algorithms and code generation.
points: Step-by-step: solve sequentially (reasoning, maths, planning)
Subtask separation: distinct modules (classification, analysis, QA, coding)
Role decomposition: several expert roles, then combine (multi-domain reasoning)
Program-like: pseudo-code blocks and logical modules
Program-like suits maths reasoning, algorithms and code generation
cards.example: 'Analyze as a legal expert, then as a financial expert, then combine insights.' 'Define variables -> derive intermediate values -> compute the final result.'
cards.say: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller ones. You can go step by step, split into modules like extract then infer then decide, view it through several expert roles, or turn it into pseudo-code for maths and coding.
covers: A8: Decomposition Patterns: Step-by-Step, Subtasks, Roles, Program-like

cards.title: Tree-of-Thought and Rewriting
cards.text: Tree-of-thought prompting has the model branch into several candidate strategies or steps, evaluate them and pick the best, instead of following a single line of reasoning. It helps in planning, optimisation and creative tasks. Rewriting the problem asks the model to restate the task in its own simpler words before solving it, which helps with ambiguous or poorly specified queries.
points: Tree-of-thought: branch into multiple candidate steps and evaluate them
Used for planning, optimisation and creative tasks
Rewriting: restate the problem in simpler terms before solving
Rewriting helps with ambiguous or poorly specified queries
cards.example: 'List 2-3 possible strategies and choose the best.' 'Rewrite the task in your own words, then solve it.'
cards.say: Tree-of-thought has the model explore several candidate strategies, score them and keep the best, which helps with planning. Rewriting asks it to restate a vague task in its own words first, so ambiguous problems become solvable.

cards.title: Style Control and Hard Constraints
cards.text: Style control adjusts the tone, voice and communication behaviour of the model - for example explaining for a twelve-year-old or writing academically - which supports a consistent user experience, tutoring and branding. Hard constraints are explicit, must-follow rules such as producing valid JSON or exactly three bullet points. Transformers follow clear, explicit constraints much better than vague ones.
points: Style control adjusts tone, voice and communication behaviour
Used for user-experience consistency, tutoring and branding
Hard constraints are explicit rules that must be followed
Clear, explicit constraints are followed better than vague ones
cards.example: Style: 'Explain this like I'm 12 years old.' Constraints: 'Respond using valid JSON', 'Limit your answer to exactly 3 bullet points', 'Do not include personal opinions'.
cards.say: Style control sets the tone and voice, for example explaining something as if the listener is twelve. Hard constraints are the strict rules, like valid JSON or exactly three bullets, and models follow clear rules far better than vague ones.
covers: A8: Style Control and Hard Constraints

cards.title: Soft Steering and Guardrails
cards.text: Soft steering nudges the model's behaviour without strict rules, for example 'be thorough but concise', and is used when the task allows variation. Guardrails through prompting combine style and constraints to prevent unsafe or undesired outputs, for instance restricting medical requests to general safety guidance only. This connects back to alignment and post-training, where such safety behaviour is partly learned.
points: Soft steering influences behaviour without enforcing strict rules
Used when flexibility and output variation are acceptable
Guardrails combine style and constraints to prevent unsafe output
Connects to alignment and post-training (Chapter 2.10)
cards.example: Soft: 'Be thorough but concise', 'Prefer factual statements over speculation.' Guardrail: 'If the user requests a medical diagnosis, provide general safety guidance only.'
cards.say: Soft steering gently nudges the model, like saying be thorough but concise, and leaves room for variation. Guardrails are firmer: they blend style and constraints to block unsafe output, for example refusing medical diagnoses and giving general guidance instead.
covers: A8: Soft Steering and Guardrails via Prompting

lessons.title: Structured Outputs & Function Calling
lessons.goal: Understand how JSON schemas and function calling turn an LLM into a reliable, tool-using software component.

cards.title: Structured Outputs (JSON Schemas)
cards.text: Many applications need predictable, machine-readable output instead of free-form prose. Structured prompting asks the model to answer in a fixed format such as JSON that follows a schema, which turns the LLM from an unreliable text generator into a dependable software component. This makes parsing and validation trivial, removes invented formats, and is essential for agents, pipelines and automation, where downstream code expects exact fields and types.
points: Goal: turn the LLM into a deterministic software component
Applications need predictable, machine-readable output
Fixed format such as JSON that follows a schema
Parsing and validation become trivial; hallucinated formats disappear
Essential for agents, pipelines and automation
cards.example: User: 'Extract the following fields and respond in valid JSON: {name: string, age: number}. Text: Alice is 29 years old.' Assistant: {"name": "Alice", "age": 29}
cards.say: Structured output asks the model to answer in a fixed format like JSON that follows a schema. That turns a chatty text generator into a reliable component you can parse and validate, which is exactly what agents and pipelines need.

cards.title: Function Calling (Tool Use)
cards.text: With function calling, an LLM can trigger external tools such as APIs, databases or calculators when it is given function schemas. Strict argument formats are enforced, and tasks like maths, search or retrieval are offloaded to real systems so the model does not invent answers, which makes LLMs production-ready. During generation the model either writes normal text or emits a special tool-call token followed by JSON-like arguments; the application runs the tool, returns the result, and the model writes the final answer.
points: LLMs trigger external tools (APIs, databases, calculators) via a function schema
Enforces strict argument formats
Offloads maths, search and retrieval to real systems
Prevents the model from inventing answers; makes LLMs production-ready
Model chooses between normal text and a special tool-call token
cards.example: The model emits a tool call, the app executes the tool, and the result is fed back so the model can finish the answer.
cards.say: Function calling lets the model trigger real tools, like an API or calculator, from a schema you give it. It enforces strict arguments and offloads maths and search to real systems, so the model stops guessing and becomes production-ready.

cards.title: Prompt-Based vs Native Tools
cards.text: There are two ways a model learns about tools. Open-weights models usually get the function schemas as ordinary text inside the system prompt; this is prompt-based tool use. Modern closed APIs instead pass the schemas through a separate structured interface, and the model is trained to select and call tools from that metadata; this is native tool use. Both follow the same five-step procedure: provide the prompt, supply the tool definitions, let the model emit text or a tool call, generate arguments, then run the tool and return its result.
points: Prompt-based tools: schemas placed as text in the system prompt (open-weights models)
Native tools: schemas via a separate structured interface (modern closed APIs)
Native models are trained to select and call tools from this metadata
Tool definitions are provided separately, outside the prompt
Five steps: prompt, provide tools, emit text or tool call, generate arguments, execute and return
cards.example: The same get_weather schema, shown as text in the system prompt for an open model, or passed on a side channel for a closed API.
cards.say: Models learn tools in two ways. Open models usually get the schemas as text in the system prompt, while modern closed APIs pass them on a separate structured channel the model was trained on. Either way the same five-step loop runs the tool.

cards.title: Example: get_weather
cards.text: The lecture shows a concrete tool-use exchange. A get_weather function is declared with a JSON schema requiring one string parameter, city. When the user asks about the weather in Berlin, the model does not answer in prose; it emits a tool call naming get_weather with the argument city equal to Berlin. The application then runs the tool and passes the result back to the LLM, which uses it to write the final answer.
points: Tool declared with type 'function', a name and a JSON-schema 'parameters' object
Parameter 'city' of type string is required
System prompt: 'You are a helpful assistant.'
Model responds with a tool call naming the function and its arguments
The tool runs and its result is returned to the LLM for the final answer
cards.example: User: 'What's the weather in Berlin?'; Assistant: <|tool_call|> {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Berlin"}}
cards.say: The example declares a get_weather tool that needs a city string. Asking about Berlin's weather makes the model emit a tool call with city Berlin, the app runs the function, and the result comes back so the model can answer.

lessons.title: Debugging & Optimizing Prompts
lessons.goal: Learn a systematic way to debug prompts and how automated prompt optimization improves them as an optimization problem.

cards.title: Name the Failure, Check Context
cards.text: Prompt engineering is iterative, and reliable applications need systematic evaluation and debugging rather than random trial and error. The first step is to name the failure mode: hallucination, ignored constraints, style drift, wrong reasoning, wrong length, or unstable output that changes between runs. The second step is to check context quality, because many failures come from poor context management - irrelevant history, buried or missing instructions, information that scrolled out of the window, an overridden system prompt, or confusing examples. Garbage context gives garbage output.
points: Evaluate systematically, not by trial and error
Failure modes: hallucination, ignored constraints, style drift
Also wrong reasoning, wrong length, unstable output
Check context: irrelevant history, buried instructions, scrolled-out info
Also an overridden system prompt and inconsistent examples
cards.example: A confident but wrong answer is labelled 'hallucination'; the root cause turns out to be an instruction buried in the middle of the context.
cards.say: Debugging starts by naming the failure: hallucination, ignored rules, style drift or unstable output. Then you inspect the context, because most failures are really context problems, like a buried instruction or stale history. Bad context gives bad output.
covers: A8: Identify the Failure Mode and Check Context Quality

cards.title: Improve, Add Structure, Test
cards.text: After diagnosis, the prompt is strengthened with explicit rules, a clear role and concrete output examples. Next, natural-language instructions are supported by structure - JSON schemas, chain-of-thought, decomposition and self-check patterns - because structure reduces randomness. Finally, the prompt is tested under many conditions: rephrased questions, edge cases, multi-turn chats and different document lengths. A prompt that breaks easily is not production-ready. This is a five-step workflow: identify the failure, check context, improve instructions, add structure, test systematically.
points: Explicit rules, e.g. 'Respond ONLY in JSON, no English text'
Role clarity, e.g. 'You are a data extraction assistant'
Output examples: clear input -> output templates
Structure: JSON schemas, CoT, decomposition, self-check reduce randomness
Test with different phrasings, edge cases, multi-turn, varying lengths
cards.example: Five-step workflow: identify the failure mode, check context quality, improve instructions, add structure, test systematically.
cards.say: Once you know what failed, you tighten the prompt with explicit rules, a clear role and examples, then add structure like JSON schemas or step-by-step reasoning. Finally you test many phrasings and edge cases, because a prompt that breaks easily is not ready.
covers: A8: Improve Instructions, Add Structure, Test Systematically

cards.title: Why Automate Prompt Optimization
cards.text: Writing prompts by hand is slow, inconsistent and hard to scale across many tasks. Automated prompt optimisation uses algorithms, or LLMs themselves, to systematically improve prompts for accuracy, robustness and reliability, reframing prompting as an optimisation problem rather than a creative task. Human-written prompts often hide assumptions, models react differently to different inputs, and production systems need consistent prompts - and automated methods can even beat human prompt authors on complex tasks.
points: Manual prompt engineering is slow, inconsistent and hard to scale
Automated prompt optimisation uses algorithms or LLMs to improve prompts
Targets accuracy, robustness and reliability
Prompting becomes an optimisation problem, not a creative task
Can outperform human prompt authors on complex tasks
cards.example: An optimiser generates and scores dozens of prompt variants per second instead of a human editing one by hand.
cards.say: Hand-writing prompts is slow and inconsistent at scale. Automated prompt optimisation uses algorithms or the model itself to improve prompts for accuracy and robustness, treating prompting as an optimisation problem, and it can even beat human prompt writers on hard tasks.
covers: A8: Motivation for Automated Prompt Optimization (APO)

cards.title: The APO Loop
cards.text: Automated prompt optimisation works like an evolutionary search loop. First, an LLM generates many new prompt candidates through mutation - rewriting, adding or removing constraints, rephrasing, inserting examples - and optionally crossover, which combines strong parts of two good prompts. Each candidate is then scored with automatic, task-appropriate metrics such as accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE, Pass@k, schema validation or rule-based checks on a test set. The best prompt is selected and the loop repeats until improvements flatten out.
points: Step 1: generate new prompts with the LLM
Mutation: rewrite, add/remove constraints, rephrase, insert examples
Crossover combines strong parts of two high-performing prompts
Step 2: score candidates with automatic metrics
Metrics: accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE, Pass@k, schema validation
Step 3: select the best; Step 4: repeat until convergence
cards.example: Loop: generate (mutation or crossover) -> evaluate -> select best -> repeat until convergence.
cards.say: Automated optimisation runs like evolution. The model generates prompt variants by mutating and crossing over good ones, each variant is scored on a test set with metrics like accuracy or BLEU, the best survive, and the loop repeats until scores stop improving.

lessons.title: Why RAG?
lessons.goal: Explain why parametric language models need external knowledge and how Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplies it.

cards.title: Parametric vs Non-Parametric Knowledge
cards.text: A language model stores what it knows inside its weights. That parametric knowledge is static after pretraining, opaque (you cannot inspect what the model knows), incomplete and often outdated, and it is prone to confident but wrong answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation adds non-parametric knowledge: it fetches facts from external sources at inference time and puts them into the prompt. This grounds the answer, reduces hallucinations, and lets knowledge be updated instantly without any expensive fine-tuning when only the facts change.
points: Parametric knowledge is static: no update after pretraining
Opaque: you cannot inspect what the model knows
Incomplete and often outdated: finite pretraining data
Hallucination-prone: confident but incorrect answers
RAG retrieves facts at inference time and injects them into the prompt
External knowledge updates instantly without fine-tuning
cards.example: The same question answered by a frozen model (outdated, hallucinated) versus by RAG, where a retrieved document snippet is highlighted as the source of the correct answer.
cards.say: Everything a plain model knows is baked into its weights, so it is frozen after training and can go stale. Retrieval-augmented generation adds outside knowledge instead, pulling real documents into the prompt at answer time so the facts are current and checkable.
covers: A8: RAG Motivation: Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge

cards.title: RAG as Conditional Language Modeling
cards.text: RAG treats answering a question as ordinary language modeling, but the model is additionally conditioned on documents fetched from an external source. Instead of relying only on facts memorized in its weights, the model receives relevant evidence in its prompt at inference time. The model itself, its training objective and its decoding are untouched, and generation stays autoregressive. The retrieval step acts like an information bottleneck: the model can only ground its answer in what retrieval delivers.
points: RAG = generation conditioned on the query plus retrieved evidence
Knowledge is injected explicitly at inference time
LLM architecture, training objective and decoding stay unchanged
The model is still autoregressive
Retrieval acts as an information bottleneck
cards.formula: p(y | x, RAG(x)): x = user query, RAG(x) = retrieved documents, y = generated answer
cards.example: Toggle retrieval on and off for the same query: with retrieval the answer cites the fetched document; without it the model answers only from memory.
cards.say: Think of RAG as normal language modeling with an extra ingredient. The model still predicts the next token, but now it is also allowed to read a few relevant documents first. Whatever retrieval fails to bring, the model simply cannot use.
covers: A9: RAG as Conditional Language Modeling

cards.title: The RAG Pipeline
cards.text: A RAG system runs in two phases. Offline, raw documents are ingested, split into chunks, embedded and stored in a vector database. Online, the user query is embedded with the same model, a similarity search returns the top-k chunks, an optional reranker reorders them with a stronger model, and the best chunks are selected, trimmed and ordered to fit the context window. Finally the LLM decodes the answer autoregressively, conditioned on those chunks.
points: Offline: ingest, chunk, embed and store documents
Query is embedded into the same vector space
Similarity search returns the top-k chunks
Optional reranker reorders candidates with a stronger model
Context assembly selects, truncates and orders chunks to fit the context window
LLM generates the answer conditioned on the selected chunks
cards.example: Pipeline: Text Splitter -> Embeddings -> Vector Database | Query -> Embeddings -> Search -> Rerank -> Context Assembly -> Prompt Template -> LLM -> Answer.
cards.say: Building a RAG system has two halves. Ahead of time we chop documents into chunks and store their vectors. At query time we vectorize the question, pull the closest chunks, clean them up, drop them into the prompt, and let the model answer.

cards.title: RAG vs. Alignment
cards.text: Alignment methods such as SFT, RLHF and DPO shape how a model responds: its tone, safety, honesty and willingness to refuse. They cannot add new facts or guarantee correctness. RAG is different: it controls what evidence the model answers with, grounding responses in retrieved documents. So alignment decides how the model answers, while RAG decides what it answers with, and the two are complementary parts of the same system.
points: Alignment (SFT, RLHF, DPO) changes behavior, not memory or knowledge
Alignment cannot add facts or guarantee factual correctness
RAG grounds answers in retrieved evidence
Alignment = how to answer; RAG = what to answer with
The two approaches are complementary
cards.example: A politely-aligned model can still state a wrong fact confidently; RAG can supply a correct document but a rude model remains rude - each fixes a different problem.
cards.say: Fine-tuning for alignment makes a model polite, safe and honest in tone, but it does not teach it new facts. Retrieval handles the facts instead. One shapes how the model talks, the other decides what information it has to talk about.
covers: A9: RAG, Alignment and Hallucinations (alignment limits)

cards.title: Hallucinations and RAG Failures
cards.text: Parametric LLMs hallucinate: they give fluent, confident and sometimes silently wrong answers that fill gaps in their knowledge. RAG reduces this by grounding generation in retrieved evidence and can even signal uncertainty when retrieval finds nothing. It is not a guarantee, though: retrieval can miss documents, return outdated or wrong text, or the model can simply ignore the context. So failures shift from fabrication to retrieval quality.
points: Parametric LLMs hallucinate: fluent, confident, silently wrong
Hallucinations persist even after alignment
RAG grounds answers and can make missing information explicit
RAG can still fail: missed documents, stale or wrong context, ignored context
Failure mode shifts from fabrication to retrieval quality
cards.example: If the relevant document is never retrieved, the model fills the gap from its parameters and produces a fluent but wrong answer, so the retrieval step now determines correctness.
cards.say: Plain models make things up in a very convincing way. Retrieval cuts a lot of that by handing the model real evidence, but it only works if the right documents actually get found, so the weak point simply moves from the model to the retriever.
covers: A9: RAG, Alignment and Hallucinations (hallucination reduction)

lessons.title: Embedding Models
lessons.goal: Understand how text becomes a dense vector, how Sentence-BERT produces sentence embeddings, and which model types suit which domains.

cards.title: Dense Vector Embeddings
cards.text: An embedding model maps a piece of text to a vector of fixed dimension so that texts with similar meaning land close together. Because closeness is measured geometrically, retrieval works on meaning rather than exact word overlap and copes with paraphrases and synonyms. In RAG both the query and every document chunk are embedded by the same model, which turns retrieval into a nearest-neighbor search in that vector space. If the embeddings are poor, retrieval fails and the LLM is more likely to hallucinate.
points: Embedding function maps text into a real vector space R^d
Typical dimensions d: 384, 768, 1536
Similar meaning gives nearby vectors: retrieval by geometry, not keywords
Handles paraphrases, synonyms and natural-language queries
Query and chunks are embedded by the same model
Retrieval becomes a nearest-neighbor search in R^d
cards.formula: e: text -> R^d (d = embedding dimension); q = e(x), d_i = e(chunk_i)
cards.example: A query and a paraphrase of it cluster together, so the nearest chunk by cosine similarity is found even though the words differ; with dimensions 384, 768 or 1536.
cards.say: An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, a point in space. Texts that mean similar things land near each other, so we can find relevant chunks just by looking at which points are closest to the question.

cards.title: Sentence-BERT and Pooling
cards.text: BERT produces a contextual vector for every token, but it was not built to compare whole sentences directly. Sentence-BERT fine-tunes BERT on sentence-pair similarity tasks and adds a pooling step that compresses the token vectors into one fixed-size sentence vector, enabling fast semantic search, clustering and RAG. Mean pooling averages all token vectors (stable, the most common choice). Max pooling takes the per-dimension maximum (highlights salient features, can be noisy). [CLS] pooling uses the final vector of BERT's special first token, which stands for Classification.
points: BERT gives token-level contextual representations, not sentence vectors
Sentence-BERT = BERT fine-tuned on sentence pairs plus pooling
Mean pooling: average of token vectors, stable default
Max pooling: per-dimension max, salient but noisy
[CLS] pooling: final hidden state of the special first token summarizes the sequence
[CLS] stands for 'Classification', its original purpose
cards.formula: Mean pooling: e = (1/n) * sum of h_i, where h_i = contextual embedding of token i and n = number of tokens
cards.example: For a short sentence each of its, say, five token vectors is averaged dimension by dimension into one sentence vector; switching to [CLS] pooling instead takes just the first token's final vector.
cards.say: BERT gives one vector per token, but we usually want one vector for the whole sentence. Pooling squeezes all those token vectors together, most often by averaging them, and the special first token is another popular choice.

cards.title: Siamese Bi-Encoder Training
cards.text: Sentence-BERT is trained by starting from a pretrained BERT encoder and feeding it pairs of sentences that are either semantically similar or dissimilar. Each sentence passes independently through the same BERT with shared weights, a siamese or bi-encoder setup, followed by pooling. The two resulting vectors are compared with cosine similarity, and a contrastive loss pulls similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart. The goal is correct relative distances rather than hitting exact similarity scores. Because sentences are encoded independently, document embeddings can be precomputed.
points: Initialize from a pretrained BERT encoder
Train on similar and dissimilar sentence pairs
Both sentences use the same encoder with shared parameters (siamese/bi-encoder)
Pooling yields one vector per sentence
Contrastive loss pulls similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart
Independent encoding means document embeddings can be precomputed
cards.formula: cos_sim(u, v) = (u . v) / (||u|| ||v||), between pooled sentence vectors u and v
cards.example: A similar pair such as two paraphrases has its two vectors pulled together, while an unrelated pair is pushed apart; only their relative distance matters, not the exact cosine value.
cards.say: Sentence-BERT is trained with two identical towers that share their weights. Each sentence goes through its own tower, and a contrastive loss pulls the vectors of similar sentences together and pushes dissimilar ones apart. Because the towers are separate, documents can be encoded ahead of time.

cards.title: Embedding Model Types
cards.text: General-purpose Sentence-BERT-style models are trained on broad web-scale data, giving strong zero-shot semantic understanding for open-domain QA and assistants, but they can miss specialized terminology and larger models cost more latency. Domain-adapted models are fine-tuned on narrow corpora such as legal, medical or code text, improving recall inside that domain at the cost of weaker generalization. Cross-lingual models share one embedding space across languages, so a query in one language can retrieve documents in another, with slightly weaker monolingual performance. Newer trends include instruction-tuned and asymmetric encoders.
points: General-purpose: broad data, strong zero-shot, may miss domain jargon
Domain-adapted: fine-tuned on legal, medical or code; higher in-domain recall
Domain use cases: enterprise RAG, scientific literature, technical docs
Cross-lingual: one shared multilingual space via parallel, translation and NLI data
Cross-lingual lets a query in one language retrieve documents in another
Newer trends: instruction-tuned encoders, joint training with LLMs, asymmetric query/document encoders
cards.example: A German query retrieves English documents in a cross-lingual model, while a legal term is clustered with the right documents only in a domain-adapted legal model.
cards.say: Not every task wants the same embedder. General models handle everyday language well, domain-adapted ones know legal or medical jargon, and cross-lingual ones line up several languages in one space so a question can find answers written in another language.

lessons.title: Chunking & Contextual Retrieval
lessons.goal: Understand how documents are split into chunks, how context is added, and why embedding quality caps retrieval recall.

cards.title: Chunking and Context Segmentation
cards.text: Chunking splits external data into contiguous text segments that are embedded and retrieved independently, so the chunk becomes the atomic unit of knowledge in RAG. Small chunks match queries precisely and raise recall but lose surrounding context; large chunks keep coherence but lower recall and drag in irrelevant text. Typical sizes are 200-500 tokens, often with overlap so information at boundaries is not cut apart, at the cost of extra storage and compute. Better strategies align chunks with semantic units such as sentences or document sections.
points: Chunk = contiguous text segment, embedded and retrieved independently
Recall = fraction of relevant chunks that appear in the retrieved results
Small chunks: higher recall, precise matching, less context
Large chunks: more coherence, lower recall, more irrelevant info
Typical size 200-500 tokens, often with overlap
Advanced: sentence-based, semantic, section-aware chunking; bad chunking cannot be fixed downstream
cards.formula: Consecutive chunks: chunk size L and overlap O share O tokens, so stride = L - O; Recall = |relevant intersect retrieved| / |relevant|
cards.example: With L = 400 and O = 100, each 400-token chunk overlaps the next by 100 tokens, so a sentence split on a boundary still appears whole in one of them.
cards.say: Documents are too big to feed whole, so we cut them into chunks and treat each chunk as one searchable unit. Overlap keeps a sentence that straddles two chunks from being lost, but it costs extra storage and work.

cards.title: Contextual Retrieval
cards.text: A chunk on its own may lack the information needed to understand it, for example a sentence saying revenue grew by 3% without naming the company or the period. Contextual retrieval fixes this by giving an LLM the full document and asking it to write a short context description for each chunk. That description is prepended to the chunk before embedding, so each chunk becomes self-contained and its embedding captures both local content and document-level meaning.
points: A chunk can be ambiguous because it lacks document-level context
An LLM reads the full document and writes a short context per chunk
The context is prepended to the chunk text
The enriched text is embedded
Chunks become self-contained; embeddings encode local plus global meaning
cards.example: Original chunk: 'The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.' Contextualized: 'This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME corp's performance in Q2 2023; the previous quarter's revenue was $314 million. The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.'
cards.say: A chunk like revenue grew by three percent is useless on its own because we do not know whose revenue. Contextual retrieval has a model read the whole document and write a short lead-in for each chunk, so the chunk explains itself before it is embedded.

cards.title: Embedding Quality and Retrieval Recall
cards.text: Embedding quality sets the ceiling for how much relevant information a RAG system can ever retrieve. A relevant chunk is found only if it is more similar to the query than the irrelevant chunks; if the geometry does not put it close, no later stage can bring it back. Recall is driven mainly by the embedding model, its domain alignment, the chunking strategy, how the query is phrased and the nearest-neighbor search. Rerankers and LLMs only reorder or use what was retrieved, so they cannot fix missing recall.
points: Embedding quality determines the maximum achievable recall
Chunks not close to the query are never retrieved
Retrieval failure is a representation problem
Recall drivers: model choice, domain alignment, chunking, query formulation, NN search
Rerankers and LLMs cannot fix missing recall
Failure chain: weak embeddings -> missing evidence -> parametric guess -> hallucination
cards.formula: Retrieval succeeds only if cos_sim(q, d_relevant) > cos_sim(q, d_irrelevant)
cards.example: Lower the embedding quality until the relevant chunk falls below the top-k cut-off: no reranker can recover it, because it never entered the candidate list.
cards.say: The embedding model decides how much you can ever find. If the right chunk does not land near the question in vector space, nothing later in the pipeline can rescue it, and the model falls back on its own memory.
covers: A9: Embedding Quality and Retrieval Recall

lessons.title: Vector Stores & ANN Search
lessons.goal: See why exact search is too slow at scale and how vector stores use approximate indexes, clustering and quantization.

cards.title: Naive Search vs. Vector Stores
cards.text: After embedding, the system must find the stored vectors most similar to the query. Doing this naively means computing similarity with every stored vector, which costs O(N) per query and is far too slow when there are millions or billions of chunks with hundreds or thousands of dimensions and a millisecond latency budget. A vector store (vector database) stores embeddings and retrieves them by similarity instead of exact keys, typically offering approximate nearest-neighbor search and metadata filtering by source, date or access rights.
points: Naive search compares q against all stored vectors: O(N) per query
Infeasible at millions to billions of chunks with millisecond latency
Vector store = storage plus retrieval of embeddings by similarity
Provides high-dimensional storage, ANN search and metadata filtering
Core idea: trade exactness for speed while preserving high recall
cards.formula: Exact search: argmax_i cos_sim(q, d_i), cost O(N) per query (N = number of stored vectors)
cards.example: With a billion chunks of hundreds of dimensions, a scan per query is hopeless against a millisecond budget, so the index must inspect only a small subset of vectors.
cards.say: The obvious way to find the closest stored vector is to compare the query with every single one, but that becomes far too slow once you have millions of chunks. A vector store keeps the same idea but adds an index so only a small part is ever examined.
covers: A9: Naive Search vs. Vector Stores

cards.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
cards.text: ANN search aims to find vectors that are close enough to the true nearest neighbors much faster than scanning everything. It works by organizing vectors into a structured index and inspecting only a small subset, reducing latency and memory traffic. In RAG this approximation is acceptable because several relevant chunks usually exist and small similarity differences rarely change answer quality, so coverage (recall) matters more than perfect ordering. The index parameters let engineers tune between fast-but-lossy and slower-but-higher-recall retrieval.
points: Goal: near-nearest neighbors, much faster than a full scan
Uses a structured index and searches only a small subset
In RAG, high recall matters more than exact ordering
The vector index determines speed, memory and recall
Recall versus latency is tunable through index parameters
ANN is the first-stage candidate retrieval that produces top-k
cards.example: An 'effort' slider on the index traces a recall-versus-latency curve: more effort visits more points for higher recall at higher latency.
cards.say: Instead of checking every vector, an approximate index checks only a promising subset. It may miss the exact best match, but for retrieval that is fine as long as the right answers stay near the top. One knob trades latency against recall.

cards.title: Inverted File Index (IVF)
cards.text: IVF speeds up search by clustering. During training, k centroids are learned with k-means and every vector is assigned to its nearest centroid. At query time the system first finds the centroids closest to the query and then searches only the vectors inside those clusters. This is much faster than a flat scan and scales to large datasets, but recall depends on how many clusters are probed: a true neighbor sitting in an unsearched cluster is missed.
points: Search within clusters instead of all vectors
Training: k-means learns k centroids; each vector is assigned to its nearest centroid
Query time: find nearest centroids, search only their clusters
Much faster than flat search and scales well
Recall depends on the number of clusters probed
Can miss neighbors in unprobed clusters, e.g. near a boundary
cards.example: A query lands in one Voronoi cell; if the right neighbor sits just across a boundary in an unprobed cell, IVF never looks at it and the match is lost.
cards.say: IVF groups the vectors into clusters ahead of time. A query only looks inside the few clusters nearest to it instead of everywhere, which is far faster, but a true neighbour could hide in a cluster you never opened.

cards.title: Quantization-Based Indexes
cards.text: Quantization reduces the memory footprint of vectors by compressing them, storing fewer bits per dimension and approximating each vector via codebooks. Distances are then computed approximately on the compressed codes, which cuts memory bandwidth and speeds up access. Product quantization and scalar quantization are the typical examples. This enables retrieval over very large collections, at the cost of lower precision and a slight loss of recall.
points: Compress vectors: fewer bits stored per dimension
Vectors are approximated using codebooks
Distances are computed approximately on the codes
Examples: product quantization, scalar quantization
Pros: much lower memory, faster memory access, very large scale
Cons: lower precision and a slight recall degradation
cards.example: A full-precision vector snaps to the nearest codebook levels, like pixelation: the memory meter drops sharply while a small similarity error appears.
cards.say: Quantization shrinks each vector by storing fewer bits per number. That saves a lot of memory and speeds up the distance calculation, at the price of a little precision, which is usually acceptable for retrieval.

cards.title: FAISS and Index Comparison
cards.text: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is Meta's open-source library for fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with CPU and GPU implementations. It focuses on algorithms and performance rather than database features and is a baseline in research and industry. It implements most major index types: Flat (exact), IVF, HNSW, Product Quantization, and IVF-PQ which combines IVF routing with PQ compression. Comparing indexes is a systems-engineering decision about the speed-accuracy trade-off, not a modeling choice.
points: FAISS: Meta/FAIR, open source, CPU and GPU
Focus on algorithms and performance, not database features
Implements Flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ and IVF-PQ
Flat: high memory, high recall, low speed
IVF: medium memory, recall and speed
HNSW: high memory, high recall, high speed; Quantized: low memory, medium recall, very high speed
cards.example: Comparison table (memory/recall/speed): Flat high/high/low; IVF medium/medium/medium; HNSW high/high/high; Quantized low/medium/very high.
cards.say: FAISS is a widely used open-source library that offers all the main index types, from exact flat search to IVF, graph-based HNSW and quantized indexes. Picking one is really about the trade-off between memory, recall and speed for your data size.

lessons.title: Graph Search: NSW & HNSW
lessons.goal: Understand how navigable small world graphs are built and searched, and how skip-list layering gives HNSW its speed.

cards.title: NSW Graphs: Building
cards.text: Navigable Small World (NSW) graphs borrow the idea of six degrees of separation: each embedding is a node connected to a few highly similar nodes, so any node can be reached in few hops, and the number of edges per node is kept small. The graph is built by inserting nodes one at a time. For a new node, a greedy search starts from an entry node and keeps moving to whichever neighbor is more similar until no closer node exists. Then connections are chosen under three constraints: at most M neighbors, prefer closer nodes, and reject a candidate very close to an already chosen neighbor to keep links diverse.
points: Inspired by six degrees of separation
Nodes are embeddings; edges connect similar nodes, kept few per node
Insertion: greedy search from the entry point, moving to a closer neighbor until no improvement
Constraint 1: maximum degree M
Constraint 2: prefer closer nodes
Constraint 3: diversity - reject a candidate very close to an already chosen neighbor
cards.example: Insert e6 with M = 2: from e1 (cos_sim 0.1) move to e4 (0.7); connect e6 to e4. Candidate e5 (0.4) is rejected because it is very close to e4 (0.8), so e6 connects to e3 (0.2) instead; the graph gains edges e6-e4 and e6-e3.
cards.say: A navigable small world graph links each vector to a handful of similar ones so any point can be reached in a few steps. To insert a new point we hop greedily toward its closest matches, then keep only a few edges, preferring close neighbors but also keeping them varied.
covers: A9: Navigable Small World Graphs: Building

cards.title: NSW Graphs: Searching
cards.text: To search, the algorithm picks a random entry node, computes the query's similarity to that node and its neighbors, records the scores, and moves to the neighbor with the highest similarity. This repeats until it reaches a node whose neighbors are all less similar, a local best. The k nodes with the highest recorded similarity scores are returned as the result. Because only a path of nodes is evaluated, search is far cheaper than scanning all vectors, though greedy search can stop at a local optimum.
points: Start at a random entry point
Compare the query to the entry and its neighbors
Store the scores of all evaluated nodes
Move to the node with the highest similarity
Stop at a local-best node
Return the top-k nodes among the evaluated scores
cards.example: Query q enters at e3 (cos_sim 0.1); its neighbors are e2 (0.4) and e6 (0.7), so move to e6. No neighbor beats 0.7, so e6 is the local best; with k = 2 the result is e6 (0.7) and e2 (0.4).
cards.say: Searching walks along the graph from a random start toward nodes that look more and more similar. It stops when no neighbour is closer, then returns the best few points it recorded along the way. It is fast, but it can get stuck at a merely local best.
covers: A9: Navigable Small World Graphs: Searching

cards.title: Skip Lists
cards.text: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure with several stacked linked lists: the bottom level holds all elements, and each higher level holds fewer, which lets a search skip over many items at once. Searching starts at the top level, moves along to the locally best element, then drops down a level and refines. In the example the similarity is alphabet distance and the target is C: at the top the search reaches B, descends, finds C closer to B than E, descends again, finds B and D equally close, descends, and finally moves right to reach C at the bottom level.
points: Multiple linked-list levels; higher levels are sparser
Fast traversal by skipping over many items
Per level: find the local best, then move down a level
Search from the top down to the full bottom level
Inspiration for the layered structure of HNSW
cards.example: Levels L3 {B}, L2 {B, E}, L1 {B, D, E}, L0 {A, B, C, D, E, F}: searching for C with alphabet distance reaches B at L3, descends through L2 and L1, then moves right from B to C at L0.
cards.say: A skip list stacks several sorted lists so that the top ones are sparse and let you jump far. You move right as far as you can, drop down a level to refine, and repeat, which is a fast way to find one item among many.

cards.title: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)
cards.text: HNSW combines NSW graphs with the skip-list idea by building multiple graph layers: upper layers contain few nodes with long-range links, and the bottom layer contains all nodes. A search begins at an entry point on the highest layer, greedily moves toward the query, then descends layer by layer and refines in the denser graphs. This gives an excellent speed-recall trade-off with high recall at low latency, which is why HNSW is widely used in production and is the typical default for RAG.
points: HNSW = NSW graph plus skip-list layering
Multi-layer graph: sparse upper layers and a full bottom layer
Search starts at the highest layer from an entry point, then descends
Excellent speed-recall trade-off: high recall at low latency
Widely used in production; the typical default for RAG
cards.example: Layer L1 contains e1 and e4 while layer L0 contains e1-e5: the search starts at L1, hops greedily, then drops to L0 to refine among all nodes.
cards.say: HNSW stacks these small-world graphs into layers, just like a skip list. Search hops quickly through the sparse top layers and then drops down to refine in the dense bottom one, giving high recall with very low latency, which is why it is the usual default.

lessons.title: Retrieval: Dense, Sparse, Hybrid
lessons.goal: Compare dense and sparse retrieval, see why they are combined, and learn how Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges their rankings.

cards.title: Dense Retrieval
cards.text: Dense retrieval embeds queries and chunks into the same vector space and returns the top-k chunks by cosine similarity, so it matches meaning rather than exact words. It is the default first stage in most RAG pipelines, tuned for high recall, and it supplies candidates to a reranker. It excels at paraphrases, synonyms, conceptual similarity and natural-language questions. It struggles with rare identifiers such as IDs or serial numbers, exact string matches, numeric constraints and rare proper names.
points: Retrieves by semantic similarity in a shared vector space
Default first stage, optimized for high recall
Produces candidates for reranking
Strong on paraphrases, synonyms, concepts and natural questions
Weak on rare IDs, exact strings, numeric constraints and rare proper names
cards.formula: Top-k = argmax_i cos_sim(q, d_i): the k chunks with the highest cosine similarity to the query embedding q
cards.example: 'How do transformers handle long-range dependencies?' retrieves relevant documents even without exact word overlap, because the meaning is captured by the vectors.
cards.say: Dense retrieval searches by meaning. It turns the question and the chunks into vectors and returns the closest ones, so it finds paraphrases well. But it can miss a rare serial number or an exact phrase where the wording really matters.

cards.title: Sparse Retrieval (BM25)
cards.text: Sparse retrieval represents text by explicit word occurrences, with one dimension per vocabulary word and mostly zeros, and scores documents by exact word overlap. BM25 (Best Matching 25, from the Okapi IR system; the number is historical) is the standard rule-based, non-learned ranking function. It rewards documents containing the query terms, especially rare terms (high IDF), counts repeated occurrences with diminishing returns (saturation), and normalizes for document length so long documents are not unfairly favored.
points: Sparse vector: one dimension per vocabulary word, mostly zeros
BM25 is rule-based, not learned; it comes from the Okapi system
IDF: rare query words weigh more than common ones
Term frequency saturates: the first occurrences help most
Length normalization treats short and long documents fairly
Strong for exact keywords, IDs, proper names and legal or technical references, but cannot match paraphrases
cards.formula: score(q, d) = sum over terms t in q of IDF(t) * TF(t, d) / (TF(t, d) + normalization(d)); TF = occurrences of t in d, IDF = rarity of t in the corpus, normalization(d) = length-dependent term
cards.example: Query 'EU AI Act Article 52' is split into terms {EU, AI, Act, Article, 52}. Common words like 'the' have low IDF while a rare word like 'RoPE' has high IDF, so matching it counts far more.
cards.say: Sparse retrieval is old-school keyword matching done well. BM25 gives extra weight to rare query words, counts repeats with diminishing returns, and normalizes for document length, so it nails exact terms like article numbers but cannot understand paraphrases.

cards.title: Hybrid Retrieval
cards.text: Dense and sparse retrieval have complementary strengths: dense captures meaning, while BM25 captures exact keywords. Hybrid retrieval runs both, obtaining semantic and lexical candidate lists, fuses the ranked lists, and passes the merged candidates on to reranking or generation. This increases robustness and recall. A popular fusion method is Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which ignores raw scores and uses only rank positions, rewarding documents ranked highly in any list and especially those ranked well in several lists.
points: Dense gives semantic similarity; sparse gives exact keyword matching
Hybrid combines both for robustness and recall
Pipeline: run dense, run BM25, fuse rankings, then rerank or generate
Fusion uses rank positions rather than raw scores
Documents high in multiple lists are strongly rewarded
cards.example: A conceptual question is answered well by the dense list while an exact article number is found by the BM25 list; merging the two recovers both kinds of relevant chunk.
cards.say: Dense and keyword search fail in opposite ways, so we simply run both. The meaning-based list and the exact-word list are then merged, and the combined ranking is more robust than either one alone.

cards.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
cards.text: RRF scores each document by summing 1/(k + rank) over every retrieval system that returned it. Higher ranks give larger contributions, lower ranks contribute rapidly less, and appearing in multiple lists accumulates score, so a document ranked first and second beats one ranked first in only one list. It is scale-invariant (no score normalization needed), robust to noisy rankings, works across very different retrievers and has a single hyperparameter k, typically about 60.
points: Score = sum of reciprocal ranks over the retrieval systems
k of about 60 smooths the differences between ranks
Scale-invariant: no score normalization needed
Robust to noisy rankings and heterogeneous retrievers
Only one hyperparameter (k)
Consistency across lists beats a single top rank
cards.formula: RRF(d) = sum over systems i of 1 / (k + rank_i(d)), where rank_i(d) is the rank of document d in system i and k is a smoothing constant, typically about 60
cards.example: Dense ranking: 1 chunk2, 2 chunk1, 3 chunk3; BM25 ranking: 1 chunk1, 2 chunk4, 3 chunk2. RRF(chunk1) = 1/(60+2) + 1/(60+1) = 123/3782 = 0.03252, RRF(chunk2) = 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+3) = 124/3843 = 0.03227, so chunk1 narrowly wins despite never ranking first everywhere.
cards.say: Reciprocal rank fusion ignores the actual scores and looks only at positions. Each list adds one over k plus the rank, so a document that appears near the top of several lists wins overall, even if it never comes first in any single one.

quiz.q: What does the 'P' in ChatGPT stand for?
quiz.answer: Pretrained
