quiz.why: GPT means Generative Pretrained Transformer: the model first learns broad knowledge from large text corpora.

quiz.q: Which of these did NOT contribute to ChatGPT's rapid adoption?
quiz.answer: Users had to write code to interact with it
distractors: A free tier lowered the entry barrier
It remembered the conversation within a session
Impressive answers were shared virally on social media
quiz.why: A central success factor was that no technical expertise was needed at all.

quiz.q: What is the key shift from traditional machine learning to generative AI?
quiz.answer: From one specialised model per task to one model handling many tasks
distractors: From neural networks to rule-based systems
From one task per model to many models per task
quiz.why: Classic ML trained a separate model for each task; a foundation model is general-purpose.

quiz.q: Which Transformer property is named as a driver of generative AI?
quiz.answer: Self-attention that can be trained in a highly parallel way
distractors: Processing one token at a time recurrently
quiz.why: Parallel self-attention made training on web-scale data with GPU clusters practical.

quiz.q: What is the main downside of the AI race described in this lesson?
quiz.answer: Pressure to release products before they are mature
distractors: Lower energy demand from data centres
quiz.why: Competition speeds progress but pushes companies to ship early.

quiz.q: For 'The cat sits on the' with mat 0.70, sofa 0.15, chair 0.10, car 0.05, what does greedy (argmax) selection output?
quiz.answer: mat
distractors: A random word weighted by probability
quiz.why: Argmax picks the single most probable candidate, which is 'mat' at 0.70.

quiz.q: What is autoregressive generation?
quiz.answer: Repeatedly predicting, selecting and appending one token at a time
distractors: Generating the whole answer in one parallel step
Regressing a continuous number from text
quiz.why: Each chosen token is appended to the input and the model predicts again.

quiz.q: Why is language model training called self-supervised?
quiz.answer: The labels (next words) come directly from the raw text
distractors: Humans label every word by hand
The model trains without any data
It uses reinforcement learning from human feedback
quiz.why: Each next word in the text serves as the target, so no manual annotation is needed.

quiz.q: A bigram model has a vocabulary of 50,000 words. Roughly how many entries does its probability table need?
quiz.answer: 2.5 billion
quiz.why: A bigram table has V^2 entries: 50,000^2 = 2.5 x 10^9. (125 trillion would be a trigram, V^3.)

quiz.q: In speech recognition, why is 'I eat ice cream' chosen over 'I eat I scream'?
quiz.answer: The language model assigns the first sentence a higher probability
distractors: The audio signals are clearly different
quiz.why: Both sound identical; the LM re-ranks acoustic hypotheses by linguistic plausibility.

quiz.q: Beyond next-token prediction, which three aspects explain a model's capabilities?
quiz.answer: Architecture; training and alignment; inference and context
quiz.why: Prediction is only the generation mechanism; capability comes from how the model is built, trained and prompted.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three scaling dimensions of LLMs?
quiz.answer: Number of human annotators
quiz.why: LLMs scale data, parameters and compute; being self-supervised, they do not depend on annotators.

quiz.q: An LLM trained only on next-token prediction can also translate and write code. What are such skills called?
quiz.answer: Emergent abilities
quiz.why: They emerge at scale from the prediction objective without explicit task training.

quiz.q: Why was 'foundation model' preferred over 'general-purpose model'?
quiz.answer: It conveys that the model is an unfinished base that needs adaptation
distractors: It refers only to text models
It describes the self-supervised learning method
It means the model never needs prompting or fine-tuning
quiz.why: 'General-purpose' signals versatility but hides that the model must be adapted to downstream tasks.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly relates LLMs, foundation models and AI systems?
quiz.answer: An LLM is a type of foundation model; an AI system combines models with context, data, tools and logic
distractors: A foundation model is a type of LLM
An AI system is just another name for an LLM
LLMs are trained only on images
quiz.why: LLMs are the text specialisation of foundation models; AI systems wrap models into usable applications.

quiz.q: Which statement about ChatGPT is correct?
quiz.answer: It uses a foundation model but is not itself a foundation model
distractors: It is a raw foundation model with no extra layers
It has used GPT-4 since its 2022 launch
quiz.why: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface, and it launched on GPT-3.5.

quiz.q: Which model is the example of an audio/speech foundation model?
quiz.answer: Whisper
quiz.why: Whisper learns from raw and transcribed speech; CLIP is vision, Sora is video, DALL-E generates images.

quiz.q: AI engineering is best described as the discipline of...
quiz.answer: building reliable, useful and maintainable systems around AI models
distractors: training foundation models from scratch only
quiz.why: It centres on building applications with foundation models as core components.

quiz.q: In the AI engineering stack, which concerns cut across all layers?
quiz.answer: Evaluation, safety and monitoring
quiz.why: Testing, red teaming, guardrails, monitoring and feedback loops apply to every layer.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six core capabilities?
quiz.answer: Blockchain
quiz.why: The six are vision, language, audio, code, tool use and reasoning.

quiz.q: What is the typical loop of a coding assistant?
quiz.answer: Generate code -> run tests -> inspect results -> refine
quiz.why: Coding assistants iterate using execution and testing tools; search-compare-decide-act is the agent pattern.

quiz.q: A demo asks 'Can the model do this?'. What does a production AI system ask?
quiz.answer: Can the system do this reliably, safely and efficiently?
distractors: Can the model produce one impressive answer?
Is this the largest model available?
quiz.why: Production requires consistent behaviour across many cases plus safety, latency and cost control.

quiz.q: The model invents a contract clause that sounds plausible but does not exist. Which failure category is this?
quiz.answer: Factuality
quiz.why: Plausible but incorrect content is a factuality failure, often called hallucination.

quiz.q: Why does 'open-weight' not mean 'open-source'?
quiz.answer: Published weights do not imply that training code, data or the full process are public
distractors: Open-weight models cannot be run locally
Open-weight models come without any license
quiz.why: Only the trained parameters are released, under a license; other artefacts may stay closed.

quiz.q: What is the role of llama.cpp within Ollama?
quiz.answer: It is the open-source inference library Ollama uses to run LLMs locally
distractors: It is a cloud API for GPT-4
It is a drag-and-drop workflow editor
It is a dataset of open-weight models
quiz.why: Ollama builds on llama.cpp and adds model downloading plus CLI, GUI and HTTP access.

quiz.q: Approximately how much weight memory does an 8B-parameter model need at 4-bit precision?
quiz.answer: About 4 GB
quiz.why: 8e9 parameters x 4 bits / 8 = 4e9 bytes, about 4 GB.

quiz.q: What is the engineering lesson of the 'find a model that fits your hardware' challenge?
quiz.answer: Model selection is a trade-off between quality, memory and speed
distractors: Always choose the largest model that fits
Speed does not matter for local models
quiz.why: A smaller or quantised model may be nearly as good while far faster and lighter.

quiz.q: What is LangFlow?
quiz.answer: A visual GUI for building LangChain workflows by connecting blocks
distractors: A local LLM runtime based on llama.cpp
quiz.why: LangFlow is the drag-and-drop front end for LangChain and can export Python code.

quiz.q: What does 'vibe coding' describe?
quiz.answer: Building software mainly by describing it to an AI and accepting its code with little review
distractors: Pair programming with a human colleague
quiz.why: The term, coined in early 2025, refers to programming through natural-language instructions to an AI.

quiz.q: In the newer course roadmap, which part contains retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
quiz.answer: Build with Models
quiz.why: Part 2, Build with Models, holds prompt engineering, agents, RAG and fine-tuning.

quiz.q: What is required to pass each graded computer lab unit?
quiz.answer: At least 50% of the points
quiz.why: Every graded unit requires at least half of the points; Unit 0 is optional.

quiz.q: What does BOF4 stand for?
quiz.answer: 4-bit Block-Wise Optimal Float
quiz.why: BOF4 is a 4-bit block-wise quantisation format for LLM weights, published at ICLR 2026.

quiz.q: Which tool is used in the lab for RAG?
quiz.answer: ChromaDB
quiz.why: The lab's RAG unit uses the ChromaDB vector database.

quiz.q: Which order correctly describes the text-to-text pipeline?
quiz.answer: Tokenization -> embedding lookup -> forward pass -> token selection -> detokenization
distractors: Embedding lookup -> tokenization -> forward pass -> detokenization -> token selection
Detokenization -> tokenization -> forward pass -> embedding lookup -> token selection
Tokenization -> forward pass -> embedding lookup -> token selection -> detokenization
quiz.why: Text becomes IDs, IDs become vectors, the model scores every token, one is chosen, and it is decoded back to text.

quiz.q: What does the LLM itself output right before a token is chosen?
quiz.answer: Logits: one raw score for every vocabulary token
distractors: The next word as a string
An embedding vector for the next word
A single token ID decided internally
quiz.why: The forward pass only scores candidates; a separate selection step makes the choice.

quiz.q: How many new tokens does one forward pass of a causal LLM produce during generation?
quiz.answer: Exactly one
distractors: One per word in the prompt
As many as fit in the context window
quiz.why: Generation is autoregressive: each pass scores only the next token, which is appended before the next pass.

quiz.q: Why does the pipeline need an embedding lookup after tokenization?
quiz.answer: Token IDs are arbitrary indices; the network needs meaningful continuous vectors
distractors: IDs are too long to store in memory
The tokenizer outputs letters, not numbers
Embeddings compress the text to save API cost
quiz.why: An ID is just a catalogue number; the learned vector is what the network computes with.

quiz.q: In the BPE example on the corpus 'low lower', which pair is merged first?
quiz.answer: (l, o)
quiz.why: (l, o) is the most frequent adjacent pair, so it becomes the new token 'lo'.

quiz.q: Why does byte-level BPE never encounter an unknown input character?
quiz.answer: Its base vocabulary holds all 256 byte values, and every UTF-8 character is 1-4 bytes
distractors: It contains a dictionary of all words in all languages
It maps unknown characters to the padding token
It retrains the tokenizer at inference time
quiz.why: Any text is a byte sequence, and each byte is already a token.

quiz.q: What is a main drawback of a word-level vocabulary?
quiz.answer: A huge vocabulary and no way to handle unseen words
quiz.why: Word-level tokenizers need an entry per word and turn new words into out-of-vocabulary tokens.

quiz.q: Why are per-token API prices of different models not directly comparable?
quiz.answer: Different tokenizers produce different token counts for the same text
distractors: All providers share the same tokenizer
quiz.why: The same text could be 120 tokens for one tokenizer and 165 for another.

quiz.q: What is true of the padding token <pad>?
quiz.answer: It aligns sequences in a batch and is ignored by the loss
distractors: It marks the end of generation
It separates user and assistant turns
It is predicted after every sentence
quiz.why: Padding exists only for batching; it is masked and never predicted by decoder-only models.

quiz.q: What happens if you replace a trained model's tokenizer with a different one?
quiz.answer: The text-to-ID mapping changes, so the model must be adapted or retrained
distractors: The model relearns the mapping automatically at inference
quiz.why: Tokenizer and model form a coupled system, and the output layer is sized to the vocabulary.

quiz.q: Why are raw token IDs not suitable as direct semantic input?
quiz.answer: They are arbitrary indices whose numeric distance has no linguistic meaning
distractors: They are too large to store
They change every time the model runs
quiz.why: ID 2317 is not closer in meaning to 2318 than to 57; embeddings provide meaningful geometry.

quiz.q: How many parameters does an embedding matrix with vocabulary size V and width d_model have?
quiz.answer: V · d_model
quiz.why: E has one row of length d_model per vocabulary entry, e.g. 100,000 × 4,096 ≈ 410 million.

quiz.q: What is the cosine similarity of two vectors pointing in exactly opposite directions?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity depends only on the angle; 180 degrees gives -1.

quiz.q: In trained embeddings, what does a large vector norm mainly indicate?
quiz.answer: The word is frequent or generic in the training data
distractors: The word has a very specific meaning
The word is an antonym of many words
quiz.why: Frequent words collect more gradient updates and longer vectors; direction carries meaning.

quiz.q: What does Word2Vec skip-gram predict?
quiz.answer: The surrounding context words from a centre word
distractors: The centre word from its context
quiz.why: Skip-gram takes the centre word as input and maximises the probability of its neighbours.

quiz.q: 'bank' appears in a finance sentence and a river sentence. What is true of its initial embedding?
quiz.answer: It is identical in both sentences
distractors: It is randomly re-sampled each time
It is zero until context is processed
quiz.why: The lookup is context-independent; contextual meaning is built later by attention layers.

quiz.q: What are logits?
quiz.answer: Raw, unnormalised scores, one for every vocabulary token
distractors: Probabilities that already sum to one
The embedding vectors of the input tokens
The IDs of the top-5 candidate tokens
quiz.why: Logits are scores; softmax turns them into probabilities and a decoding strategy then chooses a token.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical stopping condition for generation?
quiz.answer: The logit of the top token exceeds 1.0
distractors: A configured generation limit is reached
quiz.why: Generation stops on <eos>, length limits or other configured criteria, never on a logit threshold.

quiz.q: With a fixed context window, what is the effect of a longer prompt?
quiz.answer: Less room remains for generated tokens
distractors: Generated tokens no longer count toward the limit
quiz.why: Prompt and generated tokens share the same window: n_prompt + n_generated <= L.

quiz.q: What context window length did GPT-3 have?
quiz.answer: 2,048 tokens

quiz.q: Why is detokenization not simply joining token strings with spaces?
quiz.answer: Token boundaries do not match word boundaries; spaces are part of the tokens
distractors: Detokenization uses a different tokenizer than encoding
quiz.why: Tokens may be word pieces with leading spaces; decoding follows the tokenizer's byte rules.

quiz.q: During training, what is the predicted distribution compared against in the cross-entropy loss?
quiz.answer: A one-hot vector for the correct next token
quiz.why: The target is the input shifted by one; the loss is minus the log probability of the correct token.

quiz.q: Why do two occurrences of 'bank' in different sentences have the same vector right after the embedding lookup?
quiz.answer: The embedding lookup depends only on the token ID, not on context
distractors: Because the tokenizer merges both sentences
Because softmax normalizes them to the same value
Because the hidden state starts at zero
quiz.why: An embedding table maps each ID to one fixed row; context only enters through later layers.

quiz.q: In an RNN, which matrix carries information from the previous time step into the new hidden state?
quiz.answer: The recurrent hidden-to-hidden matrix W_hh
quiz.why: W_hh (H x H) multiplies h_(t-1), linking each step to the past.

quiz.q: What does the seq2seq decoder receive as its very first input token?
quiz.answer: <bos>, the beginning-of-sequence token
quiz.why: Generation starts from <bos>; afterwards each predicted token is fed back in.

quiz.q: In the example 'I love machine learning' -> 'Jag älskar maskininlärning', what does the length difference show?
quiz.answer: Input and output sequences in seq2seq can have different lengths
distractors: The decoder dropped a word by mistake
The encoder only reads three tokens
quiz.why: Four source tokens map to three target tokens plus <eos>; seq2seq decouples the lengths.

quiz.q: What is the core limitation of basic RNN seq2seq that motivates attention?
quiz.answer: All source information must pass through one fixed-size context vector
distractors: The encoder has no hidden state
quiz.why: The fixed vector cannot keep every detail of long inputs, and the decoder cannot look at individual encoder states.

quiz.q: Which scoring function does Luong-style attention typically use?
quiz.answer: A dot product between decoder state and encoder state
distractors: A learned additive network with tanh
The cosine of the token IDs
quiz.why: Luong attention scores with s . h; the additive tanh network is Bahdanau's version.

quiz.q: After softmax, what is true about the attention weights for one decoding step?
quiz.answer: They are positive and sum to 1
distractors: They sum to the number of source tokens
quiz.why: Softmax produces a probability distribution; uniform 0.25 was only an illustration.

quiz.q: How is the context vector c_t computed in attention-based seq2seq?
quiz.answer: As the attention-weighted sum of all encoder hidden states
distractors: As the final encoder state only
As the average of decoder states
As the embedding of the previous output token
quiz.why: c_t = sum of alpha_t,i h_i, recomputed at every step.

quiz.q: In the translation example, which source word gets the largest weight when 'älskar' is generated?
quiz.answer: love
quiz.why: At t = 2 attention concentrates on 'love', the source word that 'älskar' translates.

quiz.q: What does a bend away from the diagonal in a translation attention map indicate?
quiz.answer: The model learned a word reordering between the languages
distractors: That the decoder ignored the source
quiz.why: Non-monotonic alignment appears when the target language orders words differently.

quiz.q: What is the key architectural change the 2017 Transformer made compared with attention-based RNN seq2seq?
quiz.answer: It removed recurrence and relies entirely on attention
distractors: It replaced embeddings with one-hot vectors
It used a single fixed context vector
quiz.why: Without a recurrent chain, all known positions can be processed in parallel.

quiz.q: In self-attention, why must queries and keys have the same dimension d_k?
quiz.answer: Because they are compared with a dot product
distractors: Because values are summed with them
Because the vocabulary size equals d_k
quiz.why: A dot product is only defined for vectors of equal length; values may use a different size d_v.

quiz.q: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k)?
quiz.answer: To keep dot products from growing with dimension and making the softmax too peaked
distractors: To make the weights sum to one
To reduce the number of parameters
To block attention to future tokens
quiz.why: Large raw scores push softmax toward one-hot distributions; scaling keeps it smooth.

quiz.q: In the original Transformer with d_model = 512 and 8 heads, what is the per-head dimension d_k?
quiz.why: d_k = d_model / h = 512 / 8 = 64, and 8 x 64 concatenates back to 512.

quiz.q: What property holds for every row of a (softmax) attention matrix?
quiz.answer: Its weights sum to 1
distractors: It contains exactly one non-zero entry
quiz.why: Each row is a probability distribution over the keys for one query.

quiz.q: Which statement about attention head roles is correct?
quiz.answer: Roles emerge during training and may overlap or be uninterpretable
distractors: Each head is assigned a fixed linguistic role by design
quiz.why: Heads have separate learned projections; any role is an observed tendency, not a specification.

quiz.q: What happens to the outputs of unmasked self-attention without positional information if you shuffle the input tokens?
quiz.answer: The outputs are shuffled in the same way and otherwise unchanged
distractors: The model refuses to process the input
The outputs stay in the original order
quiz.why: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: SelfAttn(PX) = P SelfAttn(X).

quiz.q: How are sinusoidal positional encodings combined with token embeddings in the original Transformer?
quiz.answer: They are added element-wise
distractors: They are concatenated after the last layer
They are multiplied with the attention weights
quiz.why: x_pos = e_token + PE(pos), both of size d_model.

quiz.q: Which dimensions of the sinusoidal encoding carry fine, local position information?
quiz.answer: The low dimension indices with high-frequency waves
distractors: The high dimension indices with slow waves
None - all dimensions change equally fast
quiz.why: Low indices oscillate quickly from position to position; high indices vary slowly and encode coarse position.

quiz.q: In the causal mask, what value is placed at positions j > i before softmax?
quiz.answer: Minus infinity
quiz.why: exp(minus infinity) = 0, so future tokens receive zero weight.

quiz.q: In the masked table for 'The bank raised interest rates', what is the row for 'The'?
quiz.why: The first token can only see itself, so all weight goes to position 1.

quiz.q: Why can a decoder Transformer train in parallel but must generate sequentially?
quiz.answer: In training the full sequence is known and masked; in inference future tokens do not exist yet
distractors: Training uses an RNN, inference uses attention
The mask is removed at inference
GPUs cannot run attention during inference
quiz.why: Masking simulates the prefix-only view during training; at inference each new token must be generated before the next.

quiz.q: In the original Transformer layer, what is the order of sublayers?
quiz.answer: Multi-head attention, Add & Norm, FFN, Add & Norm
quiz.why: The original design is Post-Norm: Add & Norm follows each of the two sublayers.

quiz.q: In Transformer Base (d_model = 512, d_ff = 2048), roughly how many weights does one FFN have compared with one attention block?
quiz.answer: About 2.10M vs about 1.05M, so roughly twice as many

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a residual connection y = x + Sublayer(x)?
quiz.answer: The sublayer only learns an update and gradients flow directly backwards
distractors: It blocks attention to future tokens
It removes the need for embeddings
quiz.why: The identity path preserves information and gives gradients a shortcut to early layers.

quiz.q: Which model has d_model = 12288 and 96 layers?
quiz.answer: GPT-3 with 175B parameters
quiz.why: Transformer Base is 512 wide and Big is 1024 wide, both 6+6 layers; GPT-3 is 12288 wide with 96 layers.

quiz.q: When generating the next token after 'The cat sat on', which hidden state is projected by the LM head?
quiz.answer: Only the final state, the one for 'on'
distractors: The average of all four states
All four states, then summed logits
quiz.why: With causal attention the last state already contains all available context.

quiz.q: With V = 50,000 and d = 4,096, how many parameters does weight tying save?
quiz.answer: About 204.8M (from 409.6M down to 204.8M)
quiz.why: One V x d matrix (204.8M) is shared instead of learning two.

quiz.q: Why does Pre-LN allow much deeper Transformers than Post-LN?
quiz.answer: The residual skip path stays a pure identity, so gradients flow back without being reshaped by every norm.
distractors: It removes the residual connection entirely
It normalizes the gradients instead of the activations
It halves the number of parameters per layer
quiz.why: Post-LN puts LayerNorm on the residual path; Pre-LN only normalizes the sublayer input, leaving a direct gradient highway.

quiz.q: What does RMSNorm leave out compared with LayerNorm?
quiz.answer: Subtracting the mean (centering)
quiz.why: RMSNorm only divides by the root mean square and multiplies by gamma; it never re-centers the vector.

quiz.q: With RoPE, the attention score between a query at position m and a key at position n depends on...
quiz.answer: their content and the relative offset n - m
distractors: a lookup in a learned position table
a rotation applied to the value vectors
quiz.why: The two rotations combine into one rotation by n - m; values are not rotated at all.

quiz.q: A model has 32 query heads. How many KV heads do MHA, GQA with 8 groups and MQA have?
quiz.why: MHA keeps one K/V per query head, GQA one per group, MQA one shared by all.

quiz.q: What can a SwiGLU gate do that a sigmoid GLU gate cannot?
quiz.answer: Amplify features with gate values above 1
quiz.why: SiLU is unbounded above, while the sigmoid saturates below 1 and can only attenuate.

quiz.q: Why can the KV cache avoid recomputing earlier positions at each step?
quiz.answer: Causal masking keeps earlier keys and values unchanged when a new token is appended
distractors: The model stores only the last token
Attention is recomputed but averaged with a running mean
The prompt is split into non-overlapping blocks
quiz.why: Each token only attends to earlier ones, so appending a token never changes earlier representations, keys or values.

quiz.q: Which phase processes the whole prompt in parallel and produces the first output token?
quiz.answer: Prefill
quiz.why: Prefill builds the initial KV cache for every layer and its final position's logits pick the first token; decode then adds one token at a time.

quiz.q: A long output with a short prompt is dominated by which cost?
quiz.answer: The sequential decode steps
quiz.why: Total latency is roughly first-token time plus one decode step per token, so many output tokens make decode the dominant cost.

quiz.q: In the example model (32 layers, 32 query heads, head dimension 128, FP16), which factor do GQA's 8 KV heads and MQA's 1 KV head reduce?
quiz.answer: The number of KV heads, so the cache shrinks to 1/4 or 1/32 of full MHA
quiz.why: Cache size scales linearly with the KV-head count: MHA 16 GiB, GQA 4 GiB and MQA 512 MiB at 32,768 positions.

quiz.q: Does quantizing the model weights shrink the KV cache?
quiz.answer: No, because the cache stores activations and only KV-cache quantization reduces bytes per element
distractors: Yes, it shrinks the cache proportionally to the weights
Yes, but only for the value vectors
Only if the batch size is one
quiz.why: Weight quantization touches parameters; the cache holds keys and values, so it must be quantized separately.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of a sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer?
quiz.answer: To add trainable parameters without proportionally increasing the compute per token
distractors: To reduce the number of stored parameters
To remove the feed-forward layer entirely
quiz.why: Only a few experts run per token, so capacity grows while active compute stays low.

quiz.q: With router scores 2.0, 0.2, 1.0 and -0.5 and k equal to 2, which experts run and with what weights?
quiz.answer: Experts 1 and 3, with weights about 0.73 and 0.27
distractors: Experts 1 and 2, with weights about 0.9 and 0.1
All four experts, each weighted by its score
quiz.why: Top-k keeps the two largest scores, and the softmax is taken over only those two: exp(2.0) and exp(1.0) normalise to 0.73 and 0.27.

quiz.q: With 100M parameters per expert, what are the total and active expert parameters for 8 experts with 2 selected?
quiz.answer: 800M total and 200M active
quiz.why: Total is E * P_expert = 8 * 100M; active is k * P_expert = 2 * 100M.

quiz.q: Why is an auxiliary loss used when training a router?
quiz.answer: To encourage balanced expert usage so no expert is starved of training signals
distractors: To make the top-k selection differentiable
To reduce the number of experts stored
quiz.why: Without help routers can favour a few experts; the auxiliary loss levels the load, though perfect equality is not required.

quiz.q: What does quantizing the weights do for a MoE model's memory?
quiz.answer: It does not remove experts: weight memory does not drop, because all experts must stay stored
distractors: It deletes unselected experts at runtime
It cuts weight memory in half automatically
It only affects the KV cache
quiz.why: Sparse activation reduces compute, but every expert's weights remain in memory and available to be selected.

quiz.q: For one token, which experts receive a gradient during training?
quiz.answer: Only the selected experts, through their output vectors
distractors: Every expert, scaled by its router score
Only the router, not the experts
The unselected experts, through the top-k mask
quiz.why: Gradients reach selected experts via their outputs and the router via the softmax weights; unselected experts get none from that token.

quiz.q: In a state space model, what does the state vector represent?
quiz.answer: A fixed-size summary of everything seen so far, updated with each new token
distractors: A growing cache of every previous key and value
A copy of the current token only
The vocabulary logits of the last token
quiz.why: The SSM keeps one compact state whose size never depends on sequence length, unlike a KV cache.

quiz.q: What does Mamba add to a basic SSM?
quiz.answer: Input-dependent parameters, so the model can decide per token what to retain and write
distractors: A growing KV cache for exact lookups
quiz.why: Selectivity makes the update content-dependent, letting important tokens be remembered and filler fade.

quiz.q: In an LSTM, which gate decides how much previous cell memory to keep?
quiz.answer: The forget gate
quiz.why: The forget gate scales the old cell state, the input gate writes new content and the output gate exposes it.

quiz.q: How can Mamba and mLSTM be trained on a whole sequence in parallel despite being recurrent?
quiz.answer: Their updates depend only on the input tokens and can be combined algebraically
distractors: They discard the recurrent state during training
They replace recurrence with a KV cache
Their gates are independent of the inputs
quiz.why: Composable, input-only updates allow a parallel scan; generation is still sequential token by token.

quiz.q: What does Gated DeltaNet do that plain linear attention cannot?
quiz.answer: It forgets selectively and writes only the error (delta) between the new and predicted value
distractors: It stores every past key and value separately
It removes the feature map entirely
It grows a KV cache with context length
quiz.why: A retention gate plus an error-driven write correct stale associations instead of adding conflicting ones.

quiz.q: What is the prefill and per-token decode compute complexity of full attention in N context tokens?
quiz.answer: Quadratic prefill O(N^2) and linear decode O(N) per token
distractors: Linear prefill O(N) and constant decode O(1)
quiz.why: Full attention compares every prompt token with every other, and each decode step attends to all previous positions.

quiz.q: Which architecture class has linear prefill and constant per-token decode and state memory?
quiz.answer: Recurrent and linear-attention models such as Mamba, xLSTM and Gated DeltaNet
quiz.why: They keep a fixed-size state, so prefill is O(N) and decode and state are O(1).

quiz.q: Two models have the same Big-O. What can still make them run at different speeds?
quiz.answer: Kernel quality, memory bandwidth and GPU utilisation
distractors: Their parameter counts defined by Big-O
quiz.why: Big-O shows how cost scales, but real runtime depends on kernels, bandwidth and hardware utilisation.

quiz.q: Why is exact long-context recall harder for a fixed-state model than for full attention?
quiz.answer: It must squeeze every detail into one evolving state, so specific facts like a phone number can blur
distractors: It stores each past token in a separate cache slot
It cannot process prompts longer than one token
It uses more memory for older tokens
quiz.why: Full attention keeps token-specific keys and values for direct access, while a fixed state has limited capacity for exact detail.

quiz.q: For a service with many concurrent users and a memory limit, what does the lesson recommend?
quiz.answer: GQA or MQA, or fixed-state models, to reduce per-request memory
distractors: Full MHA with the largest context window
A looped model with many iterations
quiz.why: Fewer KV heads or a fixed state means each request needs less cache memory, which lets more users fit on one device.

quiz.q: FineWeb-Edu kept only documents with an educational score of at least 3. What happened to MMLU accuracy for a 1.71B model trained on 350B tokens?
quiz.answer: It rose from 33% to 37%
distractors: It stayed the same but training was faster
It dropped slightly because less data was used
quiz.why: Same model and token budget, better data: selecting educational text alone gave about 4 percentage points on MMLU.

quiz.q: Why is deduplication an important step in building a pretraining corpus?
quiz.answer: Repeated documents increase memorization and verbatim regurgitation and waste training compute
distractors: Deduplication is required to translate text into English
Duplicates cause the context window to overflow
quiz.why: Overrepresented copies push the model to memorize them; removing them reduces memorization and improves efficiency.

quiz.q: In a data mixture, what does upsampling a source mean?
quiz.answer: Drawing tokens from that source more often than its share of available data, possibly repeating it
distractors: Increasing the resolution of the source's text
Collecting more documents from that source with a crawler
Giving the source a larger learning rate
quiz.why: Mixture weights set token shares independent of availability; small valuable sources like code or math are sampled more often.

quiz.q: In the Phi-1 controlled experiment with a 350M model, what did adding synthetic textbook data change?
quiz.answer: The unit-test pass rate improved from 17.7% to 20.1%
distractors: The model grew from 350M to 1.3B parameters
The pass rate doubled from 20% to 40%
Training no longer needed real code at all
quiz.why: Synthetic textbooks added 2.4 percentage points without more parameters, showing data is a design lever, but not proving synthetic data always wins.

quiz.q: GPT-4 scores 85.5% on MMLU in English but 62.0% in Telugu. Which statement is most accurate?
quiz.answer: Data imbalance is a likely cause, but the evaluation alone does not prove the cause
distractors: Telugu questions were harder by design
It proves the tokenizer is the only cause
The model was never trained on any non-English text
quiz.why: Plausible causes include training-data imbalance, tokenization efficiency and translation effects; a measured disparity does not identify which one dominates.

quiz.q: Roughly how large was the August 2025 Common Crawl archive?
quiz.answer: About 2.44 billion web pages
quiz.why: The CC-MAIN-2025-33 crawl contained around 2.44 billion pages, roughly 47 TB.

quiz.q: The model assigns probability 0.10 to the correct next token. What is the cross-entropy loss at that position?
quiz.answer: About 2.30, since -ln(0.10) ≈ 2.30
distractors: Zero, because the model was confident
quiz.why: Cross-entropy is the negative log of the target probability: a low probability gives a large loss.

quiz.q: Using the ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token rule, how many FLOPs does one step of a 7B model with 2,048 tokens per step need?
quiz.answer: About 8.6e13 FLOPs
quiz.why: 6 * 7e9 * 2048 ≈ 8.6e13; a 70B model would be about ten times higher, near 8.6e14.

quiz.q: Why does LLM training begin with a linear learning-rate warm-up?
quiz.answer: Adam's moment estimates are still unreliable early, so large steps could destabilize training
distractors: To increase the effective batch size
To let the tokenizer adapt to the data
Because the FLOP count is unknown at the start
quiz.why: Warm-up ramps the rate from near zero so the optimizer can build trustworthy mean and variance estimates before taking big steps.

quiz.q: How do batch sizes affect gradient estimates in pretraining?
quiz.answer: Small batches give noisy gradients; large batches give smoother gradients and better hardware efficiency
distractors: Small batches always converge faster to lower loss
Batch size does not affect gradient noise
Large batches remove the need for an optimizer
quiz.why: A larger batch averages more examples, reducing gradient noise, though it does not automatically speed up convergence.

quiz.q: Which numbers describe the NVIDIA H100 used for LLM training?
quiz.answer: 80 GB HBM3 memory, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth, up to 700 W
quiz.why: The H100 SXM has 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth, NVLink up to 900 GB/s and up to 700 W.

quiz.q: A batch has 2,048 token sequences of length 4,096. Roughly how many tokens does one optimizer step process?
quiz.answer: About 8.4 million tokens
quiz.why: Tokens per batch = B * L = 2,048 * 4,096 ≈ 8.4 million.

quiz.q: Why is BF16 the standard format for LLM training rather than FP16?
quiz.answer: BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits, giving a wide range at 16-bit cost, while FP16's smaller range can overflow
distractors: BF16 has more fraction bits than FP32
BF16 needs loss scaling but FP16 does not
BF16 uses 24 exponent bits for extra precision
quiz.why: Exponent bits set range: BF16 matches FP32's 8 exponent bits with only 7 fraction bits, so it is stable and half the size.

quiz.q: Why can a 70B-parameter model not be trained on a single H100?
quiz.answer: Its BF16 weights alone need about 140 GB, more than the H100's 80 GB, before gradients and activations
distractors: The H100 cannot run matrix multiplications
BF16 weights need only 35 GB but the CPU cannot copy them
The model would fit, but the tokenizer is too large
quiz.why: 70B * 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB for weights alone, and gradients, optimizer states and activations add much more.

quiz.q: What does gradient accumulation do?
quiz.answer: It sums gradients over N micro-batches and applies one averaged optimizer step, simulating a large batch
distractors: It updates the weights after every micro-batch
It splits the model across several GPUs
It speeds up training by running micro-batches in parallel on one GPU
quiz.why: Micro-batches run sequentially into one averaged update, keeping peak activation memory low but not accelerating training.

quiz.q: In data parallelism, what is replicated on every GPU and what is combined?
quiz.answer: The full model is replicated; gradients are averaged across GPUs before each synchronized update
distractors: Weight matrices are split by columns; outputs are concatenated
Layers are split into stages; activations flow between them
Only optimizer states are sharded across the GPUs
quiz.why: DP gives each GPU the whole model and different data, then all-reduces gradients so all copies update identically.

quiz.q: What does ZeRO stage 3 add over stages 1 and 2?
quiz.answer: It also shards the model parameters, on top of optimizer states and gradients
distractors: It shards only the optimizer states
It shards gradients but not optimizer states
It removes the need for any GPU-to-GPU communication
quiz.why: ZeRO shards optimizer states (stage 1), then gradients (stage 2), then parameters (stage 3), cutting per-GPU memory at the cost of more communication.

quiz.q: Which description fits the Llama 3.1 8B base model?
quiz.answer: A decoder-only causal Transformer with 32 blocks, hidden size 4096, 32 heads and up to 128k context
distractors: An encoder-decoder with 8 blocks and a 512-token context
A mixture-of-experts with 4096 layers and 8 heads
A bidirectional Transformer trained with masked language modeling
quiz.why: Llama 3.1 8B base is a decoder-only causal Transformer: ~8B parameters, 32 blocks, d_model 4096, 32 heads, FFN ~14,336, 128k context.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a data mixture and a data schedule in a training recipe?
quiz.answer: The mixture sets the token proportion per domain; the schedule decides when each domain appears during training
distractors: The mixture sets the learning rate; the schedule sets the batch size
The mixture controls parallelism; the schedule controls precision
They are the same thing described in different units
quiz.why: Both matter: the same 30% code share can be uniform, early or late, and timing changes the capabilities the model ends up with.

quiz.q: How is the final OLMo 2 7B model produced?
quiz.answer: Three midtraining runs of 50B tokens from the same checkpoint, averaged element-wise
distractors: One single run of 4T tokens with no midtraining
Training three separate models and picking the best one
Concatenating three checkpoints into a larger model
quiz.why: Stage 1 is ~4T tokens; stage 2 is three 50B-token continuations on Dolmino Mix with different shuffles, averaged into one model.

quiz.q: Why does Llama 3 extend its context length in stages rather than training at 128K from the start?
quiz.answer: Attention cost grows quadratically with length, so short-context training is much cheaper
distractors: Long contexts cannot be tokenized at the start
The 128K model needs a different objective function
The optimizer cannot handle sequences longer than 8K
quiz.why: The 8K -> 128K extension took six progressive stages and about 800B extra tokens, because attention compute is quadratic in sequence length.

quiz.q: In the 7B, 1T-token experiment, what did upsampling selected domains only in the final 20% of training do?
quiz.answer: It raised math and code scores, e.g. GSM8K 14.71 -> 22.97, while language understanding dipped slightly
distractors: It had no measurable effect without more tokens
It doubled the token budget while keeping the mixture
quiz.why: MMLU 35.69 -> 42.59, GSM8K 14.71 -> 22.97 and HumanEval 17.23 -> 23.40 rose, but language understanding eased from 61.52 to 60.08: capabilities shift, not lift everywhere.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures why a training recipe matters?
quiz.answer: With the same model, data, token count and compute, different scheduling decisions yield different capabilities
distractors: Only the number of tokens affects a model's final abilities
The optimizer settings alone determine the outcome
Scheduling only changes training speed, never the result
quiz.why: Order matters because each update changes the starting point for later gradients, so how data is exposed over time shapes what the model learns.

quiz.q: In Kaplan's fit L(N) ~ (N_c / N)^0.076, what happens to held-out loss when the model size doubles?
quiz.answer: Loss is multiplied by 2^-0.076, about 0.949, roughly 5.1% lower
distractors: Loss stays the same but training is faster
quiz.why: The exponent 0.076 is tiny, so doubling N gives a constant ratio 2^-0.076 ~ 0.949, a small relative gain.

quiz.q: In the dense-Transformer formula C ~ 6 N D, where does the factor six come from?
quiz.answer: About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward plus about 4 backward
quiz.why: Each parameter is used per token: roughly 2 operations going forward and 4 in the backward pass, ignoring attention overhead.

quiz.q: Chinchilla found that for a 10x compute increase the model and the data should grow about equally. Which exponents describe this?
quiz.answer: N_opt ~ C^0.49 and D_opt ~ C^0.51, giving about 3.09x parameters and 3.24x tokens
distractors: N ~ C^0.73 and D ~ C^0.27, giving 5.37x and 1.86x
quiz.why: Chinchilla's near-equal exponents corrected Kaplan, whose implied recipe grew parameters far faster than tokens.

quiz.q: What is the Chinchilla rule of thumb for compute-optimal training?
quiz.answer: About 20 training tokens per parameter
quiz.why: Chinchilla used 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens, about 20 tokens per parameter, and beat the larger but data-starved Gopher.

quiz.q: Why do many production models use far more than 20 tokens per parameter?
quiz.answer: Inference cost dominates over many requests, so an overtrained smaller model is cheaper lifetime-wise
distractors: More tokens always improve accuracy with no cost
Inference is free once the model is trained
Larger models are always cheaper to serve
quiz.why: Deployment-optimal training trades extra one-time training cost for lower per-request cost, which pays off above the break-even request count.

quiz.q: What defines in-context learning?
quiz.answer: The model learns a task from examples in the prompt without any change to its weights
distractors: The model fine-tunes its weights during the conversation
The model stores the examples in a database for later
The model retrains on the prompt after answering
quiz.why: ICL adapts hidden states to the prompt pattern at inference time; parameters are never updated.

quiz.q: Why does a base model ramble about a Paris trip instead of answering?
quiz.answer: A base model continues text in a statistically likely way rather than following instructions
distractors: Its context window is too small
It was trained only on travel text
quiz.why: Pretraining only teaches next-token continuation, so a bare base model imitates the expected genre, here a blog-style narrative.

quiz.q: Why does ending a list like 'Milch -> milk, ..., Blume ->' make a base model answer with just 'flower'?
quiz.answer: Every example ends with a single English word, so the format constrains the continuation to one word
distractors: The model looks the word up online
The model was fine-tuned on German
The model counts the number of examples
quiz.why: The model predicts the most probable continuation; consistent one-word examples make a one-word answer most probable.

quiz.q: What are the two modes of in-context learning?
quiz.answer: Algorithmic ICL (copying, sorting, sequence patterns) and semantic ICL (inferring a task from stored knowledge)
quiz.why: Algorithmic skills come from self-attention and scale, while semantic skills use world knowledge learned during pretraining.

quiz.q: What role do induction heads play?
quiz.answer: They look back for an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed, driving algorithmic ICL
distractors: They store the model's facts permanently
quiz.why: Induction heads are attention circuits that complete patterns such as 'A B C A B ?' -> C, and they appear as models scale up.

quiz.q: Why are pretraining and post-training kept as separate stages?
quiz.answer: Pretraining is expensive and done once, while alignment is cheaper to iterate without destroying pretrained knowledge
distractors: Because post-training deletes the pretrained weights
Because the two stages use different tokenizers
quiz.why: Separating them gives clearer control over alignment while protecting the costly knowledge acquired during pretraining.

quiz.q: What data does supervised fine-tuning train on?
quiz.answer: High-quality human-written instruction-response pairs, using the same next-token loss
quiz.why: SFT reuses the pretraining loss but on curated demonstrations such as 'Summarize this text' followed by a clean summary.

quiz.q: In the InstructGPT work, roughly how much human data was used?
quiz.answer: About 13,000 examples written by about 40 trained annotators
quiz.why: A small, carefully curated set under strict guidelines proved more valuable than a much larger noisy one.

quiz.q: How is ChatGPT best described?
quiz.answer: A foundation model plus alignment (instruction tuning and RLHF) plus an interface layer
distractors: A foundation model on its own
An interface with no underlying model
quiz.why: ChatGPT is a product; the foundation model, alignment and interface together produce the assistant behaviour.

quiz.q: Which is a fundamental limitation of SFT?
quiz.answer: It only imitates correct answers, so it has no negative signal to penalize bad or unsafe responses
quiz.why: Every example counts as correct, so SFT cannot learn relative quality; this motivates preference-based methods like RLHF.

quiz.q: Why are absolute 1-7 ratings not used to align models to preferences?
quiz.answer: They are noisy and uncalibrated: annotators disagree and drift, the scale does not transfer across tasks, and models game high-score traits
distractors: They are too slow to collect
They always agree with human rankings
quiz.why: Relative comparisons are more stable because 'A beats B' does not depend on a shifting internal scale.

quiz.q: What does one entry in a human preference dataset contain?
quiz.answer: A prompt, a preferred answer and a less preferred answer, (x, y_w, y_l)
distractors: A prompt and a single numeric score
quiz.why: Each human ranking is broken into pairwise winner-loser triples used for reward-model and DPO training.

quiz.q: What is the reward model in RLHF?
quiz.answer: A model with the base architecture but a scalar output head that scores a prompt-answer pair, trained with the Bradley-Terry logistic loss
distractors: A copy of the LLM that writes better answers
A random number generator that sets the reward
quiz.why: It never generates text; it learns to give preferred answers a higher score than rejected ones on preference pairs.

quiz.q: What is the job of the KL penalty in the RLHF objective?
quiz.answer: It keeps the policy close to the SFT reference model to prevent reward hacking and preserve fluent language
distractors: It increases the reward-model score without limit
It removes the need for preference data
quiz.why: The beta-weighted KL term limits how far the model may drift from the reference policy while chasing reward.

quiz.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF?
quiz.answer: DPO skips the reward model and RL, using a closed-form loss on preference pairs derived from the RLHF objective
distractors: DPO needs an extra reward model and PPO
DPO trains only on raw web text
quiz.why: DPO's log-ratio to the reference model acts as an implicit reward, giving RLHF-quality alignment more cheaply and stably.

quiz.q: What did the InstructGPT human evaluations show about model size?
quiz.answer: A 1.3B PPO-aligned model was preferred over the 175B GPT-3
distractors: Size had no effect at all
quiz.why: Alignment through RLHF mattered more than raw parameter count in human preference for helpful, on-instruction answers.

quiz.q: Why is the maximum logit subtracted before computing the softmax?
quiz.answer: To avoid floating-point overflow while keeping the probabilities identical
distractors: To make the probabilities sum to more than one
To remove the most likely token
quiz.why: exp(z - m) stays <= 1 and the shift cancels in the ratio, so the result is unchanged but safe.

quiz.q: With greedy decoding and the candidates store 0.30, restaurant 0.20, park 0.15, ..., which token is always produced?
quiz.answer: store (0.30)
quiz.why: Greedy takes the argmax at every step, so the highest-probability token always wins.

quiz.q: What happens to the next-token distribution when the temperature T is below 1?
quiz.answer: It becomes sharper and more deterministic
distractors: It becomes flatter and more random
quiz.why: Dividing logits by T < 1 enlarges the differences between them, sharpening the distribution.

quiz.q: With top-k sampling (k = 3) and top probabilities 0.30, 0.20, 0.15, what is the renormalized probability of the top token?
quiz.answer: about 0.46

quiz.q: In the top-p example with p = 0.8, how many tokens form the nucleus and what is the largest renormalized probability?
quiz.answer: 5 tokens (mass 0.83), top probability 0.36
quiz.why: The cumulative mass first reaches 0.8 at the 5th token, and 0.30 / 0.83 = 0.36.

quiz.q: In random sampling, a draw gives r between 0.65 and 0.75. Which token is chosen?
quiz.answer: cinema
quiz.why: The cumulative range for cinema is 0.65 to 0.75, so the first boundary crossing r selects it.

quiz.q: How is perplexity related to the loss?
quiz.answer: It is the exponential of the cross-entropy loss
distractors: It is the average loss divided by the token count
It is unrelated to the loss
quiz.why: PPL = exp(cross-entropy), so it measures next-token prediction quality and lower is better.

quiz.q: What does a perplexity of 10 mean intuitively?
quiz.answer: The model is about as uncertain as a uniform choice among 10 tokens
distractors: The model needs 10 tokens of context
quiz.why: Perplexity equals the effective number of equally likely choices; PPL = k means uniform uncertainty among k tokens.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly describes BLEU and ROUGE?
quiz.answer: BLEU is precision-oriented (translation); ROUGE is recall-oriented (summarisation)
distractors: BLEU is recall-oriented; ROUGE is precision-oriented
quiz.why: BLEU counts how many of the model's n-grams are in the reference; ROUGE counts how many reference n-grams the model covered.

quiz.q: For a pass@k estimate, the model generates 10 samples and 3 are correct. What is pass@1?
quiz.why: pass@1 equals c/n = 3/10 only as a simple fraction, and the unbiased estimator confirms 0.30.

quiz.q: Using the same n = 10, c = 3, what is pass@5 approximately?
quiz.why: With five attempts the chance that at least one is correct rises to about 0.917.

quiz.q: A model has very low perplexity on held-out text. What can we conclude?
quiz.answer: It predicts the next token well, but this says nothing about reasoning, tool use or factuality
distractors: It will definitely follow instructions well
It is always safe to deploy
quiz.why: Perplexity only measures token prediction, not reasoning, instruction following, tool use, factuality or safety.

quiz.q: How many subjects does MMLU cover, and how is it scored?
quiz.answer: 57 subjects, scored as multiple-choice accuracy
quiz.why: MMLU uses four-option multiple choice over 57 subjects, so guessing yields 25%.

quiz.q: What makes BIG-Bench different from a knowledge test like MMLU?
quiz.answer: It is a suite of about 200 diverse tasks probing human-like thinking, with no single score
quiz.why: BIG-Bench mixes logic, puzzles, symbolic and off-distribution tasks with task-specific metrics.

quiz.q: In HumanEval, when is a solution counted as correct?
quiz.answer: When every hidden unit test passes
distractors: When it looks similar to the reference
When at least half the tests pass
When it runs without an error
quiz.why: Grading is objective pass/fail; any failing test makes the solution wrong, and scores are reported as pass@k.

quiz.q: Why does Tau-2 Bench include a simulated user who also acts through tools (dual-control)?
quiz.answer: To test realistic agent behaviour where both the agent and the user change the environment
distractors: To reduce the number of API calls
To measure perplexity of the user
quiz.why: Dual-control mirrors real support scenarios, as in the 'No Service' example where the agent guides the user to a working 5G connection.

quiz.q: Which statement about multi-turn instruction following is correct?
quiz.answer: It is shaped mainly by alignment training and does not correlate with perplexity or MMLU
distractors: It equals task accuracy on MMLU
It can be ignored for assistants
quiz.why: Remembering and revising constraints over turns depends on SFT, RLHF and DPO, not on classical metrics.

quiz.q: Why can a high MMLU score be misleading for choosing a deployed model?
quiz.answer: Benchmarks can be contaminated by training data and MMLU is saturated above 90%, so it poorly predicts real product performance
quiz.why: Test-set leakage and saturation inflate and flatten scores, while domain tasks, long instructions and tool calls need their own evaluation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended engineering principle for adapting an LLM?
quiz.answer: First maximize what prompting can achieve, then finetune or post-train if a gap remains
distractors: Always finetune first, then add prompts
Retrain the model from scratch for each task
Avoid prompting because it changes model weights
quiz.why: Prompting is fast, cheap and reversible and does not change weights, so it comes first on the adaptation ladder.

quiz.q: What is the priority order when system, user and assistant-history instructions conflict?
quiz.answer: System > User > Assistant history
quiz.why: Chat models are trained during post-training and alignment to follow the system prompt first, then the user, then history.

quiz.q: Which role is the best place for a rule like 'Always answer in JSON'?
quiz.answer: The system prompt
quiz.why: The system prompt defines global rules, persona and formatting constraints with the highest priority.

quiz.q: What are the assistant messages in a chat template?
quiz.answer: The model's own previous replies, forming the conversation history
quiz.why: Assistant-role content is the model's earlier output; it builds ongoing context and strongly influences later turns via recency bias.

quiz.q: Why does the system-first role hierarchy exist?
quiz.answer: It is taught during post-training and alignment for safety and consistency
distractors: It is hard-coded in the transformer block
It comes from the tokenizer vocabulary
It is set by the context window size
quiz.why: The hierarchy is not architectural; alignment training makes models follow the system prompt first, which underpins safety and tool use.

quiz.q: What defines zero-shot prompting?
quiz.answer: The model receives only an instruction, with no examples
distractors: The model receives exactly one example
The model is finetuned on zero labelled data
The model gets no instruction, only examples
quiz.why: Zero-shot relies entirely on pretrained knowledge and alignment; a single example would make it one-shot.

quiz.q: If a prompt contains exactly one worked example, what is it called?
quiz.answer: One-shot prompting
quiz.why: Few-shot uses a handful of examples; exactly one example is specifically called one-shot.

quiz.q: Why does adding a few examples raise accuracy?
quiz.answer: The model infers the input-output pattern from the demonstrations through in-context learning, with no weight updates
distractors: The examples permanently update the weights
The examples shrink the context window
quiz.why: Few-shot triggers in-context learning: the examples fix the format and pattern, improving accuracy without any training.

quiz.q: What did Wei et al. show about chain-of-thought?
quiz.answer: CoT unlocks latent reasoning mainly in large models, evidence of an emergent ability
distractors: CoT works equally well in all model sizes
CoT is a hidden multi-pass planning loop
CoT replaces the need for any examples
quiz.why: The CoT effect appears strongly only past a certain scale; small models gain little, which is read as an emergent ability.

quiz.q: How is chain-of-thought actually produced?
quiz.answer: In a single autoregressive inference run, as ordinary tokens generated one after another
distractors: By an internal planner looping over subtasks
By calling a hidden calculator tool
By several separate model passes merged at the end
quiz.why: CoT is just step tokens emitted in one pass; there is no internal loop, planner or independent subtask execution.

quiz.q: Where should a key document be placed to be most reliably used?
quiz.answer: At the very start or the very end of the context, not in the middle
distractors: In the exact middle, where it is easiest to find
quiz.why: Accuracy follows a U-shape: primacy and recency peaks at the start and end, with a weak 'dead zone' in the middle.

quiz.q: Where should output-format requirements go?
quiz.answer: At the end, near the query, because later instructions override earlier ones
distractors: Buried in the middle of the history
quiz.why: Recency bias means the end of the context strongly shapes the next token, so repeating format rules there keeps them obeyed.

quiz.q: What is the key rule when chunking a document?
quiz.answer: Split at natural boundaries without cutting mid-sentence or mid-concept, and label each chunk
distractors: Split into fixed character counts ignoring content
Keep the whole document as one chunk
Delete all headings from the chunks
quiz.why: Coherent, labelled chunks keep meaning intact and let you feed only the relevant pieces to the model.

quiz.q: What does instruction reiteration do?
quiz.answer: Repeats critical rules, especially formats, at the end of the context to counter recency bias and forgetting
distractors: Moves all rules into the weights
quiz.why: Restating key rules last keeps them reliably obeyed in long sessions, since the context end has the strongest influence.

quiz.q: Which describes the recommended prompt order?
quiz.answer: Global rules, task instructions, examples/schemas, supporting context, then the user's task last
distractors: User task first, then examples, then system rules
Examples first, then rules, then the task
Random order, since position does not matter
quiz.why: Because both ends are weighted heavily, key rules go first, format and examples go last, and the user's immediate task closes the prompt.

quiz.q: What does the persona pattern do?
quiz.answer: Assigns the model a role that shifts its tone, assumed expertise and style
distractors: Forces the output to be valid JSON
quiz.why: Personas change tone and expertise, useful for domain framing, formality and teaching.

quiz.q: Which pattern is especially helpful for extraction tasks?
quiz.answer: The example (few-shot) pattern, showing input-output demonstrations
quiz.why: Demonstrations fix the input-output mapping and structure, which improves extraction accuracy.

quiz.q: What is the critique-and-refine pattern?
quiz.answer: The model evaluates its own draft for weaknesses and then produces an improved version
distractors: The model randomises its output until it is correct
The model calls an external reviewer API
The model asks the user to rewrite the prompt
quiz.why: It is a self-improvement loop used for writing, code review and refactoring, followed by a refined output.

quiz.q: What does role decomposition do?
quiz.answer: Analyses a problem from several expert viewpoints and merges the results
distractors: Splits the model into separate weight sets
Rewrites the task in simpler words
Restricts the output to a fixed JSON schema
quiz.why: Role decomposition views a problem as multiple experts, which suits multi-domain reasoning before combining insights.

quiz.q: How does tree-of-thought differ from a single chain of reasoning?
quiz.answer: It branches into several candidate strategies, evaluates them and keeps the best
distractors: It runs the model on multiple GPUs in parallel
It repeats the same step until it converges
quiz.why: ToT explores and scores multiple paths, which helps with planning, optimisation and creative tasks.

quiz.q: What is the difference between hard constraints and soft steering?
quiz.answer: Hard constraints are explicit must-follow rules; soft steering gently nudges behaviour and allows variation
distractors: Both are strict, fixed ranges of output length
Hard constraints only affect tone; soft steering only affects facts
Soft steering always forbids certain outputs, hard constraints never do
quiz.why: Hard constraints such as valid JSON are strictly followed, while soft steering like 'be concise' guides without enforcing.

quiz.q: Why is structured output important for applications?
quiz.answer: It produces predictable, machine-readable output that downstream code can parse and validate reliably
distractors: It makes the model run faster
It removes the need for a tokenizer
It lowers the model's perplexity on training data
quiz.why: A fixed schema turns the LLM into a deterministic component, eliminating invented formats and enabling automation.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of function calling?
quiz.answer: The model offloads maths, search and retrieval to real external tools instead of inventing answers
distractors: It fine-tunes the model on the user's data
quiz.why: Function calling enforces strict arguments and delegates real work to APIs and databases, making the LLM production-ready.

quiz.q: How do open-weights models typically receive tool schemas?
quiz.answer: As text inside the system prompt (prompt-based tools)
distractors: Via a separate trained metadata channel
They cannot use tools at all
quiz.why: Open-weights models usually get schemas as prompt text, while modern closed APIs pass them through a structured side channel.

quiz.q: In the get_weather example, what is the required parameter?
quiz.answer: city, a string
quiz.why: The schema declares a single required string parameter, city, and the model fills it with 'Berlin'.

quiz.q: Instead of prose, what does the model emit when it wants to use a tool?
quiz.answer: A special tool-call token followed by JSON-like arguments
quiz.why: The model chooses between normal text and a tool-call token; the app executes the tool and returns the result for the final answer.

quiz.q: What is the first step of systematic prompt debugging?
quiz.answer: Naming the failure mode, such as hallucination, ignored constraints or style drift
quiz.why: You must classify the failure before fixing it; the second step then checks context quality for the root cause.

quiz.q: Why check the context when a prompt fails?
quiz.answer: Many failures come from poor context management, like buried instructions or irrelevant history
distractors: The context window is always the model's limit
quiz.why: Garbage context gives garbage output: irrelevant history, scrolled-out info or an overridden system prompt are common root causes.

quiz.q: Why does adding structure such as JSON schemas help?
quiz.answer: Structure reduces randomness and makes the model's behaviour more deterministic
distractors: It makes the model run faster
It removes the need to test
quiz.why: Structured instructions plus explicit rules and examples constrain the output, so behaviour becomes more reliable.

quiz.q: What are the two generators of new prompts in the APO loop?
quiz.answer: Mutation (rewriting, adding or removing constraints) and crossover (combining strong parts of two good prompts)
distractors: Hand-editing and A/B testing by people
quiz.why: The optimiser uses mutation and optional crossover to create candidates, which are then scored and selected.

quiz.q: How are candidate prompts scored in automated prompt optimization?
quiz.answer: With automatic, task-appropriate metrics such as accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE, Pass@k or schema validation on a test set
distractors: By asking a single human to rank them
By the model's perplexity on pretraining data
quiz.why: Each candidate is evaluated on a test set with the right metric, then the best prompt is kept and the loop repeats until convergence.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of parametric knowledge in an LLM?
quiz.answer: It is static after pretraining, opaque, incomplete or outdated, and hallucination-prone
distractors: It is stored in a separate database
It updates instantly when facts change
It can be inspected directly by the user
quiz.why: Knowledge baked into the weights cannot be edited and may be stale or wrong, which is exactly the gap RAG fills at inference time.

quiz.q: In RAG, how is the model conditioned on retrieved evidence?
quiz.answer: The retrieved documents are placed in the prompt, so the model computes p(y | x, RAG(x))
distractors: The model weights are updated for each query
The documents are used to retrain the tokenizer
quiz.why: RAG leaves architecture, training and decoding unchanged; it only changes what the model is allowed to condition on.

quiz.q: Which phase of the RAG pipeline is done offline, before any query arrives?
quiz.answer: Ingesting documents, chunking them, embedding them and storing them in a vector database
quiz.why: Documents are processed ahead of time so that at query time only the query must be embedded and searched against the stored vectors.

quiz.q: Why can alignment methods such as SFT, RLHF and DPO not replace RAG?
quiz.answer: They change how the model responds but cannot add new facts or guarantee correctness
quiz.why: Alignment shapes tone, safety and honesty; RAG supplies the evidence the answer is grounded in.

quiz.q: What kind of failure does RAG mostly shift the system toward?
quiz.answer: Retrieval quality: missed, stale or ignored documents rather than pure fabrication
quiz.why: RAG removes many hallucinations but only works if the right chunks are retrieved, so the bottleneck moves to retrieval.

quiz.q: What does an embedding model do in a RAG system?
quiz.answer: It maps text to a fixed-dimension vector so that similar meanings lie close together, enabling retrieval by geometry
distractors: It compresses documents into a single word
It translates text between languages only
It replaces the LLM during generation
quiz.why: Both queries and chunks are embedded by the same model, so retrieval becomes a nearest-neighbor search in vector space.

quiz.q: Which pooling method averages all token vectors and is the stable default for Sentence-BERT?
quiz.answer: Mean pooling
quiz.why: Mean pooling averages the token vectors dimension by dimension, giving a stable sentence vector, while max and [CLS] pooling serve other purposes.

quiz.q: Why is Sentence-BERT described as a siamese bi-encoder?
quiz.answer: Both sentences pass through the same encoder with shared weights and are compared with cosine similarity
distractors: It uses two different models trained separately
It only encodes one sentence at a time
It uses a single decoder to generate sentences
quiz.why: Shared weights and independent encoding let document embeddings be precomputed, which is what makes fast retrieval possible.

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off of a domain-adapted embedding model?
quiz.answer: Higher in-domain recall but poorer generalization outside the domain and a need for curated data
distractors: It always outperforms general-purpose models everywhere
It removes the need for chunking
quiz.why: Fine-tuning on legal, medical or code text sharpens that domain while narrowing the model's broader usefulness.

quiz.q: What does a cross-lingual embedding model enable?
quiz.answer: A query in one language can retrieve documents written in another, because all languages share one embedding space
distractors: It only works for English documents
It translates the LLM's answer instead of retrieving
It removes the need for a vector store
quiz.why: Training on parallel, translation and cross-lingual NLI data aligns many languages, with slightly weaker monolingual performance as the price.

quiz.q: What is trade-off between small and large chunks?
quiz.answer: Small chunks match precisely and raise recall but lose context; large chunks keep coherence but lower recall and add noise
distractors: Large chunks are always more precise
Chunk size has no effect on retrieval
quiz.why: Chunk size governs how precisely a query matches the stored knowledge and how much surrounding context travels with it.

quiz.q: Why are chunks often given overlap in RAG?
quiz.answer: So information that sits on a boundary is not cut apart and lost
distractors: To remove the need for embeddings
quiz.why: With chunk size L = 400 and overlap O = 100, neighbouring chunks share 100 tokens, protecting boundary sentences at the cost of storage.

quiz.q: What does contextual retrieval add to a chunk before embedding it?
quiz.answer: A short LLM-written context description, prepended so the chunk is self-contained
quiz.why: Giving an LLM the full document lets it write context such as the company and period, so an ambiguous chunk embeds with document-level meaning.

quiz.q: Why can a reranker not fix missing recall?
quiz.answer: It can only reorder chunks that were already retrieved; if the relevant chunk was never in the candidate list it cannot recover it
distractors: Rerankers are slower than the LLM
quiz.why: If the geometry never places the relevant chunk close to the query, it never enters the top-k, so no downstream stage can bring it back.

quiz.q: What sets the upper bound on achievable recall in a RAG system?
quiz.answer: The quality of the embedding model (plus chunking and query formulation)
distractors: The size of the vector store
quiz.why: Embedding quality, domain alignment, chunking and query phrasing decide whether relevant chunks are close enough to be found at all.

quiz.q: Why is naive similarity search impractical at scale?
quiz.answer: It compares the query with every stored vector, costing O(N) per query at millions or billions of chunks
quiz.why: With hundreds of dimensions and millisecond latency goals, scanning all vectors per query is far too slow.

quiz.q: Why is approximate nearest neighbor search acceptable in RAG?
quiz.answer: Several relevant chunks usually exist and small similarity differences rarely change answer quality, so recall matters more than exact ordering
distractors: Approximation always finds the exact best match
RAG never needs more than one chunk
ANN removes the need for embeddings
quiz.why: Coverage of relevant chunks is what counts; the index's effort parameter trades latency for higher recall.

quiz.q: How does an IVF index speed up search?
quiz.answer: It learns k centroids with k-means, assigns vectors to clusters, and at query time searches only the nearest clusters
distractors: It stores fewer bits per dimension
It removes all but the first chunk
quiz.why: Searching a few clusters is much faster than a flat scan, but a true neighbor in an unprobed cluster is missed, so recall depends on how many clusters are probed.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit and cost of quantization?
quiz.answer: Much lower memory and faster access at very large scale, at the cost of lower precision and slight recall loss
distractors: Higher precision with the same memory
No effect on memory but slower search
Removal of the need for an index
quiz.why: Product and scalar quantization compress vectors via codebooks and compute distances approximately on the codes.

quiz.q: According to the index comparison, which index has high memory, high recall and high speed?
quiz.answer: HNSW
quiz.why: Flat is slow, IVF is medium on all three, and quantized indexes trade recall for very high speed and low memory.

quiz.q: What is FAISS?
quiz.answer: Meta's open-source library for fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with CPU and GPU support
distractors: A database that only stores exact keys
A tool that only builds skip lists
quiz.why: FAISS focuses on algorithms and performance and implements Flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ and IVF-PQ index types.

quiz.q: What are the three constraints for choosing edges when building an NSW graph?
quiz.answer: At most M neighbors, prefer closer nodes, and reject a candidate very close to an already chosen neighbor for diversity
distractors: Use all neighbors, ignore distance, duplicate edges
Connect only the two oldest nodes
quiz.why: The maximum degree M bounds the cost, closer nodes are better neighbors, and the diversity rule avoids redundant links.

quiz.q: In the NSW insertion example, why was candidate e5 (cos_sim 0.4) rejected for the new node e6?
quiz.answer: It is very close to the already chosen neighbor e4 (cos_sim 0.8), so it would not add diversity
distractors: It was too far from e6
quiz.why: The diversity heuristic keeps links spread out, so e6 connected to e3 (0.2) instead, yielding edges e6-e4 and e6-e3.

quiz.q: When does an NSW search stop?
quiz.answer: When it reaches a node whose neighbors are all less similar (a local best)
distractors: When the graph runs out of nodes
quiz.why: Only the path of visited nodes is evaluated, so search is cheap but can stop at a local optimum rather than the global best.

quiz.q: How does a skip list speed up search?
quiz.answer: It stacks linked lists with sparser higher levels so a search jumps over many items, finding the local best per level then dropping down
distractors: It stores vectors in a database
quiz.why: The layered structure is the inspiration for HNSW's multiple graph layers.

quiz.q: Why is HNSW the typical default for RAG?
quiz.answer: It combines NSW graphs with skip-list layering for an excellent speed-recall trade-off: high recall at low latency
distractors: It stores the fewest bits per dimension
It guarantees the exact nearest neighbor
quiz.why: Search starts on a sparse top layer and descends through denser layers to refine, which is fast to build on and widely used in production.

quiz.q: What is dense retrieval good at and what does it struggle with?
quiz.answer: Good at paraphrases, synonyms and concepts; weak on rare IDs, exact strings, numeric constraints and rare proper names
distractors: Good at exact keywords; weak at meaning
quiz.why: Dense retrieval matches meaning in vector space, which covers paraphrases but not exact tokens such as serial numbers.

quiz.q: Which three mechanisms shape the BM25 score?
quiz.answer: IDF (rare terms weigh more), term-frequency saturation, and length normalization
distractors: Learning rate, batch size and warm-up
quiz.why: BM25 is a rule-based function that rewards rare query terms, saturates repeated occurrences and fairly treats short and long documents.

quiz.q: Why is hybrid retrieval more robust than dense or sparse alone?
quiz.answer: It combines semantic matching with exact keyword matching, increasing recall and robustness
distractors: It uses only the dense list
quiz.why: Dense and sparse fail in complementary ways, so running both and fusing the rankings covers more relevant chunks.

quiz.q: How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion score a document?
quiz.answer: It sums 1/(k + rank) over every retrieval list that returned the document, using k of about 60
distractors: It multiplies the raw retrieval scores
It counts only the number of appearances
quiz.why: RRF is scale-invariant and rewards documents that rank well in several lists, not just one.

quiz.q: In the RRF example, why did chunk1 beat chunk2?
quiz.answer: Chunk1 was 2nd in dense and 1st in BM25 (RRF 0.03252), while chunk2 was 1st in dense but only 3rd in BM25 (RRF 0.03227)
distractors: Chunk1 was first in both lists
Chunk2 was missing from both lists
Both had identical scores and tied
quiz.why: Consistency across both lists gave chunk1 a slightly higher fused score than chunk2's single top rank.

quiz.q: What does the term 'saturation' mean in BM25?
quiz.answer: Repeated occurrences of a term add less and less, so the first occurrences matter most
distractors: Long documents are always ranked higher
quiz.why: Diminishing returns on term frequency stop a document from ranking high just by repeating a word.
